\chapter*{Preface}\label{preface}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Preface}

\markboth{Preface}{Preface}

Welcome to \textbf{STAT 303-1 (Data Science with Python I), Section 20}
at Northwestern University.

This book is designed to support your journey into data science,
blending foundational concepts with hands-on practice. It builds on the
original work of \textbf{Professor Arvind Krishna}, whose materials
inspired the structure and spirit of this resource. The content has been
thoughtfully updated to meet the evolving needs of students and the
goals of the course.

In this first course, you will:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Learn to use essential Python libraries for data science, including
  but not limited to \textbf{NumPy}, \textbf{Pandas}, and
  \textbf{Matplotlib}. These three are the main focus, but you will also
  be introduced to other useful libraries and tools as needed for
  real-world data analysis.
\item
  Develop skills in \textbf{Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)},
  transforming messy, real-world datasets into meaningful insights
  through visualization, summarization, and pattern discovery
\end{itemize}

The book is organized to guide you step-by-step:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapters 1--3}: Set up your coding environment in VS Code,
  understand Python environments, and enhance your workflow
\item
  \textbf{Chapters 4--5}: Review key concepts from STAT 201. If you need
  a refresher, visit the
  \href{https://lizhen0909.github.io/Intro_to_programming_for_data_sci/}{STAT
  201 ebook}.
\item
  New material begins in \textbf{Chapter 6 -- \emph{Reading Data}}
\end{itemize}

Throughout the quarter, this resource will be updated and refined to
improve clarity, depth, and alignment with our teaching objectives.

As a \textbf{living document}, your feedback and suggestions are always
welcome. Contributions from students, instructors, and the broader
academic community help make this book stronger and more effective.

If you have ideas for improving the textbook, please share your feedback
or suggestions using our dedicated
\href{https://edstem.org/us/courses/86347/discussion}{Textbook
Improvement Form}. Your input is invaluable in making this resource
better for everyone.

Thank you for joining us on this learning adventure. We hope this book
becomes a valuable companion as you build your skills and confidence in
data science with Python.

\part{Getting started}

\chapter{Setting up your environment with VS
Code}\label{setting-up-your-environment-with-vs-code}

\begin{verbatim}
<IPython.core.display.Image object>
\end{verbatim}

\section{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives}

Setting up your Python data science environment is the foundation for
all your work in this course. A well-configured setup will save you
time, prevent errors, and make your workflow smoother. Whether you're
new to VS Code or Python, these steps will help you build a reliable
environment for coding, analysis, and reproducibility.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Install and configure \textbf{Visual Studio Code (VS Code)} for Python
  and Jupyter Notebooks.\\
\item
  Create and manage a \textbf{virtual environment} for this course.\\
\item
  Install essential \textbf{Python libraries} for data science.\\
\item
  Verify that your environment is working properly.
\end{itemize}

\section{Why Choose Visual Studio Code (VS
Code)?}\label{why-choose-visual-studio-code-vs-code}

Choosing the right editor can make a big difference in your productivity
and learning experience. VS Code is a top choice for data science and
Python development because it combines power, flexibility, and ease of
use.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Free and Lightweight}\\
  VS Code is free, open-source, and runs efficiently on most systems
  without being resource-heavy.
\item
  \textbf{Cross-Platform}\\
  Works consistently on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
\item
  \textbf{Rich Python Support}\\
  With the official Python extension, you get:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Syntax highlighting and IntelliSense (auto-completion, code
    hints).\\
  \item
    Built-in debugging tools.\\
  \item
    Easy integration with virtual environments and Jupyter Notebooks.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Integrated Jupyter Notebook Support}\\
  You can open and run \texttt{.ipynb} notebooks directly in VS Code.
\item
  \textbf{Customizable and Extensible}\\
  Large marketplace of extensions (e.g., formatting, linting, Git,
  Docker, AI tools).
\item
  \textbf{Version Control Integration}\\
  Built-in Git and GitHub support for managing and sharing code.
\item
  \textbf{Unified Workflow}\\
  One place for editing, running, debugging, documenting, and
  version-controlling Python code.
\end{itemize}

Whether you're just starting out or working on advanced projects, VS
Code provides a modern, unified environment for all your coding needs.

\section{Quick Start: Setting Up Python \& VS
Code}\label{quick-start-setting-up-python-vs-code}

VS Code is a versatile editor. To use it for data science, you'll
complete a few extra setup steps (e.g., Python \& Jupyter extensions).
Follow this step-by-step setup guide to get started quickly and avoid
common pitfalls.

\textbf{Step 1: Install Python}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Download and install the latest version from
  \href{https://www.python.org}{python.org}.
\item
  On Windows, check the box \textbf{``Add Python to PATH.''} This makes
  Python available in your terminal.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 2: Install VS Code \& Extensions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Download VS Code from
  \href{https://code.visualstudio.com}{code.visualstudio.com}.
\item
  Open VS Code, go to the Extensions panel (\texttt{Ctrl+Shift+X}), and
  install:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Python (Microsoft)}
  \item
    \textbf{Jupyter (Microsoft)}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 3: Create a Course Folder}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Make a folder for your notebooks (e.g., \texttt{datasci} on Desktop or
  Documents).
\item
  Open this folder in VS Code.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 4: Create Your First Notebook}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In VS Code, go to \textbf{File → New File → Save as →
  \texttt{test.ipynb}}.
\item
  Add a code cell:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"hello world"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Run the cell. VS Code may prompt you to select or create a Python
  environment.
  \pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{images/env_create_option.png}}:
\item
  If prompted, create a new environment using the GUI (recommended for
  beginners).
\item
  Make sure the kernel (top right) shows \textbf{.venv (Python 3.xx.x)}.
\item
  ✅ If you see \texttt{hello\ world} printed, your setup is working!
\end{itemize}

\textbf{If everything works, you can skip the Full Setup below.}

❌ If you run into issues, continue with the detailed setup and
troubleshooting steps in the next section.

This quick start helps you get coding fast, but the full setup ensures
your environment is robust and reproducible for all course projects.

\section{Full Setup: Reliable Python Environment in VS
Code}\label{full-setup-reliable-python-environment-in-vs-code}

If the quick start didn't work, or you want a more robust setup, follow
these step-by-step instructions to ensure your Python environment is
reproducible and ready for data science.

\textbf{Step 1: Install Python}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Go to the \href{https://www.python.org/downloads/}{official Python
  website} and download the latest version for your operating system.
\item
  \textbf{Important:} During installation, check the box \textbf{``Add
  Python to PATH''} so Python is available in your terminal.
\item
  After installation, restart your terminal in VS Code.
\item
  Verify installation by running:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{python }\OperatorTok{{-}{-}}\NormalTok{version}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  You should see the installed Python version.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 2: Install VS Code Extensions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Open VS Code.
\item
  Go to Extensions (\texttt{Ctrl+Shift+X}).
\item
  Install:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Python} (by Microsoft)
  \item
    \textbf{Jupyter} (by Microsoft)
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 3: Set Up Your Workspace}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Create a new folder for your course work (e.g., \texttt{STAT303-1} on
  Desktop or Documents).
\item
  Open the folder in VS Code
  (\texttt{File\ \textgreater{}\ Open\ Folder}).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 4: Create a Notebook for Your Work}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In VS Code, go to \texttt{File\ \textgreater{}\ New\ File} and select
  \texttt{Jupyter\ Notebook}.
\item
  Save the file as \texttt{your\_notebook.ipynb}.
\item
  Add a code cell:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"hello world"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Make sure to select the \texttt{.venv} kernel for your notebook (see
  next step).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 5A: Create a Virtual Environment (GUI Method)}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Run the cell. If prompted, create a Python environment using
  \texttt{venv} in the current workspace.
\item
  Wait for Jupyter to start and install necessary components (e.g.,
  ipykernel).
\item
  After installation, ensure the selected kernel in the top right of the
  notebook says \textbf{.venv (Python 3.xx.x)}.
\item
  If not, select the \texttt{.venv} kernel manually.
\end{itemize}

\emph{If you successfully created the environment using the GUI, skip
Step 5B.}

\textbf{Step 5B: Create a Virtual Environment (Command Line Method)}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If not prompted to create your environment, use the terminal:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Open the terminal in VS Code.
  \item
    Run:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{python }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{m venv }\OperatorTok{.}\FunctionTok{venv}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
  \item
    Activate the environment:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item
      On Windows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{.}\NormalTok{\textbackslash{}}\OperatorTok{.}\FunctionTok{venv}\NormalTok{\textbackslash{}Scripts\textbackslash{}activate}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
    \item
      On macOS/Linux:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{source}\NormalTok{ .venv/bin/activate}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    You should see \texttt{(.venv)} at the start of your terminal
    prompt.
  \item
    Install essential packages:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pip install numpy pandas matplotlib}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 6: Verify Your Setup}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Run the code cell again. You should see \texttt{hello\ world} printed
  out.
\item
  In the terminal, check your Python version and installed packages:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{python }\OperatorTok{{-}{-}}\NormalTok{version}
\NormalTok{pip list}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Troubleshooting Tips}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If the kernel does not show \texttt{.venv}, restart VS Code and ensure
  the environment is activated.
\item
  Make sure the Python and Jupyter extensions are installed and enabled.
\item
  If you see errors, check that your notebook is saved with the
  \texttt{.ipynb} extension and the correct kernel is selected.
\end{itemize}

A reliable environment is essential for reproducible data science. These
steps will help you avoid common issues and set yourself up for success
throughout the course.

\section{Jupyter Notebooks in VS
Code}\label{jupyter-notebooks-in-vs-code}

After setting up your environment, you can take full advantage of
Jupyter Notebooks directly in VS Code. This integration lets you:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Create, edit, and run \texttt{.ipynb} notebooks without leaving VS
  Code
\item
  Use interactive code cells for data analysis, visualization, and
  documentation
\item
  Access rich outputs (plots, tables, markdown) inline with your code
\item
  Switch kernels to use different Python environments for each notebook
\item
  Debug, refactor, and version-control your notebooks with built-in
  tools
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Getting Started:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Open or create a notebook file (\texttt{.ipynb}) in VS Code
\item
  Make sure the correct Python kernel/environment is selected (top right
  corner)
\item
  Add code and markdown cells as needed
\item
  Run cells individually or all at once
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Learn More:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Explore the official guide:
  \href{https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/datascience/jupyter-notebooks}{Jupyter
  Notebooks in VS Code}
\end{itemize}

Jupyter Notebooks in VS Code provide a powerful, flexible workflow for
data science and Python development.

\section{Rendering notebook as HTML using
Quarto}\label{rendering-notebook-as-html-using-quarto}

Quarto is designed for high-quality, customizable, and publishable
outputs, making it suitable for reports, blogs, or presentations. We'll
use Quarto to print the **.ipynb* file as HTML for your assignment
submission.

\subsection{Installing and Verifying
Quarto}\label{installing-and-verifying-quarto}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Download and install Quarto from the
  \href{https://quarto.org/}{official website}.
\item
  Follow the installation instructions for your operating system.
\item
  Open your terminal within VS Code:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Go to \texttt{Terminal} -\textgreater{} \texttt{New\ Terminal}.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Run the following command to verify that Quarto and its dependencies
  are correctly installed: \texttt{quarto\ -\/-version}
\item
  You should see the installed quarto version. If the command line
  doesn't work, you might see an error message like:

\begin{verbatim}
- `quarto is not recognized`
- `quarto command is not found` 
\end{verbatim}

  This issue is often caused by Quarto not being added to the PATH
  environment variable. Similar to how you added the Python path to the
  environment variable above, you need to add the Quarto path to the
  system environment variable so that the command can be recognized by
  your operating system's shell.

  On Windows, if you used the default installation path (without
  changing it), Quarto is installed in:
  \texttt{C:\textbackslash{}Users\textbackslash{}\textless{}USER\textgreater{}\textbackslash{}AppData\textbackslash{}Local\textbackslash{}Programs\textbackslash{}Quarto\textbackslash{}bin}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Note:}\\
Before moving forward, ensure that the command
\texttt{quarto\ -\/-version} successfully prints the version of your
installed quarto. If it does not, you may need to troubleshoot your
quarto installation or add it to the PATH environment variable.

\subsection{Converting the Notebook to
HTML}\label{converting-the-notebook-to-html}

Check the procedure for rendering a notebook as HTML
\href{https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html}{here}.
You have several options to format the file. Here are some points to
remember when using Quarto to render your notebook as HTML:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The
  \href{https://nbsphinx.readthedocs.io/en/0.9.3/raw-cells.html}{\texttt{Raw\ NBConvert}}
  cell type is used to render different code formats into HTML or LaTeX.
  This information is stored in the notebook metadata and converted
  appropriately. \textbf{Use this cell type to put the desired
  formatting settings for the HTML file.}
\item
  In the formatting settings, remember to use the setting
  \textbf{\href{https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html\#self-contained}{\texttt{embed-resources:\ true}}}.
  This will ensure that the rendered HTML file is self-contained, and is
  not dependent on other files. This is especially important when you
  are sending the HTML file to someone, or uploading it somewhere. If
  the file is self-contained, then you can send the file by itself
  without having to attach the dependent files with it.
\end{enumerate}

Once you have entered the desired formatting setting in the
\texttt{Raw\ NBConver} cell, you are ready to render the notebook to
HTML. Open the terminal, navigate to the directory containing the
notebook \emph{(.ipynb file)}, and use the command:
\texttt{quarto\ render\ filename.ipynb\ -\/-to\ html}.

\section{Independent Study}\label{independent-study}

\textbf{Goal:} Get hands-on experience creating a reproducible Python
environment using \texttt{pip} and \texttt{.venv} in VS Code.

\subsection{Step-by-Step Instructions}\label{step-by-step-instructions}

\textbf{Step 1: Create Your Workspace}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Make a folder named \texttt{STAT303\_1} for your course work.
\item
  Open this folder in VS Code.
\item
  Create a new notebook: \texttt{setup\_test.ipynb}.
\item
  Add a code cell:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Hello, VS Code \& .venv!"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Run the cell. If prompted, create/select a Python environment (choose
  \texttt{.venv}).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 2: Create the \texttt{.venv} Environment}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  If VS Code does not prompt you, open the terminal in VS Code.
\item
  Run:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{python }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{m venv }\OperatorTok{.}\FunctionTok{venv}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Activate the environment:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{.}\NormalTok{\textbackslash{}}\OperatorTok{.}\FunctionTok{venv}\NormalTok{\textbackslash{}Scripts\textbackslash{}activate}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Install essential packages:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pip install numpy pandas matplotlib}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 3: Verify Environment Consistency}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In the terminal, check your Python version:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{python }\OperatorTok{{-}{-}}\NormalTok{version}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  In the notebook, run:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ sys}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(sys.executable)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Make sure the Python path in the notebook matches the one in your
  terminal. This confirms you are using the same environment.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 4: Generate html from the notebook using Quarto}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  In the terminal, make sure you are in the directory that contains your
  notebook

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{quarto render setup\_test}\OperatorTok{.}\FunctionTok{ipynb}  \OperatorTok{{-}{-}}\NormalTok{to html}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Make sure the html file was generated in the same directory
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Troubleshooting Tips}

If you run into issues (e.g., kernel not showing \texttt{.venv}, code
cell errors):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Restart VS Code.
\item
  Deactivate/reactivate \texttt{.venv}.
\item
  Make sure \textbf{Python} \& \textbf{Jupyter} extensions are
  installed.
\item
  Save your notebook with the \texttt{.ipynb} extension.
\item
  If the kernel is missing, use the kernel picker (top right) to select
  \texttt{.venv}.
\item
  If you see an error like \emph{``No such file or directory''} or
  \emph{``No valid input files passed to render''}:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Check your current location:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      macOS / Linux: \texttt{pwd}\\
    \item
      Windows: \texttt{cd}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    List files in the current directory:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      macOS / Linux: \texttt{ls}\\
    \item
      Windows: \texttt{dir}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    If the notebook isn't there:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      Use \texttt{cd} to move into the correct folder, or\\
    \item
      Provide the full (absolute) path to the file.
    \end{itemize}
  \end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Extra:}

\end{itemize}

\chapter{Python Environments and Package
Management}\label{python-environments-and-package-management}

\begin{verbatim}
<IPython.core.display.Image object>
\end{verbatim}

\section{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-1}

Managing Python environments and packages is essential for reproducible,
error-free data science. Understanding these concepts will help you
avoid common pitfalls and collaborate more effectively. This chapter
will guide you through the tools and best practices for setting up,
sharing, and troubleshooting Python environments.

By the end of this chapter , you will be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain why virtual environments are important.\\
\item
  Install essential data science packages in your Python environment.\\
\item
  Create a \texttt{requirements.txt} file and use it to quickly recreate
  an environment.\\
\item
  Recognize why dependency conflicts happen.\\
\item
  Describe how tools like \texttt{conda} or \texttt{poetry} can help
  resolve dependency conflicts.
\end{itemize}

\section{Data Science packages in
Python}\label{data-science-packages-in-python}

Python has a rich ecosystem of packages that make data analysis easier
and more powerful.\\
In this course, you will install and use several core packages:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{NumPy} → numerical computing and array operations\\
\item
  \textbf{pandas} → data manipulation and analysis\\
\item
  \textbf{Matplotlib} → data visualization\\
\item
  \textbf{Seaborn} → statistical data visualization (built on top of
  Matplotlib)
\end{itemize}

These packages give you the essential tools to load, clean, analyze, and
visualize data.\\
👉 Before using them, you need to install them in your Python
environment.

In your previous VS Code setup lesson, you created a Python environment
using \texttt{.venv} and selected it as the kernel to run your notebook.
This created a folder called \texttt{.venv}, which contains: - A
dedicated Python interpreter for your project - A \texttt{Lib} folder
where all packages you install are stored

Any packages you install (e.g., with \texttt{pip\ install\ ...}) will
only affect this environment, keeping your project isolated from others.

Using virtual environments is considered best practice for Python
development, especially in data science projects. This isolation helps
you: - Avoid version conflicts between packages - Keep project
dependencies separate - Make your code more reproducible and shareable

Before we dive in, let's clarify what a Python environment is and why
isolation matters.

\section{Python Virtual Environments}\label{python-virtual-environments}

A Python virtual environment is an \textbf{isolated workspace} with its
own Python interpreter and its own set of installed packages.

This isolation makes it easy to manage dependencies for different
projects and prevents package version conflicts.

\textbf{Why use virtual environments?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Keep each project's dependencies separate
\item
  Avoid breaking code by accidentally upgrading/downgrading packages
\item
  Share your code with others and ensure it works the same way on their
  machine
\end{itemize}

Virtual environments are a key tool for professional, reproducible
Python workflows.

\section{Install Data Science Packages Within Your
Environment}\label{install-data-science-packages-within-your-environment}

Python's power for data science comes from its rich ecosystem of
packages. These packages provide essential tools for scientific
computing, data analysis, visualization, and machine learning.

Packages like \texttt{numpy}, \texttt{pandas}, and \texttt{matplotlib}
are not included in the Python standard library---you need to install
them in your environment before you can use them.

\textbf{Test your setup:} Add the following code to your
\texttt{test.ipynb} notebook to check if your environment is ready:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Setup complete!"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

👉 If you see a \texttt{ModuleNotFoundError}, it means the package is
not installed in your current environment. Use \texttt{pip\ install} to
add missing packages.

\textbf{Tip:} Always install packages inside your active virtual
environment to keep your project isolated and reproducible.

\subsection{How to Install Packages}\label{how-to-install-packages}

There are two main ways to install data science packages in your
environment:

\subsubsection{Installing from the
Terminal}\label{installing-from-the-terminal}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Open a New Terminal:} Check that your terminal is using the
  same environment as your notebook kernel.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    If you see \texttt{(.venv)} at the start of the prompt, your virtual
    environment is active and matches the notebook kernel.
  \item
    If you see \texttt{(base)}, it means the base conda environment is
    active (common if you have Anaconda installed).
  \item
    To confirm which Python is being used, run:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      On macOS/Linux: \texttt{which\ python}
    \item
      On Windows: \texttt{where.exe\ python}
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Note:} If you have both Anaconda and VS Code installed,
environments can sometimes conflict. If the terminal and notebook use
different environments, packages may be installed in the wrong place,
causing import errors in your notebook.
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Install packages with pip:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{pip}\NormalTok{ install numpy pandas}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Installing from the
Notebook}\label{installing-from-the-notebook}

You can also install packages directly from a Jupyter Notebook cell
using a magic command. This is convenient for quick installs without
leaving the notebook interface.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Add a new code cell and run:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pip install numpy pandas}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Best Practice:} Always make sure you are installing packages
into the correct environment. Double-check your kernel and terminal
environment before running installation commands.

\subsection{Backing Up and Sharing Your
Environment}\label{backing-up-and-sharing-your-environment}

Reproducibility is a cornerstone of good data science. To ensure your
code works for you, your collaborators, and on other machines, you need
a way to recreate your Python environment exactly.

Backing up your environment makes it easy to share your work and avoid
``it works on my machine'' problems.

\textbf{How to back up your environment:}

Step 1: \textbf{Create a \texttt{requirements.txt} file}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  This file lists all installed packages and their versions, so anyone
  can recreate your environment.
\end{itemize}

Run the following command in your terminal to list all installed
packages and their versions:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pip freeze}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}

colorama==0.4.6
comm==0.2.2

Using the redirection operator \texttt{\textgreater{}}, you can save the
output of \texttt{pip\ freeze} to a \texttt{requirement.txt}. This file
can be used to install the same versions of packages in a different
environment.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pip freeze }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ requirement.txt}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.
\end{verbatim}

working directory

\end{Highlighting}

Step 2: \textbf{Share the file}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Send the \texttt{requirements.txt} file to your collaborator, or save
  it for future use.
\end{itemize}

Step 3: \textbf{Recreate the environment elsewhere}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  On a new machine or environment, run:

\ExtensionTok{pip}\NormalTok{ install }\AttributeTok{{-}r}\NormalTok{ requirements.txt}

\end{Shaded}

Requirement already satisfied: wcwidth==0.2.13 in c:\users\lsi8012\onedrive - northwestern university\fa24\303-1\test_env\.venv\lib\site-packages (from -r requirement.txt (line 39)) (0.2.13)
Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.

Once you run the install command, all packages listed in your
\texttt{requirements.txt} file will be installed, matching the exact
versions you used in your original environment.

This ensures your code runs the same way everywhere---whether on your
computer, a collaborator's machine, or a server.

\textbf{Why is this important?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Guarantees everyone is using the same package versions, reducing
  errors and ``works on my machine'' problems.
\item
  Makes it easy to set up your project on a new computer, server, or
  cloud environment.
\item
  Simplifies troubleshooting and collaboration---everyone starts from
  the same setup.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pro Tip:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Update your \texttt{requirements.txt} after installing or upgrading
  packages to keep it current.
\item
  Consider version-controlling your \texttt{requirements.txt} file
  (e.g., with Git) so changes are tracked and shared with collaborators.
\end{itemize}

A well-maintained environment file is essential for reproducible,
shareable, and professional data science projects.

\section{Dependency Conflicts}\label{dependency-conflicts}

A \textbf{dependency conflict} occurs when two or more packages in your
Python environment require different or incompatible versions of the
same library.\\
This can cause errors, unexpected behavior, or even break your code.

\subsection{Why do dependency conflicts
happen?}\label{why-do-dependency-conflicts-happen}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Many Python packages rely on other packages (called
  \emph{dependencies}) to work.\\
\item
  If you install packages that depend on different versions of the same
  dependency, they may not work together.\\
\item
  This is especially common in data science, where libraries evolve
  quickly and have complex interdependencies.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Example:} Suppose you install two packages:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{PackageA} requires \texttt{numpy==1.24.0}\\
\item
  \texttt{PackageB} requires \texttt{numpy==2.2.0}
\end{itemize}

If you install both with \texttt{pip}, the \textbf{last specified
version wins}. One of the packages may then fail because it cannot use
the version of \texttt{numpy} that was actually installed.

\subsection{How to avoid dependency
conflicts}\label{how-to-avoid-dependency-conflicts}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  ✅ Use \textbf{virtual environments} to isolate dependencies for each
  project.\\
\item
  ✅ Check package requirements before installing new libraries.\\
\item
  ✅ Use tools like \textbf{Poetry} or \textbf{Conda} to detect and
  resolve conflicts automatically.
\end{itemize}

\section{How to Resolve Conflicts and Manage
Environments}\label{how-to-resolve-conflicts-and-manage-environments}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Use \texttt{conda} for Robust Environment
Management}{Use conda for Robust Environment Management}}\label{use-conda-for-robust-environment-management}

\texttt{conda} is a powerful tool for managing both Python environments
and packages, especially in data science workflows. It helps you avoid
and resolve dependency conflicts by handling package versions and system
dependencies more effectively than \texttt{pip} alone.

\textbf{Why use conda?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Create fully isolated environments for different projects
\item
  Install packages and all their dependencies from the Anaconda
  repository
\item
  Easily switch between environments for different tasks
\item
  Export and share environment configurations for reproducibility
\end{itemize}

\textbf{How conda prevents dependency conflicts:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When you install a package, conda automatically checks for compatible
  versions of all dependencies and installs them together.
\item
  If a conflict is detected, conda will warn you, suggest solutions, or
  prevent incompatible installations.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Essential conda commands:}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Create a new environment:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ create }\AttributeTok{{-}{-}name}\NormalTok{ myenv numpy pandas matplotlib}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Activate an environment:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ activate myenv}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Install a package in an environment:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ install seaborn}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  List all environments:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ env list}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Export environment configuration:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ env export }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ environment.yml}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Recreate an environment from a file:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ env create }\AttributeTok{{-}f}\NormalTok{ environment.yml}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Example:} Suppose you need to work on two projects that require
different versions of \texttt{scikit-learn}. You can create two separate
environments:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ create }\AttributeTok{{-}{-}name}\NormalTok{ projectA scikit{-}learn=0.24}
\ExtensionTok{conda}\NormalTok{ create }\AttributeTok{{-}{-}name}\NormalTok{ projectB scikit{-}learn=1.2}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Each environment will have its own compatible dependencies, so you avoid
conflicts.

\textbf{Summary:} Using \texttt{conda} is highly recommended for
managing complex dependencies, system-level packages, and reproducible
environments in data science.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Use \texttt{poetry} for Modern Python
Projects}{Use poetry for Modern Python Projects}}\label{use-poetry-for-modern-python-projects}

\texttt{poetry} is a modern tool for managing Python dependencies and
packaging. It streamlines environment setup, ensures reproducibility,
and makes sharing your project easy.

\textbf{Why use poetry?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Automatically creates and manages virtual environments for each
  project
\item
  Uses a \texttt{pyproject.toml} file to specify and lock project
  requirements
\item
  Prevents dependency conflicts with a lock file (\texttt{poetry.lock})
\item
  Simplifies publishing packages to PyPI and sharing with others
\end{itemize}

\textbf{How poetry helps with dependency management:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Resolves and installs compatible versions of all dependencies
  automatically
\item
  Keeps your environment reproducible and up-to-date
\item
  Makes it easy to add, update, or remove packages
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Essential poetry commands:}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2214}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.7786}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Command / File
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Description
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\texttt{poetry\ install} & \textbf{Installs all dependencies.} If a
\texttt{poetry.lock} file exists, installs exact versions from it. If
not, resolves dependencies, creates the \texttt{poetry.lock} file, and
installs. \\
\texttt{poetry\ add\ \textless{}package\textgreater{}} & Adds a package,
resolves the new dependency tree, updates the \texttt{pyproject.toml}
and updates the \texttt{poetry.lock} file. \\
\texttt{poetry\ remove\ \textless{}package\textgreater{}} & Removes a
package, resolves the new dependency tree, updates the
\texttt{pyproject.toml} and updates the \texttt{poetry.lock} file. \\
\texttt{poetry\ show} & Lists all installed packages (and their
versions) as recorded in the \texttt{poetry.lock} file. \\
\texttt{poetry\ show\ -\/-tree} & Displays the dependency tree based on
the resolved dependencies in the \texttt{poetry.lock} file. \\
\texttt{poetry\ show\ -\/-outdated} & Compares versions in the
\texttt{poetry.lock} file against the latest available on the remote
repository. \\
\texttt{poetry\ run\ \textless{}command\textgreater{}} & Runs a command
in the virtual environment whose packages are defined by the
\texttt{poetry.lock} file. \\
\texttt{poetry.lock} (File) & \textbf{The most important file for
reproducibility.} Pins exact versions of every package and dependency.
\textbf{Always commit this to version control} to ensure all developers
and deployments use identical dependencies. \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Core Files to Know}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{pyproject.toml}}:\\
  The \emph{declarative} file where you define your project's metadata,
  dependencies, and build system.\\
  This file is meant to be edited by humans.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{poetry.lock}}:\\
  The \emph{definitive record} of the exact versions of every package
  that makes your project work.\\
  This file is generated and managed by Poetry.\\
  \textbf{You should commit this to version control} to ensure everyone
  (and your deployments) uses identical dependencies.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Summary:} \texttt{poetry} is highly recommended for modern
Python projects where you want reliable dependency management, easy
environment setup, and reproducible results.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Difference Between \texttt{conda} and
\texttt{poetry}}{Difference Between conda and poetry}}\label{difference-between-conda-and-poetry}

Both \texttt{conda} and \texttt{poetry} are tools for managing Python
environments and dependencies, but they have different strengths and use
cases.

\textbf{conda:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Manages both Python environments and packages, including non-Python
  dependencies (e.g., C libraries, compilers)
\item
  Works with multiple languages (Python, R, etc.)
\item
  Uses the Anaconda repository, which includes many scientific and data
  science packages
\item
  Great for data science workflows, especially when you need packages
  with compiled code or system-level dependencies
\item
  Handles complex dependency resolution and environment isolation
\end{itemize}

\textbf{poetry:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Focuses on Python projects and packages
\item
  Uses \texttt{pyproject.toml} and \texttt{poetry.lock} for reproducible
  builds
\item
  Automatically creates and manages virtual environments
\item
  Excellent for modern Python application development and publishing to
  PyPI
\item
  Handles dependency resolution and version locking for Python packages
  only
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Key differences:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{conda} can install system-level and non-Python dependencies;
  \texttt{poetry} only manages Python packages
\item
  \texttt{conda} environments can include packages from the Anaconda
  repository; \texttt{poetry} uses PyPI
\item
  \texttt{poetry} is ideal for pure Python projects and reproducible
  builds; \texttt{conda} is better for scientific computing and
  mixed-language projects
\end{itemize}

\textbf{When to use each:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Use \texttt{conda} if you need scientific libraries, compiled code, or
  non-Python dependencies
\item
  Use \texttt{poetry} for modern Python projects, apps, and libraries
  where you want easy dependency management and publishing
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Summary Table:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2927}}

Non-Python dependencies & Yes & No \\
Environment isolation & Yes & Yes \\
Dependency resolution & Excellent & Excellent \\
Reproducibility & Good & Excellent \\
Publishing to PyPI & No & Yes \\
\end{longtable}

Choose the tool that best fits your project needs!

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Modern Python Package Managers:
\texttt{pip}, \texttt{conda}, \texttt{poetry},
\texttt{uv}}{Modern Python Package Managers: pip, conda, poetry, uv}}\label{modern-python-package-managers-pip-conda-poetry-uv}

Python package management has evolved rapidly, making it easier to
install, update, and manage dependencies for any project.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{pip} is the standard tool for installing Python packages from
  PyPI. It works well for most projects and is simple to use.
\item
  \textbf{.venv} helps you create isolated environments so each project
  has its own dependencies.
\item
  \textbf{conda} offers advanced environment and package management,
  especially for scientific computing and projects with non-Python
  dependencies.
\item
  \textbf{poetry} provides modern dependency management, automatic
  environment creation, and reproducibility for Python projects.
\item
  \textbf{uv} is a new, high-performance package manager written in
  Rust. It's designed for speed and supports modern workflows. Learn
  more: \href{https://github.com/astral-sh/uv}{uv GitHub page}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{For this course:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  You'll use \texttt{pip} and \texttt{.venv} for installing packages and
  managing your environment.
\item
  As you tackle larger or more complex projects, consider exploring
  \texttt{conda}, \texttt{poetry}, and \texttt{uv} for better
  performance, reproducibility, and ease of use.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Summary:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Choose the tool that fits your workflow and project needs.
\item
  Stay curious---new tools like \texttt{uv} are making Python
  development faster and more reliable.
\end{itemize}

A good package manager and environment strategy will save you time,
prevent headaches, and make your code more reproducible and shareable.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Independent Study: Practice Environment Setup
with
\texttt{pip}}{Independent Study: Practice Environment Setup with pip}}\label{independent-study-practice-environment-setup-with-pip}

\textbf{Objective:} Build hands-on skills in creating, managing, and
verifying Python environments and packages using \texttt{pip}.

\subsection{Instructions}\label{instructions}

\textbf{Step 1: Create Your Workspace}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Make a folder named \texttt{test\_pip\_env}.
\item
  Open the folder in VS Code.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  create a \texttt{.venv} environment
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 3: Install Required Packages}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  With the environment active, install packages using \texttt{pip}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 4: Export Your Environment Configuration}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Save your environment's package list to a file:

\begin{Shaded}

\end{Shaded}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 5: Deactivate and Remove the Environment}

\begin{itemize}

  Deactivate the environment:

\textbf{Step 6: Recreate the Environment from the Exported File}

\begin{itemize}

\item
  Install packages from your saved file:

\end{Shaded}
\item
  Verify that \texttt{numpy}, \texttt{pandas}, \texttt{matplotlib}, and
  (if installed) \texttt{scikit-learn} are present.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Step 7: Run a Jupyter Notebook}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Create a notebook in the recreated environment.
\item
  Import \texttt{numpy}, \texttt{pandas}, \texttt{matplotlib}, and
  \texttt{scikit-learn}.
\item
  Print the versions of these packages to confirm setup.
\item
  Generate html file from the notebook using quarto

This exercise will help you master environment management and

\section{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-2}

In this lecture, we'll explore how to optimize your workflow in Jupyter
notebooks by leveraging \textbf{magic commands} and \textbf{shell
commands}, understanding \textbf{file paths}, and interacting with the
\textbf{filesystem} using the \texttt{os} module.

By completing this lecture, you will be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Run shell commands directly within a notebook.\\
\item
  Navigate and manipulate files and directories efficiently.\\
\item
  Integrate external tools and scripts seamlessly into your workflow.
\end{itemize}

By mastering these techniques, you'll be able to work more efficiently
and handle complex data science tasks with ease.

\section{Magic Commands}\label{magic-commands}

\subsection{What are Magic Commands?}\label{what-are-magic-commands}

Magic commands in Jupyter are shortcuts that extend the functionality of
the notebook environment. There are two types of magic commands:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Line magics}: Commands that operate on a single line.
\item
  \textbf{Cell magics}: Commands that operate on the entire cell.
\end{itemize}

You can access the full list of magic commands by typing:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# show all the avaiable magic commands on the system}
\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{lsmagic  }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Available line magics:
%alias  %alias_magic  %autoawait  %autocall  %automagic  %autosave  %bookmark  %cd  %clear  %cls  %code_wrap  %colors  %conda  %config  %connect_info  %copy  %ddir  %debug  %dhist  %dirs  %doctest_mode  %echo  %ed  %edit  %env  %gui  %hist  %history  %killbgscripts  %ldir  %less  %load  %load_ext  %loadpy  %logoff  %logon  %logstart  %logstate  %logstop  %ls  %lsmagic  %macro  %magic  %mamba  %matplotlib  %micromamba  %mkdir  %more  %notebook  %page  %pastebin  %pdb  %pdef  %pdoc  %pfile  %pinfo  %pinfo2  %pip  %popd  %pprint  %precision  %prun  %psearch  %psource  %pushd  %pwd  %pycat  %pylab  %qtconsole  %quickref  %recall  %rehashx  %reload_ext  %ren  %rep  %rerun  %reset  %reset_selective  %rmdir  %run  %save  %sc  %set_env  %store  %sx  %system  %tb  %time  %timeit  %unalias  %unload_ext  %uv  %who  %who_ls  %whos  %xdel  %xmode

Available cell magics:
%%!  %%HTML  %%SVG  %%bash  %%capture  %%cmd  %%code_wrap  %%debug  %%file  %%html  %%javascript  %%js  %%latex  %%markdown  %%perl  %%prun  %%pypy  %%python  %%python2  %%python3  %%ruby  %%script  %%sh  %%svg  %%sx  %%system  %%time  %%timeit  %%writefile

Automagic is ON, % prefix IS NOT needed for line magics.
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Line Magic}\label{line-magic}

In Jupyter notebooks, line magic commands are invoked by placing a
single percentage sign (\texttt{\%}) in front of the statement, allowing
for quick, inline operations.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\texttt{\%time}: Timing the execution of
code}{\%time: Timing the execution of code}}\label{time-timing-the-execution-of-code}

In data science, it is often crucial to evaluate the performance of
specific code snippets or algorithms, and the \texttt{\%time} magic
command provides a simple and efficient way to measure the execution
time of individual statements, helping you identify bottlenecks and
optimize your code for better performance.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ my\_dot(a, b): }
    \CommentTok{"""}
\CommentTok{   Compute the dot product of two vectors}
\CommentTok{ }
\CommentTok{    Args:}
\CommentTok{      a (ndarray (n,)):  input vector }
\CommentTok{      b (ndarray (n,)):  input vector with same dimension as a}
\CommentTok{    }
\CommentTok{    Returns:}
\CommentTok{      x (scalar): }
\CommentTok{    """}
\NormalTok{    x}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(a.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]):}
\NormalTok{        x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ a[i] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ b[i]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ x}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\NormalTok{np.random.seed(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{a }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.rand(}\DecValTok{10000000}\NormalTok{)  }\CommentTok{\# very large arrays}
\NormalTok{b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.rand(}\DecValTok{10000000}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let's use \texttt{\%time} to measure the execution time of a single line
of code.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Example: Timing a list comprehension}
\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{time np.dot(a, b)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
CPU times: total: 15.6 ms
Wall time: 32.9 ms
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
2501072.5816813153
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{time my\_dot(a, b)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
CPU times: total: 1.88 s
Wall time: 1.86 s
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
2501072.5816813707
\end{verbatim}

To capture the output of \texttt{\%time} (or \texttt{\%timeit}), you
cannot directly assign it to a variable as it's a magic command that
prints the result to the notebook's output. However, you can use
Python's built-in \texttt{time} module to manually time your code and
assign the execution time to a variable.

Here's how you can do it using the \texttt{time} module:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ time}
\NormalTok{tic }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ time.time()  }\CommentTok{\# capture start time}
\NormalTok{c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.dot(a, b)}
\NormalTok{toc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ time.time()  }\CommentTok{\# capture end time}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"np.dot(a, b) =  }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{c}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Vectorized version duration: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\DecValTok{1000}\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{(toc}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{tic)}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ ms "}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{tic }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ time.time()  }\CommentTok{\# capture start time}
\NormalTok{c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ my\_dot(a,b)}
\NormalTok{toc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ time.time()  }\CommentTok{\# capture end time}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"my\_dot(a, b) =  }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{c}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"loop version duration: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\DecValTok{1000}\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{(toc}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{tic)}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ ms "}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{del}\NormalTok{(a)}\OperatorTok{;}\KeywordTok{del}\NormalTok{(b)  }\CommentTok{\#remove these big arrays from memory}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.dot(a, b) =  2501072.5817
Vectorized version duration: 2.9922 ms 
my_dot(a, b) =  2501072.5817
loop version duration: 2004.3225 ms 
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\texttt{\%matplotlib\ inline}: Displaying
plots
inline}{\%matplotlib inline: Displaying plots inline}}\label{matplotlib-inline-displaying-plots-inline}

This command allows you to embed plots within the notebook.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Example: Using \%matplotlib inline to display a plot}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{matplotlib inline}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linspace(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.sin(x)}
\NormalTok{plt.plot(x, y)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{workflow_enhance_files/figure-pdf/cell-9-output-1.png}}

\subsection{Cell Magic Commands}\label{cell-magic-commands}

While cell magic commands are denoted with double percentage signs
(\texttt{\%\%}) at the beginning of the cell, enabling you to apply
commands to the entire cell for more complex tasks. Note that a cell
magic command in Jupyter notebook has to be the first line in the code
cell!

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\texttt{\%\%time}: Timing cell
execution}{\%\%time: Timing cell execution}}\label{time-timing-cell-execution}

This cell magic is useful for measuring the execution time of an entire
cell.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{\%\%}\NormalTok{time}
\CommentTok{\# Example: Timing a cell with matrix multiplication}

\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.rand(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{B }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.rand(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{C }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.dot(A, B)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
CPU times: total: 219 ms
Wall time: 23 ms
\end{verbatim}

Question: there are several timing magic commands that can be confusing
due to their similarities, they are \texttt{\%time},\texttt{\%timeit},
\texttt{\%\%time}, and \texttt{\%timeit}. Do your own research on the
differences among them

\section{Shell Commands in Jupyter
Notebooks}\label{shell-commands-in-jupyter-notebooks}

\textbf{What are Shell Commands?}

Shell commands let you interact directly with your computer's operating
system from within a Jupyter notebook. This means you can manage files,
check your environment, and run system tools without leaving your
notebook. To run a shell command in Jupyter, start the line with an
exclamation mark (\texttt{!}). For example, \texttt{!ls} lists files on
macOS/Linux, while \texttt{!dir} does the same on Windows.

\textbf{How does it work?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Python code is executed by the IPython kernel inside the notebook.
\item
  Shell commands (lines starting with \texttt{!}) are sent to your
  computer's shell (like Bash, Command Prompt, or PowerShell), not to
  Python.
\item
  This separation means you can use both Python and shell commands in
  the same notebook, but they run in different environments.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Using Shell Commands}\label{using-shell-commands}

\subsubsection{Print the current working
directory}\label{print-the-current-working-directory}

To see where your notebook is running, use: - On macOS/Linux:
\texttt{!pwd} - On Windows: \texttt{!cd}

This helps you understand where files will be saved or loaded from.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{!}\NormalTok{cd}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{!}\NormalTok{cd}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
c:\Users\lsi8012\mydev\STAT303-1-class-notes
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\texttt{!ls} (\texttt{!dir} on Windows):
Listing files and
directories}{!ls (!dir on Windows): Listing files and directories}}\label{ls-dir-on-windows-listing-files-and-directories}

To view all files and folders in your current directory, use a shell
command:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  On macOS/Linux: \texttt{!ls}
\item
  On Windows: \texttt{!dir}
\end{itemize}

This is useful for quickly checking what data, scripts, or notebooks are
available in your workspace. If you want to see hidden files (those
starting with a dot), use \texttt{!ls\ -a} on macOS/Linux or
\texttt{!dir\ /a} on Windows.

\textbf{Tip:} If you get an error, double-check that you are using the
correct command for your operating system.

\section{Installing Required Packages Within Your
Notebook}\label{installing-required-packages-within-your-notebook}

When working in Jupyter notebooks, you often need to install new Python
packages. There are two main ways to do this:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Shell Command (not recommend):}

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Use an exclamation mark (\texttt{!}) before the command:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      \texttt{!pip\ install\ package\_name}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    This runs the command in your system shell, which may not always
    install the package in the same environment as your notebook kernel.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Magic Command:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    Use a percent sign (\texttt{\%}) before the command:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      \texttt{\%pip\ install\ package\_name}
    \end{itemize}
  \item
    This is Jupyter-specific and ensures the package is installed in the
    environment where your notebook is running.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Example:}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \texttt{\%pip\ install\ numpy} \# Installs numpy in the notebook's
  environment
\item
  \texttt{!pip\ install\ numpy} \# Installs numpy using the system shell
  (may differ from notebook environment)
\end{itemize}

Unlike shell commands, the \texttt{\%pip} magic command is designed
specifically for Jupyter notebooks. It automatically installs packages
into the exact environment your notebook kernel is using, reducing
confusion and installation errors.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{pip install numpy}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Requirement already satisfied: numpy in c:\users\lsi8012\appdata\local\anaconda3\lib\site-packages (1.26.4)
Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.
\end{verbatim}

In most cases, you don't need to type \texttt{\%} before
\texttt{pip\ install\ numpy} because Jupyter's ``automagic'' feature is
enabled by default. Automagic lets you use line magics without the
\texttt{\%} (unless their name conflicts with Python variables or
commands).

\textbf{How automagic works:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If you type \texttt{pip\ install\ numpy}, Jupyter will interpret it as
  \texttt{\%pip\ install\ numpy} automatically.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Best practice:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Use \texttt{\%pip\ install\ ...} for clarity and to avoid conflicts.
\item
  Automagic is convenient, but explicit magic commands are safer in
  shared or complex notebooks.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Note:} Cell magics still require the \texttt{\%\%} prefix.

\section{File Paths in Python}\label{file-paths-in-python}

Understanding how to specify file paths in Python is essential for
loading and saving data. File paths tell Python where to find or store
your files (e.g., datasets, results, or scripts).

There are two main types of file paths: \textbf{absolute paths} and
\textbf{relative paths}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Absolute Path:} Gives the complete location of a file or
  folder from the root of your file system. It always points to the same
  place, no matter where your code is running.
\item
  \textbf{Relative Path:} Specifies the location of a file or folder in
  relation to your current working directory. It is shorter and more
  flexible, making your code easier to share and reuse.
\end{itemize}

Choosing the right type of path helps avoid errors and makes your code
more portable across different computers and operating systems.

\subsection{Absolute Path}\label{absolute-path}

An \textbf{absolute path} provides the full address to a file or
directory, starting from the root of your system. It does \textbf{not}
depend on where your code is running.

\textbf{Example (Windows):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Absolute path example (Windows)}
\NormalTok{file\_path }\OperatorTok{=} \VerbatimStringTok{r"C:\textbackslash{}Users\textbackslash{}Username\textbackslash{}Documents\textbackslash{}data.csv"}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\OperatorTok{!}\NormalTok{conda env }\BuiltInTok{list}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
# conda environments:
#
base                  *  C:\Users\lsi8012\AppData\Local\anaconda3
\end{verbatim}

The path associated with each conda env is absolute path.

\subsection{Relative Path}\label{relative-path}

A \textbf{relative path} describes the location of a file or folder in
relation to your current working directory. It is shorter, more
flexible, and makes your code easier to share and run on different
computers.

Relative paths are especially useful in projects with organized folder
structures, because they allow you to move your code and data together
without changing file references.

To find your current working directory in your notebook, you can use a
magic command:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Magic command: \texttt{\%pwd}
\end{itemize}

Knowing your current working directory helps you understand where Python
will look for files when using relative paths.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Magic command}
\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{pwd}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
'c:\\Users\\lsi8012\\Documents\\Courses\\FA24\\DataScience_Intro_python_fa24_Sec20_21'
\end{verbatim}

Example of a Relative Path:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Example of relative path}
\NormalTok{file\_path }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"sample.txt"}  \CommentTok{\# Relative to the current directory}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The relative path \texttt{sample.txt} means that there is a file in the
current working directory.

\subsection{Methods to Specify File Paths in
Windows}\label{methods-to-specify-file-paths-in-windows}

Specifying file paths correctly is crucial for avoiding errors and
making your code portable. Windows uses backslashes
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}}) to separate folders, but in Python, a single
backslash is an escape character (e.g., \texttt{\textbackslash{}n} for
newline), which can lead to mistakes if not handled properly.

Here are four reliable ways to specify file paths in Windows:

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Method 1: \textbf{Using Escaped
Backslashes}}{Method 1: Using Escaped Backslashes}}\label{method-1-using-escaped-backslashes}

Use double backslashes (\texttt{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}}) to
prevent Python from interpreting them as escape characters.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{file\_path }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"C:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}}\StringTok{Users}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}}\StringTok{Username}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}}\StringTok{Documents}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}}\StringTok{data.csv"}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Method 2: \textbf{Using Raw
Strings}}{Method 2: Using Raw Strings}}\label{method-2-using-raw-strings}

Prefix the path with \texttt{r} to tell Python to treat backslashes as
literal characters.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{file\_path }\OperatorTok{=} \VerbatimStringTok{r"C:\textbackslash{}Users\textbackslash{}Username\textbackslash{}Documents\textbackslash{}data.csv"}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Method 3: \textbf{Using forward slashes
(\texttt{/})}}{Method 3: Using forward slashes (/)}}\label{method-3-using-forward-slashes}

Python accepts forward slashes (\texttt{/}) in file paths, even on
Windows. This is often the simplest and most portable method.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{file\_path }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"C:/Users/Username/Documents/data.csv"}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Method 4: \textbf{Using
\texttt{os.path.join}}}{Method 4: Using os.path.join}}\label{method-4-using-os.path.join}

Use \texttt{os.path.join()} to build paths programmatically. This method
automatically uses the correct separator for your operating system,
making your code cross-platform.

Using these methods helps prevent bugs, makes your code easier to share,
and ensures it works on different computers and operating systems.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ os}
\NormalTok{file\_path }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ os.path.join(}\StringTok{"C:"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Users"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Username"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Documents"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data.csv"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This method works across different operating systems because
\texttt{os.path.join} automatically uses the correct path separator
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}} for Windows and \texttt{/}for Linux/Mac).

\subsection{File paths in macOS and
Linux}\label{file-paths-in-macos-and-linux}

macOS and Linux use forward slashes (\texttt{/}) as path separators,
which is exactly what Python expects by default. This means you can
specify file paths directly, like
\texttt{/Users/yourname/Documents/data.csv}, without worrying about
escape characters or compatibility issues.

\textbf{Why is this helpful?} - Forward slashes work seamlessly in
Python on macOS, Linux, and even Windows. - You avoid common errors
caused by backslashes (which are escape characters in Python). - Code
written with forward slashes is portable and recommended for all
platforms.

\subsubsection{Best Practices for File Paths in Data
Science}\label{best-practices-for-file-paths-in-data-science}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Prefer \textbf{relative paths} within your project folders---this
  makes your code portable and easy to share or move.
\item
  Use \textbf{absolute paths} only for files outside your project or
  when you need a fixed location.
\item
  Always check your \textbf{current working directory} before reading or
  writing files to avoid confusion and errors.
\item
  Avoid hardcoding file paths directly in your code; use variables or
  configuration files for flexibility.
\item
  For cross-platform compatibility, use \textbf{forward slashes
  (\texttt{/})} in file paths or build paths programmatically with
  \texttt{os.path.join()}.
\item
  Document your file structure and path conventions in your project
  README to help collaborators.
\item
  When sharing code, test file paths on both Windows and macOS/Linux to
  ensure portability.
\end{itemize}

\section{Interacting with the OS and
Filesystem}\label{interacting-with-the-os-and-filesystem}

In data science projects, you often work with data files (such as CSV,
Excel, or JSON) stored in various folders. Managing these files
efficiently is essential for reproducible workflows and organized
projects.

The Python \texttt{os} module provides powerful tools to interact with
your operating system and manage files and directories directly from
your notebook. With \texttt{os}, you can: - Check your current working
directory - List files and folders - Create, rename, or delete
directories - Move between folders - Check if files or folders exist
before using them

Let's import the \texttt{os} module and explore some of its most useful
functions for data science tasks.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ os}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We can get the location of the current working directory using the
\texttt{os.getcwd} function.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{os.getcwd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
'c:\\Users\\lsi8012\\mydev\\STAT303-1-class-notes'
\end{verbatim}

The command \texttt{os.chdir(\textquotesingle{}..\textquotesingle{})} in
Python changes the current working directory to the parent directory of
the current one.

Note that \texttt{..} as the path notation for the parent directory is
universally true across all major operating systems, including Windows,
macOS, and Linux. It allows you to move one level up in the directory
hierarchy, which is very useful when navigating directories
programmatically, especially in scripts where directory traversal is
needed.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{os.chdir(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}..\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{os.getcwd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
'c:\\Users\\lsi8012\\mydev'
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{os.chdir()} is used to change the current working directory.

For example:
\texttt{os.chdir(\textquotesingle{}./week2\textquotesingle{})}

\texttt{./week2} is a relative path:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{.} refers to the current directory.
\item
  week2 is a folder inside the current directory.
\end{itemize}

The \texttt{os.listdir()} function in Python returns a list of all files
and directories in the specified path. If no path is provided, it
returns the contents of the current working directory.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{os.listdir()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
['limonstar-web',
 'llm2005spring',
 'llm2005spring_back',
 'mcdc_2025su',
 'mcdc_2025su_new',
 'STAT201',
 'STAT303-1-class-notes',
 'STAT303-2-class-notes',
 'STAT303-3-class-notes',
 'stat359_su25',
 'stat362']
\end{verbatim}

Check whether a specific folder/file exist in the current working
directory

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\textquotesingle{}data\textquotesingle{}} \KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ os.listdir(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}.\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
False
\end{verbatim}

\section{Navigate between directories and understand . and .. in
paths}\label{navigate-between-directories-and-understand-.-and-..-in-paths}

In Python, you can use the \texttt{os} module to work with directories
and paths, and it's important to understand how relative paths work:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{.} refers to the \textbf{current directory}\\
\item
  \texttt{..} refers to the \textbf{parent directory}
\end{itemize}

This knowledge is essential for organizing files and writing portable
code.

From the command line, you can use the \texttt{cd} (change directory)
command to move between folders:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{cd\ \textless{}folder\_name\textgreater{}} moves \textbf{down}
  into a child folder\\
\item
  \texttt{cd\ ..} moves \textbf{up} to the parent folder
\end{itemize}

By combining these commands, you can navigate to the desired location.

\section{Python Variables}\label{python-variables}

Variables are fundamental building blocks in Python---they allow you to
store, update, and reference data throughout your code. Choosing clear
and descriptive variable names makes your code easier to read, debug,
and share with others.

\subsection{Rules for variable names}\label{rules-for-variable-names}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Variable names must start with a letter (a--z, A--Z) or an underscore
  (\texttt{\_}). They cannot begin with a number.
\item
  Names can include letters, digits, and underscores
  (\texttt{a\_variable}, \texttt{profit\_margin},
  \texttt{the\_3\_musketeers}).
\item
  Variable names are case-sensitive: \texttt{score}, \texttt{Score}, and
  \texttt{SCORE} are all different variables.
\item
  Avoid using Python reserved words (like \texttt{for}, \texttt{if},
  \texttt{class}, etc.) as variable names.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Tip:} Use descriptive names that reflect the purpose of the
variable. This helps you and others understand your code at a glance.

Here are some examples of good variable names:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Examples of valid variable names}

\NormalTok{a\_variable }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{23}
\NormalTok{is\_today\_Saturday }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{False}
\NormalTok{my\_favorite\_car }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"Delorean"}
\NormalTok{the\_3\_musketeers }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"Athos"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Porthos"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Aramis"}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
If you use an invalid variable name, Python will raise a
\texttt{SyntaxError} and stop running your code. Always follow the
naming rules to avoid these errors and keep your code readable.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Dynamic Typing in Python
Variables}\label{dynamic-typing-in-python-variables}

Python variables are dynamically typed, meaning you don't need to
declare their type before using them. You can assign a value of any type
to a variable, and even change its type later in your code:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}      \CommentTok{\# x is an integer}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"cat"} \CommentTok{\# now x is a string}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To check the type of a variable, use the built-in \texttt{type()}
function:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This flexibility makes Python easy to use, but it's important to keep
track of your variable types to avoid confusion in your code.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Print the variables defined above their values and their types}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"a\_variable:"}\NormalTok{, a\_variable, }\StringTok{"| type:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(a\_variable))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"is\_today\_Saturday:"}\NormalTok{, is\_today\_Saturday, }\StringTok{"| type:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(is\_today\_Saturday))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"my\_favorite\_car:"}\NormalTok{, my\_favorite\_car, }\StringTok{"| type:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(my\_favorite\_car))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"the\_3\_musketeers:"}\NormalTok{, the\_3\_musketeers, }\StringTok{"| type:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(the\_3\_musketeers))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
a_variable: 23 | type: <class 'int'>
is_today_Saturday: False | type: <class 'bool'>
my_favorite_car: Delorean | type: <class 'str'>
the_3_musketeers: ['Athos', 'Porthos', 'Aramis'] | type: <class 'list'>
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Multiple Variable Assignment in
Python}\label{multiple-variable-assignment-in-python}

Python allows you to assign values to several variables at once in a
single line. This technique is especially useful for initializing
related variables and can make your code cleaner and more efficient.

\textbf{Example:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{color1, color2, color3 }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"red"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"green"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"blue"}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

After this assignment: - \texttt{color1} is ``red'' - \texttt{color2} is
``green'' - \texttt{color3} is ``blue''

This approach works for any number of variables, as long as the number
of values matches the number of variable names.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{color1, color2, color3 }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"red"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"green"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"blue"}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(color1)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(color3)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
red
blue
\end{verbatim}

The same value can be assigned to multiple variables by chaining
multiple assignment operations within a single statement.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{color4 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ color5 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ color6 }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"magenta"}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(color4)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(color6)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
magenta
magenta
\end{verbatim}

\section{Built-in data types}\label{built-in-data-types}

Python has several built-in data types for storing different kinds of
information in variables.

\begin{verbatim}
<IPython.core.display.Image object>
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{Primitive Types}\\
In Python, \textbf{integers, floats, booleans, and \texttt{None}} are
often called \emph{primitive data types} because they represent a single
value.

\textbf{Container (Data Structure) Types}\\
Types such as \textbf{strings, lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries}
are \emph{containers} because they can hold multiple values (characters
in a string, items in a list, key--value pairs in a dictionary, etc.).
We'll explore these container types in more detail in the next chapter.

\textbf{Identifying Types}\\
You can check the type of any object using Python's built-in
\texttt{type()} function. For example:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{))         }\CommentTok{\# int}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(}\FloatTok{3.14}\NormalTok{))       }\CommentTok{\# float}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{))       }\CommentTok{\# bool}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{))       }\CommentTok{\# NoneType}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"hello"}\NormalTok{))    }\CommentTok{\# str (a sequence / container of characters)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]))  }\CommentTok{\# list}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'bool'>
<class 'NoneType'>
<class 'str'>
<class 'list'>
\end{verbatim}

\section{Python Standard Library}\label{python-standard-library}

The \href{https://docs.python.org/3/library/}{Python Standard Library}
provides a wide range of modules and built-in functions that support
everyday programming tasks. These tools allow you to write code that is
both efficient and readable without reinventing common functionality.

\textbf{Examples of built-in functions:} - \texttt{print()}: Displays
output to the screen. - \texttt{len()}: Returns the length of an object
(like a list or string). - \texttt{type()}: Shows the type of a
variable. - \texttt{sum()}: Adds up all items in an iterable (like a
list). - \texttt{range()}: Generates a sequence of numbers, often used
in loops.

You can explore more built-in functions and modules in the official
documentation. Using these tools makes your code more readable and
powerful.

\textbf{Example:}

\textbf{range():} The \texttt{range()} function returns a sequence of
evenly-spaced integer values. It is commonly used in \texttt{for} loops
to define the sequence of elements over which the iterations are
performed.

Below is an example where the \texttt{range()} function is used to
create a sequence of whole numbers upto 10:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{Date and Time:}

Python includes a powerful built-in module called
