\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{nums }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Use \texttt{lambda} with \texttt{filter()} to keep only names starting
  with a vowel:
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{names }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"Alice"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Bob"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Eve"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Uma"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Sam"}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Use \texttt{lambda} with \texttt{map()} to convert Celsius to
  Fahrenheit:
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{temps\_c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{37}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{}\label{section}

You are given a list of strings representing student names. Some
students appear more than once because they signed up for multiple
activities.

Write a Python function that:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Removes duplicate names} while \emph{preserving the first
  occurrence order}.\\
\item
  \textbf{Returns a list of tuples} \texttt{(index,\ name\_length)} for
  each \textbf{unique name}, where:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \texttt{index} is the original position of the name in the list
    (first occurrence).\\
  \item
    \texttt{name\_length} is the length of the name.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Finally, \textbf{sort the output list by \texttt{name\_length} in
descending order}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{names }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"Alice"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Bob"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Alice"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Charlie"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Bob"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Dave"}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\part{Core library foundations}

\chapter{Reading Data}\label{reading-data}

\begin{verbatim}
<IPython.core.display.Image object>
\end{verbatim}

\section{Types of Data: Structured
vs.~Unstructured}\label{types-of-data-structured-vs.-unstructured}

Understanding the format of your data is crucial before you can analyze
it effectively. Data exists in two primary formats:

\subsection{Structured Data}\label{structured-data}

\textbf{Structured data} is organized in a tabular format with clearly
defined relationships between data elements. Key characteristics
include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Rows} represent individual \textbf{observations} (records or
  data points)
\item
  \textbf{Columns} represent \textbf{variables} (attributes or features)
\item
  Data follows a consistent schema or format
\item
  Easy to search, query, and analyze using standard tools
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Example:} The dataset below contains movie information where
each row represents one movie (observation) and each column contains
specific attributes like title, rating, or budget (variables). Since all
data in a row relates to the same movie, this is also called
\textbf{relational data}.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& Title & US Gross & Production Budget & Release Date & Major Genre &
Creative Type & Rotten Tomatoes Rating & IMDB Rating \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & The Shawshank Redemption & 28241469 & 25000000 & Sep 23 1994 & Drama
& Fiction & 88 & 9.2 \\
1 & Inception & 285630280 & 160000000 & Jul 16 2010 & Horror/Thriller &
Fiction & 87 & 9.1 \\
2 & One Flew Over the Cuckoo\textquotesingle s Nest & 108981275 &
4400000 & Nov 19 1975 & Comedy & Fiction & 96 & 8.9 \\
3 & The Dark Knight & 533345358 & 185000000 & Jul 18 2008 &
Action/Adventure & Fiction & 93 & 8.9 \\
4 & Schindler\textquotesingle s List & 96067179 & 25000000 & Dec 15 1993
& Drama & Non-Fiction & 97 & 8.9 \\
\end{longtable}

\emph{Common formats:} CSV files, Excel spreadsheets, SQL databases

\subsection{Unstructured Data}\label{unstructured-data}

\textbf{Unstructured data} lacks a predefined organizational structure,
making it more challenging to analyze with traditional methods.

\emph{Examples include:} Text documents, images, audio files, videos,
social media posts, sensor data

While harder to analyze directly, unstructured data can often be
converted into structured formats for analysis (e.g., extracting
features from images or sentiment scores from text).

\textbf{In this sequence, we will focus on analyzing structured data.}

\section{Introduction to Pandas}\label{introduction-to-pandas}

\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/}{\textbf{Pandas}} is Python's premier
library for data manipulation and analysis. Think of it as Excel for
Python - it provides powerful tools for working with tabular data (like
spreadsheets) and supports reading from various file formats:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{CSV} (Comma-Separated Values)
\item
  \textbf{Excel} spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls)
\item
  \textbf{JSON} (JavaScript Object Notation)
\item
  \textbf{HTML} tables
\item
  \textbf{SQL} databases
\item
  And many more!
\end{itemize}

\section{Reading CSV Files with
Pandas}\label{reading-csv-files-with-pandas}

\subsection{Understanding CSV Files}\label{understanding-csv-files}

\textbf{CSV (Comma-Separated Values)} is the most popular format for
storing structured data. Here's what makes CSV files special:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Simple structure}: Each row represents one record/observation
\item
  \textbf{Comma delimiter}: Values within a row are separated by commas
\item
  \textbf{Plain text}: Human-readable and lightweight
\item
  \textbf{Universal compatibility}: Supported by virtually all data
  tools
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{💡 Pro Tip}: When you open a CSV file in Excel, the commas are
automatically converted to column separators, so you won't see them
visually!
\end{quote}

\subsection{CSV File Structure
Example}\label{csv-file-structure-example}

Here's a sample CSV file containing daily COVID-19 data for Italy:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{date,new\_cases,new\_deaths,new\_tests}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}21,2256.0,454.0,28095.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}22,2729.0,534.0,44248.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}23,3370.0,437.0,37083.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}24,2646.0,464.0,95273.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}25,3021.0,420.0,38676.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}26,2357.0,415.0,24113.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}27,2324.0,260.0,26678.0}
\NormalTok{2020{-}04{-}28,1739.0,333.0,37554.0}
\NormalTok{...}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Structure breakdown:} - \textbf{Header row}: Column names
(\texttt{date}, \texttt{new\_cases}, \texttt{new\_deaths},
\texttt{new\_tests}) - \textbf{Data rows}: Each row contains values for
one day - \textbf{Delimiter}: Commas separate each value within a row

\subsection{Getting Started: Importing
Pandas}\label{getting-started-importing-pandas}

Before we can work with data, we need to import the pandas library. By
convention, pandas is imported with the alias \texttt{pd} - this is a
universal practice that makes your code more readable and concise.

\textbf{Why use \texttt{pd}?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Shorter syntax}: \texttt{pd.read\_csv()} instead of
  \texttt{pandas.read\_csv()}
\item
  \textbf{Industry standard}: Everyone in the data science community
  uses this alias
\item
  \textbf{Cleaner code}: Makes your scripts more readable
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ os}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Loading Data with
\texttt{pd.read\_csv()}}{Loading Data with pd.read\_csv()}}\label{loading-data-with-pd.read_csv}

\textbf{What is \texttt{pd.read\_csv()}?}

The \texttt{pd.read\_csv()} function is your gateway to loading CSV data
into Python. It converts CSV files into a pandas \textbf{DataFrame} -
think of it as a powerful, interactive spreadsheet that you can
manipulate with code.

\textbf{Key Features:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Automatic data type detection}: Pandas intelligently guesses
  column types (numbers, text, dates)
\item
  \textbf{Header recognition}: Automatically uses the first row as
  column names
\item
  \textbf{Missing data handling}: Gracefully handles empty cells
\item
  \textbf{Flexible parsing}: Can handle various CSV formats and
  delimiters
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movie\_ratings.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Understanding the DataFrame Display:}

When you display a DataFrame, you'll notice several key components:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{The Index Column (leftmost)}: The first column shows row
  indices (0, 1, 2, 3\ldots). When you create a DataFrame without
  specifying an index, pandas automatically assigns a
  \textbf{RangeIndex}, which is a sequence of integers starting from 0.
\item
  \textbf{Column Headers}: The top row shows column names from your CSV
  file
\item
  \textbf{Data Cells}: The intersection of rows and columns contains
  your actual data
\item
  \textbf{Data Types}: Pandas automatically detects whether columns
  contain numbers, text, dates, etc.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
💡 \textbf{Key Point}: The index is \textbf{not} part of your original
data - it's added by pandas to help identify and access rows
efficiently.
\end{quote}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Index range: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_ratings}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{index[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ to }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_ratings}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{index[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Total rows: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(movie\_ratings.index)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\end{Highlighting}

\subsection{Indexing}\label{indexing}

Alternatively, we can use the \texttt{index\_col} parameter in the
\texttt{pd.read\_csv()} function to set a specific column as the
\texttt{index} when reading a CSV file in pandas. This allows us to
directly specify which column should be used as the index of the
resulting DataFrame.

\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Understanding Pandas Data
Structures}\label{understanding-pandas-data-structures}

Before diving deeper into data manipulation, it's crucial to understand
the \textbf{two fundamental data structures} that pandas provides. Think
of these as the building blocks for all data science operations.

\subsection{Series - Your First Pandas Data
Structure}\label{series---your-first-pandas-data-structure}

A \texttt{pandas.Series} is like a \textbf{smart column} of data -
imagine a single column from an Excel spreadsheet, but with superpowers!

\textbf{📝 Definition}: A Series is a \textbf{one-dimensional array} of
data with an associated \textbf{index} (labels for each data point).

\textbf{🔍 Key Characteristics:}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2903}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4194}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2903}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Feature
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Description
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{One-dimensional} & Holds data in a single column/row &
\texttt{{[}85,\ 92,\ 78,\ 95{]}} \\
\textbf{Indexed} & Each element has a label/index &
\texttt{{[}\textquotesingle{}Alice\textquotesingle{},\ \textquotesingle{}Bob\textquotesingle{},\ \textquotesingle{}Carol\textquotesingle{},\ \textquotesingle{}David\textquotesingle{}{]}} \\
\textbf{Homogeneous} & Ideally same data type (but flexible) & All
numbers or all text \\
\textbf{Size immutable} & Fixed size once created (values can change) &
4 elements stay 4 elements \\
\end{longtable}

** Think of it as**: A single column from your DataFrame with smart
labeling capabilities.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# 🎬 Creating a Series from the \textquotesingle{}Title\textquotesingle{} column}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"="} \OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{" Movie Titles Series (first 10):"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(movie\_titles.head(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{()}

\CommentTok{\# Let\textquotesingle{}s explore what we just created}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{" Series Details:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Type: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(movie\_titles)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Shape: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_titles}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Size: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_titles}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{size}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Data Type: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_titles}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{dtype}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Name: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_titles}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{name}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{DataFrame}: Two-Dimensional
Data}{DataFrame: Two-Dimensional Data}}\label{dataframe-two-dimensional-data}

A \textbf{DataFrame} is the star of pandas - it's like a complete
spreadsheet or database table:

\textbf{Key Characteristics:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Two-dimensional}: Organized in rows and columns
\item
  \textbf{Heterogeneous}: Different columns can have different data
  types
\item
  \textbf{Labeled axes}: Both rows (index) and columns have names/labels
\item
  \textbf{Flexible}: Easy to filter, sort, group, and analyze
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Structure:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Rows (Index)}: Each row represents one \textbf{observation}
  (e.g., one movie, customer, transaction)
\item
  \textbf{Columns}: Each column represents one \textbf{variable/feature}
  (e.g., title, price, rating, date)
\item
  \textbf{Cells}: Individual data points where rows and columns
  intersect
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Default Behavior:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Row indices}: Automatically numbered 0, 1, 2, 3\ldots{} (but
  customizable)
\item
  \textbf{Column names}: Taken from the first row of your CSV file (the
  header)
\item
  \textbf{Data types}: Automatically detected (numbers, text, dates,
  etc.)
\end{itemize}

\section{DataFrame Exploration: Attributes and
Methods}\label{dataframe-exploration-attributes-and-methods}

Now that you understand what DataFrames and Series are, let's learn how
to \textbf{explore and understand} your data. Think of these tools as
your data detective kit!

\subsection{Essential DataFrame
Attributes}\label{essential-dataframe-attributes}

These attributes help you quickly understand your dataset's structure
and characteristics.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Data Types with
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dtypes.html}{\texttt{dtypes}}}{Data Types with dtypes}}\label{data-types-with-dtypes}

\textbf{What it shows}: The data type of each column\\
\textbf{Why it matters}: Understanding data types helps you: - ✅
Identify if numbers are stored as text (and need conversion) - ✅ Know
which operations work with each column\\
- ✅ Optimize memory usage and performance\\
- ✅ Catch data quality issues early

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# 🔍 Examine data types of all columns}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"📊 Data Types in Our Movie Dataset:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"="} \OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(movie\_ratings.dtypes)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{()}

\CommentTok{\# Count how many columns of each type we have}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"📈 Data Type Summary:"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{dtype\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ movie\_ratings.dtypes.value\_counts()}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ dtype, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ dtype\_counts.items():}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"  }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{dtype}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{count}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ columns"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Title                 object
US Gross               int64
Worldwide Gross        int64
Production Budget      int64
Release Date          object
MPAA Rating           object
Source                object
Major Genre           object
Creative Type         object
IMDB Rating          float64
IMDB Votes             int64
dtype: object
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Understanding Pandas Data
Types}\label{understanding-pandas-data-types}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1857}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2714}}

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Pandas Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Python Equivalent
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Real-World Example
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
When You'll See It
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}

\textbf{object} & string/mixed & Movie titles, categories, mixed data &
Text columns, categorical data \\
\textbf{int64} & int & Year (2023), count (50 movies) & Whole numbers,
counts, IDs \\
\textbf{float64} & float & Rating (7.5), budget (\$50.5M) & Decimal
numbers, measurements \\
\textbf{bool} & True/False & Is\_Popular, Has\_Sequel & Yes/no
questions \\
\textbf{datetime64} & datetime & Release dates, timestamps & Dates and
times \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{🚨 Common Data Type Issues:} - \textbf{Numbers stored as
`object'}: Often means there are non-numeric characters (like `\$' or
`,') - \textbf{Dates as `object'}: Need to convert using
\texttt{pd.to\_datetime()} - \textbf{Missing values in integers}: Forces
conversion to float64

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Dataset Dimensions with
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.shape.html}{\texttt{shape}}}{Dataset Dimensions with shape}}\label{dataset-dimensions-with-shape}

\textbf{What it shows}: Returns dimensions as
\texttt{(rows,\ columns)}\\
\textbf{Why it matters}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Understand your dataset size at a glance
\item
  Know if you have a ``tall'' (many rows) or ``wide'' (many columns)
  dataset
\item
  Estimate memory requirements
\item
  Spot issues (e.g., fewer rows than expected after filtering)
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Check the dimensions of our movie dataset}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Dataset shape: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_ratings}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Number of rows (movies): }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_ratings}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Number of columns (features): }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{movie\_ratings}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.columns.html}{\texttt{columns}}}{columns}}\label{columns}

\textbf{Why useful}: See what variables/features are available in your

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.info.html}{\texttt{info()}}}{info()}}\label{info}

\textbf{Purpose}: Provides a comprehensive summary of the DataFrame

\textbf{Returns}: Information about data types, non-null counts, and
memory usage

\section{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Putting It All Together: Understanding
Pandas Data
Structures}}{Putting It All Together: Understanding Pandas Data Structures}}\label{putting-it-all-together-understanding-pandas-data-structures}

Now that we've explored DataFrames and Series in detail, let's
consolidate your understanding with a comprehensive comparison and key
takeaways.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{DataFrame vs Series: The Complete
Picture}}{DataFrame vs Series: The Complete Picture}}\label{dataframe-vs-series-the-complete-picture}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2286}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4286}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3429}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Aspect
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{DataFrame}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Series}
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
** Dimensions** & 2D (rows × columns) & 1D (single column) \\
** Purpose** & Complete dataset/table & Single variable/column \\
** Structure** & Multiple columns, each can be different type & Single
column of one data type \\
** Access** &
\texttt{df{[}\textquotesingle{}column\textquotesingle{}{]}} or
\texttt{df.column} & Direct indexing \texttt{series{[}0{]}} \\
** Example** & Entire movie database & Just the `Rating' column \\
** Relationship** & Contains multiple Series & One column extracted from
DataFrame \\
\end{longtable}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Key Concepts You Now
Understand}}{Key Concepts You Now Understand}}\label{key-concepts-you-now-understand}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{DataFrames are Collections of
Series}}{DataFrames are Collections of Series}}\label{dataframes-are-collections-of-series}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# When you do this:}
\NormalTok{ratings }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ movie\_ratings[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Rating\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]  }\CommentTok{\# You get a Series}
\NormalTok{titles }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ movie\_ratings[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Title\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]    }\CommentTok{\# You get another Series}

\CommentTok{\# The DataFrame is made up of these Series working together!}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Index: The Hidden
Hero}}{Index: The Hidden Hero}}\label{index-the-hidden-hero}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Every row has a label} (0, 1, 2, 3\ldots{} by default)
\item
  \textbf{Links related data} across different columns
\item
  \textbf{Enables precise data selection} and alignment
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Data Types
Matter}}{Data Types Matter}}\label{data-types-matter}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Numerical columns} (\texttt{int64}, \texttt{float64}) →
  Mathematical operations
\item
  \textbf{Text columns} (\texttt{object}) → String operations,
  categories\\
\item
  \textbf{Date columns} (\texttt{datetime64}) → Time-based analysis
\item
  \textbf{Boolean columns} (\texttt{bool}) → True/False filtering
\end{itemize}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{What You Can Do
Now}}{What You Can Do Now}}\label{what-you-can-do-now}

✅ \textbf{Load data} from CSV files into DataFrames\\
✅ \textbf{Understand the structure} using \texttt{.shape},
\texttt{.dtypes}, \texttt{.info()}\\
✅ \textbf{Extract specific columns} as Series for focused analysis\\
✅ \textbf{Identify data quality issues} through data type inspection\\
✅ \textbf{Navigate between 1D and 2D data} structures confidently

\section{Writing Data to CSV Files}\label{writing-data-to-csv-files}

After cleaning, analyzing, or transforming your data, you'll often need
to \textbf{save your results} for future use or sharing. Pandas makes
this easy with the
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.to_csv.html}{\texttt{to\_csv()}}
method.

\subsection{Basic CSV Export}\label{basic-csv-export}

The simplest way to export a DataFrame is using the \texttt{to\_csv()}
method with just a filename:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Basic export {-} saves DataFrame to CSV file}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movie\_ratings\_exported.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"✅ Data exported successfully!"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
✅ Data exported successfully!
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Verify the file was created}
\ControlFlowTok{if} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movie\_ratings\_exported.csv\textquotesingle{}} \KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\SpecialStringTok{f\textquotesingle{}./datasets/}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{f}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{\textquotesingle{}} \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ f }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ os.listdir(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)]:}

    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"✅ File successfully exported!"}\NormalTok{)    }
\ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"❌ Export failed"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
✅ File successfully exported!
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Important CSV Export
Parameters}\label{important-csv-export-parameters}

By default, pandas includes row indices in the exported CSV. Often you
don't want this:

The \texttt{to\_csv()} method has many useful parameters to customize
your output:

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Index
Control}}{Index Control}}\label{index-control}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Export WITHOUT row indices (most common)}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_no\_index.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Export WITH row indices (default behavior)}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_with\_index.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Column
Selection}}{Column Selection}}\label{column-selection}

Export only specific columns:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Export only selected columns}
\NormalTok{columns\_to\_export }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Title\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}IMDB Rating\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Worldwide Gross\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings[columns\_to\_export].to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_selected\_columns.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Custom
Separators}}{Custom Separators}}\label{custom-separators}

Change the delimiter (useful for different regional standards):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Use semicolon instead of comma (common in European locales)}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_semicolon.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, sep}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{};\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Use tab separator (creates TSV file)}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_tab.txt\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, sep}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}t}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Handling Missing
Values}}{Handling Missing Values}}\label{handling-missing-values}

Control how missing/null values are represented:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Replace NaN values with custom text}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_custom\_na.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }
\NormalTok{                     index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{, }
\NormalTok{                     na\_rep}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Missing\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Encoding
Specification}}{Encoding Specification}}\label{encoding-specification}

Ensure proper character encoding (important for international data):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Specify UTF{-}8 encoding (recommended for international characters)}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings.to\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movies\_utf8.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }
\NormalTok{                     index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{, }
\NormalTok{                     encoding}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}utf{-}8\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Best Practices for CSV
Export}\label{best-practices-for-csv-export}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2889}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4222}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2889}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Practice}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Why Important}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Example}
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Always use \texttt{index=False}} & Prevents unnecessary row
numbers &
\texttt{df.to\_csv(\textquotesingle{}file.csv\textquotesingle{},\ index=False)} \\
\textbf{Specify encoding} & Ensures international characters display
correctly &
\texttt{encoding=\textquotesingle{}utf-8\textquotesingle{}} \\
\textbf{Use descriptive filenames} & Makes files easy to identify later
&
\texttt{\textquotesingle{}cleaned\_movie\_data\_2024.csv\textquotesingle{}} \\
\textbf{Check file paths} & Avoid overwriting important files & Use
relative or absolute paths carefully \\
\textbf{Handle missing data} & Define how NaN values should appear &
\texttt{na\_rep=\textquotesingle{}N/A\textquotesingle{}} or
\texttt{na\_rep=\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} \\
\end{longtable}

\subsection{Complete Export Example}\label{complete-export-example}

Here's a comprehensive example combining multiple parameters:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Professional CSV export with all best practices}
\NormalTok{export\_filename }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movie\_analysis\_final.csv\textquotesingle{}}

\CommentTok{\# Select relevant columns for export}
\NormalTok{columns\_for\_analysis }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Title\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}IMDB Rating\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}IMDB Votes\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}US Gross\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Worldwide Gross\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Production Budget\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{]}

\CommentTok{\# Export with professional settings}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings[columns\_for\_analysis].to\_csv(}
\NormalTok{    export\_filename,}
\NormalTok{    index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{,           }\CommentTok{\# No row numbers}
\NormalTok{    encoding}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}utf{-}8\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,      }\CommentTok{\# International characters}
\NormalTok{    na\_rep}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}N/A\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,         }\CommentTok{\# Clear missing value indicator}
\NormalTok{    float\_format}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\SpecialCharTok{\%.2f}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}    \CommentTok{\# 2 decimal places for numbers}
\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"✅ Analysis data exported to: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{export\_filename}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"📊 Exported }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(columns\_for\_analysis)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ columns for }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(movie\_ratings)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ movies"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
✅ Analysis data exported to: ./datasets/movie_analysis_final.csv
📊 Exported 6 columns for 2228 movies
\end{verbatim}

require different reading approaches.

\subsection{What You'll Learn}\label{what-youll-learn}

In this section, we'll explore how to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Read text files} with different delimiters (tabs, semicolons,
  etc.)
\item
  \textbf{Handle JSON data} from APIs and web services
\item
  \textbf{Access live data} directly from URLs and APIs
\item
  \textbf{Extract tables} from HTML web pages
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
💡 \textbf{Key Insight}: The same \texttt{pd.read\_csv()} function can
read many text-based formats by adjusting parameters!
\end{quote}

\subsection{Reading Text Files (.txt)}\label{reading-text-files-.txt}

\textbf{Text files offer maximum flexibility} for storing tabular data
with custom delimiters.

\textbf{Key Differences from CSV:}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{CSV files}: Always use commas (\texttt{,}) as delimitersLet's
  read a file where values are separated by tab characters:
\item
  \textbf{Text files}: Can use \textbf{any character} as a delimiter
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Reading Tab-Separated
Files}\label{reading-tab-separated-files}

\textbf{Common Delimiters in Text Files:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Space} (\texttt{}) → Simple space-separated files
\item
  \textbf{Tab character} (\texttt{\textbackslash{}t}) → Creates TSV
  (Tab-Separated Values) files- \textbf{Pipe symbol}
  (\texttt{\textbar{}}) → Used when data contains commas
\item
  \textbf{Semicolon} (\texttt{;}) → Common in European data files
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Read tab{-}separated file using \textbackslash{}t as separator}
\CommentTok{\# Note: We still use pd.read\_csv() but specify the separator}
\NormalTok{movie\_ratings\_txt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movie\_ratings.txt\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, sep}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}t}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{movie\_ratings\_txt.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Rating & IMDB Votes \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

Adapted screenplay & Drama & Fiction & 6.5 & 468 \\
1 & 1 & Major Dundee & 14873 & 14873 & 3800000 & Apr 07 1965 & PG/PG-13
& Adapted screenplay & Western/Musical & Fiction & 6.7 & 2588 \\

Adapted screenplay & Horror/Thriller & Fiction & 5.2 & 7595 \\

\begin{itemize}

  The function automatically handles headers and data types

\CommentTok{\# Different separator examples (these are demonstrations)}

\CommentTok{\# df\_semicolon = pd.read\_csv(\textquotesingle{}file.txt\textquotesingle{}, sep=\textquotesingle{};\textquotesingle{})}

\CommentTok{\# Pipe{-}separated (when data contains commas)}

\subsubsection{Automatic Delimiter
Detection}\label{automatic-delimiter-detection}

Pandas can automatically detect delimiters using the Python engine:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Let pandas automatically detect the delimiter}
\CommentTok{\# This uses the \textquotesingle{}python\textquotesingle{} engine with a \textquotesingle{}sniffer\textquotesingle{} tool}
\ControlFlowTok{try}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{    auto\_detected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/movie\_ratings.txt\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }
\NormalTok{                               sep}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{,           }\CommentTok{\# Auto{-}detect}
\NormalTok{                               engine}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}python\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)    }\CommentTok{\# Use Python engine}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{" Delimiter detected automatically!"}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Shape: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{auto\_detected}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{except} \PreprocessorTok{FileNotFoundError}\NormalTok{:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{" File not found {-} this is just a demonstration"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
 Delimiter detected automatically!
 Shape: (2228, 12)
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{When to use automatic detection:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  ✅ When you're unsure about the delimiter
\item
  ✅ For quick data exploration
\item
  ❌ Avoid in production code (be explicit for reliability)
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
💡 \textbf{Pro Tip}: Always check the
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html}{pandas
documentation} for parameter details!
\end{quote}

\subsection{Reading JSON Data}\label{reading-json-data}

\textbf{JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)} is the \textbf{standard
format for web APIs} and modern data exchange.

\textbf{Why JSON is Everywhere:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Web APIs}: Most modern APIs return JSON data
\item
  \textbf{Mobile Apps}: Standard format for app-server communication
\item
  \textbf{Cloud Services}: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure all use JSON
\item
  \textbf{IoT Devices}: Smart devices send data in JSON format
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Key Advantages over CSV:}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1892}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3919}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4189}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Feature}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{CSV}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{JSON}
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Structure} & Flat tables only & \textbf{Nested /
hierarchical} \\
\textbf{Data Types} & Text and numbers & \textbf{Objects, arrays,
booleans} \\
\textbf{Metadata} & Must be stored separately or encoded in headers &
\textbf{Supports metadata inline (keys + values in the same
document)} \\
\textbf{Complex / Nested Records} & Must be flattened into multiple
columns & \textbf{Native support for nested objects and arrays} \\
\end{longtable}

\subsubsection{Reading JSON with Pandas}\label{reading-json-with-pandas}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  📊 \textbf{Data type inference} (numbers, dates, etc.)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\texttt{pd.read\_json()}} automatically converts JSON data into
pandas DataFrames:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  📋 \textbf{DataFrame conversion} when possible
\item
  🤖 \textbf{Smart detection} of JSON structure
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Automatic Processing:}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  ✅ \textbf{Local files}:
  \texttt{pd.read\_json(\textquotesingle{}data.json\textquotesingle{})}
\item
  ✅ \textbf{URLs}:
  \texttt{pd.read\_json(\textquotesingle{}https://api.example.com/data\textquotesingle{})}
\item
  ✅ \textbf{Various orientations}: Records, index, values, etc.
\item
  ✅ \textbf{JSON strings}: Direct JSON text
\end{itemize}

\end{Highlighting}

\subsubsection{Reading Data from URLs and
APIs}\label{reading-data-from-urls-and-apis}

\textbf{Modern data science often involves accessing live data} from web
APIs (Application Programming Interfaces). This allows you to get
real-time information directly into your analysis pipeline.

\textbf{Using the \texttt{requests} Library}

The \texttt{requests} library is the standard tool for making HTTP
requests in Python. You'll need to install it if not already available:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{pip}\NormalTok{ install requests}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Basic API Request Pattern:} 1. \textbf{Send request} to the API
URL 2. \textbf{Check response} status (success/error) 3. \textbf{Parse
JSON data} into usable format 4. \textbf{Convert to DataFrame} for
analysis

Let's demonstrate with the \textbf{CoinGecko API}, which provides
cryptocurrency market data:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ requests}

\CommentTok{\# Define the API endpoint}
\NormalTok{api\_url }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/coins/markets\textquotesingle{}}

\CommentTok{\# Add parameters to get USD prices for top 10 cryptocurrencies}
\NormalTok{params }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}vs\_currency\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}usd\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,  }\CommentTok{\# Price in US Dollars}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}order\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}market\_cap\_desc\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,  }\CommentTok{\# Sort by market cap}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}per\_page\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{,  }\CommentTok{\# Get top 10 coins}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}page\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,  }\CommentTok{\# First page}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}sparkline\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\VariableTok{False}  \CommentTok{\# Don\textquotesingle{}t include price history}
\NormalTok{\}}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{" Requesting cryptocurrency data from CoinGecko API..."}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Send GET request with parameters}
\NormalTok{response }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ requests.get(api\_url, params}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{params)}

\CommentTok{\# Check HTTP status codes}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Response Status Code: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{response}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{status\_code}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ response.status\_code }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{200}\NormalTok{:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"✅ Request successful!"}\NormalTok{)}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Parse JSON response}
\NormalTok{    crypto\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ response.json()}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Display basic info about the response}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"📊 Received data for }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(crypto\_data)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ cryptocurrencies"}\NormalTok{)}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Show raw JSON structure (first item only)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\SpecialStringTok{ Sample JSON structure:"}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Keys available: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(crypto\_data[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{].keys())}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
    
\ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
    \CommentTok{\# Handle different error codes}
\NormalTok{    error\_messages }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
        \DecValTok{400}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Bad Request {-} Check your parameters"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{401}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Unauthorized {-} API key might be required"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{403}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Forbidden {-} Access denied"}\NormalTok{, }
        \DecValTok{404}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Not Found {-} Invalid endpoint"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{429}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Rate Limited {-} Too many requests"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Server Error {-} Try again later"}
\NormalTok{    \}}
    
\NormalTok{    error\_msg }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ error\_messages.get(response.status\_code, }\StringTok{"Unknown error"}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ Request failed: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{error\_msg}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    crypto\_data }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{None}
\end{Highlighting}

\begin{Shaded}

\NormalTok{api\_url }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\_per\_capita\textquotesingle{}}
\CommentTok{\# Use pandas to read all tables from the webpage}
\NormalTok{wiki\_response }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ requests.get(api\_url)}
\CommentTok{\# Check HTTP status codes}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f" Response Status Code: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{wiki\_response}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{status\_code}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ wiki\_response.status\_code }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{200}\NormalTok{:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"✅ Request successful!"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
    \CommentTok{\# output error message based on the status code}
\NormalTok{    error\_messages }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
        \DecValTok{400}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Bad Request {-} Check your parameters"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{401}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Unauthorized {-} API key might be required"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{403}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Forbidden {-} Access denied"}\NormalTok{, }
        \DecValTok{404}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Not Found {-} Invalid endpoint"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{429}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Rate Limited {-} Too many requests"}\NormalTok{,}
        \DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"Server Error {-} Try again later"}
\NormalTok{    \}}
\NormalTok{    error\_msg }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ error\_messages.get(wiki\_response.status\_code, }\StringTok{"Unknown error"}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ Request failed: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{error\_msg}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
 Response Status Code: 403
❌ Request failed: Forbidden - Access denied
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Understanding HTTP 403 Errors with
Wikipedia}}{Understanding HTTP 403 Errors with Wikipedia}}\label{understanding-http-403-errors-with-wikipedia}

\textbf{Why Wikipedia Returns 403 ``Forbidden'' Errors:}

Wikipedia and many other websites block requests that appear to be
automated bots or scrapers. When you make a request without proper
headers, the server sees it as suspicious and blocks it with a 403
error.

\textbf{Common Causes of 403 Errors:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  ❌ \textbf{Missing User-Agent}: No browser identification
\item
  ❌ \textbf{Suspicious headers}: Looks like automated scraping\\
\item
  ❌ \textbf{Rate limiting}: Too many requests too quickly
\item
  ❌ \textbf{IP blocking}: Your IP has been flagged
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Solution: Add Proper
Headers}}{Solution: Add Proper Headers}}\label{solution-add-proper-headers}

The key is to make your request look like it's coming from a real web
browser by adding appropriate headers:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{headers }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}User{-}Agent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}My Data Analysis Project (your\_email@example.com)\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{url }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\textquotesingle{}}

\CommentTok{\# Pass the headers to read\_html}
\NormalTok{tables }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_html(url, header}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, attrs}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{headers)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let's define a helper function for this purpose

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ read\_html\_tables\_from\_url(url, match}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, user\_agent}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, timeout}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{kwargs):}
    \CommentTok{"""}
\CommentTok{    Read HTML tables from a website URL with error handling and customizable options.}
\CommentTok{    }
\CommentTok{    Parameters:}
\CommentTok{    {-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}}
\CommentTok{    url : str}
\CommentTok{        The website URL to scrape tables from}
\CommentTok{    match : str, optional}
\CommentTok{        String or regex pattern to match tables (passed to pd.read\_html)}
\CommentTok{    user\_agent : str, optional}
\CommentTok{        Custom User{-}Agent header. If None, uses a default Chrome User{-}Agent}
\CommentTok{    timeout : int, default 10}
\CommentTok{        Request timeout in seconds}
\CommentTok{    **kwargs : dict}
\CommentTok{        Additional arguments passed to pd.read\_html()}
\CommentTok{    }
\CommentTok{    Returns:}
\CommentTok{    {-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}}
\CommentTok{    list of DataFrames or None}
\CommentTok{        List of pandas DataFrames (one per table found), or None if error occurs}
\CommentTok{    }
\CommentTok{    Examples:}
\CommentTok{    {-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}{-}}
\CommentTok{    \# Basic usage}
\CommentTok{    tables = read\_html\_tables\_from\_url("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\_per\_capita")}
\CommentTok{    }
\CommentTok{    \# Filter tables containing specific text}
\CommentTok{    tables = read\_html\_tables\_from\_url(url, match="Country")}
\CommentTok{    }
\CommentTok{    \# With custom user agent}
\CommentTok{    tables = read\_html\_tables\_from\_url(url, user\_agent="MyBot/1.0")}
\CommentTok{    """}
    \ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}
    \ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ requests}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Default User{-}Agent if none provided}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ user\_agent }\KeywordTok{is} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        user\_agent }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/91.0.4472.124 Safari/537.36\textquotesingle{}}
    
\NormalTok{    headers }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}User{-}Agent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: user\_agent\}}
    
    \ControlFlowTok{try}\NormalTok{:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"🌐 Fetching data from: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{url}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
        
        \CommentTok{\# Make the HTTP request}
\NormalTok{        response }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ requests.get(url, headers}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{headers, timeout}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{timeout)}
\NormalTok{        response.raise\_for\_status()  }\CommentTok{\# Raise an exception for bad status codes (4xx or 5xx)}
        
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"✅ Successfully retrieved webpage (Status: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{response}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{status\_code}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{)"}\NormalTok{)}
        
        \CommentTok{\# Parse HTML tables}
\NormalTok{        read\_html\_kwargs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}match\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: match\} }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ match }\ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ \{\}}
\NormalTok{        read\_html\_kwargs.update(kwargs)  }\CommentTok{\# Add any additional arguments}
        
\NormalTok{        tables }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_html(response.content, }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{read\_html\_kwargs)}
        
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"📊 Found }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tables)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ table(s) on the page"}\NormalTok{)}
        
        \CommentTok{\# Display table information}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tables:}
            \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\SpecialStringTok{📋 Table Overview:"}\NormalTok{)}
            \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, table }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(tables):}
                \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"  Table }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{i}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{table}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ (rows × columns)"}\NormalTok{)}
                \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ i }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{:  }\CommentTok{\# Limit output for readability}
                    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"  ... and }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tables) }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{5}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ more tables"}\NormalTok{)}
                    \ControlFlowTok{break}
        
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ tables}
        
    \ControlFlowTok{except}\NormalTok{ requests.exceptions.HTTPError }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ err:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ HTTP Error: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{err}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}
    \ControlFlowTok{except}\NormalTok{ requests.exceptions.}\PreprocessorTok{ConnectionError} \ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ err:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ Connection Error: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{err}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}
    \ControlFlowTok{except}\NormalTok{ requests.exceptions.Timeout }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ err:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ Timeout Error: Request took longer than }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{timeout}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ seconds"}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}
    \ControlFlowTok{except}\NormalTok{ requests.exceptions.RequestException }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ err:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ Request Error: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{err}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}
    \ControlFlowTok{except} \PreprocessorTok{ValueError} \ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ err:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ No tables found on the page or parsing error: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{err}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}
    \ControlFlowTok{except} \PreprocessorTok{Exception} \ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ e:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"❌ An unexpected error occurred: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{e}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{None}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now let's demonstrate how to use our new function with different
options:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Example 1: Basic usage {-} Get all tables from GDP Wikipedia page}
\NormalTok{url }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\_per\_capita\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{tables }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ read\_html\_tables\_from\_url(url)}

\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tables:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\SpecialStringTok{ Successfully retrieved }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tables)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ tables!"}\NormalTok{)}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Display info about the largest table}
\NormalTok{    largest\_table }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(tables, key}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\SpecialStringTok{📊 Largest table has }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{largest\_table}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ rows and }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{largest\_table}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ columns"}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Columns: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(largest\_table.columns)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"❌ Failed to retrieve tables"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Independent Study}\label{independent-study-3}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Practice exercise 1: Reading \texttt{.csv}
data}{Practice exercise 1: Reading .csv data}}\label{practice-exercise-1-reading-.csv-data}

Read the file \emph{Top 10 Albums By Year.csv}. This file contains the
top 10 albums for each year from 1990 to 2021. Each row corresponds to a
unique album.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-1}

Print the first 5 rows of the data.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-2}

How many rows and columns are there in the data?

\subsubsection{}\label{section-3}

Print the summary statistics of the data, and answer the following
questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What proportion of albums have 15 or lesser tracks? Mention a range
  for the proportion.
\item
  What is the mean length of a track (in minutes)?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Practice exercise 2: Reading \texttt{.txt}
data}{Practice exercise 2: Reading .txt data}}\label{practice-exercise-2-reading-.txt-data}

Read the file \emph{bestseller\_books.txt}. It contains top 50
best-selling books on amazon from 2009 to 2019. Identify the delimiter
without opening the file with Notepad or a text-editing software. How
many rows and columns are there in the dataset?

Alternatively, you can use the argument \texttt{sep\ =\ None}, and
\texttt{engine\ =\ \textquotesingle{}python\textquotesingle{}}. The
default engine is C. However, the `python' engine has a `sniffer' tool
which may identify the delimiter automatically.

\subsection{Practice exercise 3: Reading HTML
data}\label{practice-exercise-3-reading-html-data}

Read the table(s) consisting of attendance of spectators in FIFA worlds
cup from this \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup}{page}.
Read only those table(s) that have the word \emph{`reaching'} in them.
How many rows and columns are there in the table(s)?

\subsection{Practice exercise 4: Reading JSON
data}\label{practice-exercise-4-reading-json-data}

Read the movies dataset from
\href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega-datasets/master/data/movies.json}{here}.
How many rows and columns are there in the data?

\chapter{Pandas Fundamentals}\label{pandas-fundamentals}

\begin{verbatim}
