\subsection{Pyplot Interface}\label{pyplot-interface}

In the previous chapter, our plotting is completely based on pyplot
interface of Matplotlib, which is just for basic plotting. You can
easily generate plots using pyplot module in the matplotlib library just
by importing \texttt{matplotlib.pyplot} module.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  pyplot interface is a \textbf{state-based interface.} It implicitly
  tracks the plot that it wants to reference
\item
  Simple functions are used to \textbf{add plot elements and/or modify
  the plot} as we need, whenever we need it.
\item
  The Pyplot interface \textbf{shares a lot of similarities in syntax
  and methodology with MATLAB.}
\end{itemize}

However, The \texttt{pyplot} interface has limited functionality in
these two cases:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  when there is a need to make multiple plots
\item
  when we have to make plots that require a lot of customization.
\end{itemize}

For more advanced plotting with Matplotlib, you have to learn
Object-Oriented Interface.

\section{Plotting with Object-Oriented Interface of
Matplotlib}\label{plotting-with-object-oriented-interface-of-matplotlib}

\subsection{Matplotlib Object Anatomy}\label{matplotlib-object-anatomy}

To use Matplotlib's object-oriented interface effectively, it's
important to understand the anatomy of a plot---how different visual
elements are structured within a figure:

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{images/anatomy-of-a-figure.png}}

\subsection{Matplotlib Object
Hierarchy}\label{matplotlib-object-hierarchy}

Matplotlib plots follow a \textbf{hierarchical structure}, with two core
components:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Figure: The overall container for one or more plots.
\item
  Axes: The individual plot area where data is visualized.
\end{itemize}

Each Axes contains further elements such as:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \texttt{Axis} (x-axis and y-axis)
\item
  \texttt{Title}, \texttt{Labels}, \texttt{Ticks}
\item
  Drawable objects like \texttt{Lines}, \texttt{Text}, and
  \texttt{Patches} (collectively called \textbf{Artists})
\end{itemize}

Here's a simplified view of this hierarchy:

\begin{verbatim}
Figure
 └── Axes (1 or more)
      ├── Axis (XAxis, YAxis)
      ├── Title
      ├── Label
      ├── Tick
      └── Artist objects (Lines, Text, Patches, etc.)
\end{verbatim}

Understanding this structure is key to using Matplotlib's
object-oriented interface, as it allows you to \textbf{access and
customize each component directly}.

\subsubsection{Figure}\label{figure}

The outermost object is the figure which is an instance of
\texttt{figure.Figure}. It is the \textbf{top level container} for all
the plot elements. The Figure is the final image that may contain one or
more Axes and it keeps track of all the Axes. Figure is only a container
and you can not plot data on figure.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# To begin with, we create a fiture instance which provides an empty canvas}
\NormalTok{fig }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.figure()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
<Figure size 640x480 with 0 Axes>
\end{verbatim}

Figure is just a container, note that creating figure using
\texttt{plt.figure()} does not automatically create an axes and hence
all you can see is the figure object.

\subsubsection{Axes}\label{axes}

\texttt{Axes} is the instance of \texttt{matplotlib.axes.Axes}. Axes
\textbf{is the area on which data are plotted}. A given figure can
contain many Axes, but a given Axes object can only be in one Figure.

\paragraph{Creating an Axes Object
Explicitly}\label{creating-an-axes-object-explicitly}

In the OOP interface, Axes objects are usually created using
\texttt{plt.subplots()} or \texttt{plt.figure().add\_subplot()}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# A figure only contains one axes by default}
\NormalTok{fig }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.figure()}
\CommentTok{\# add axes to the figure}
\NormalTok{ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ fig.add\_subplot()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-7-output-1.png}}

We create a blank axes (area) for plotting, if we need to add more axes
to the figure

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# create a figure with 4 axes, arranged in 2 rows and 2 columns}
\NormalTok{fig, axes }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-8-output-1.png}}

\paragraph{Components of an Axes
Object}\label{components-of-an-axes-object}

The \texttt{Axes} object contains several elements that make up the plot

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Data plotting area: Contains the data (lines, bars, points, etc.).
\item
  X-axis and Y-axis: Controls the axis limits, labels, and ticks.
\item
  Title and Labels: The overall title and labels for each axis.
\item
  Gridlines: Optional lines to help align the data visually.
\item
  Spines: The borders around the plot.
\item
  Legend: An optional component to explain the data series.
\item
  Annotations: Text or arrows highlighting points of interest.
\end{itemize}

This is what makes the \texttt{Axes} object central to any plot in the
OOP interface of Matplotlib.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# create data for plotting}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x}\OperatorTok{**}\DecValTok{2} 

\CommentTok{\# create a figure and axes}
\NormalTok{fig,ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }

\CommentTok{\# plot the data}
\NormalTok{ax.plot(x,y)}

\CommentTok{\# set the title}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_title(}\StringTok{"Exponential Plot"}\NormalTok{)}
 
\CommentTok{\# set the labels of x and y axes}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_xlabel(}\StringTok{"age"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_ylabel(}\StringTok{"Cell growth"}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# set the limits of x and y axes}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_xlim([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_ylim([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{])}

\CommentTok{\# set the ticks of x and y axes}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_xticks(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{11}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_yticks(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{101}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{))}

\CommentTok{\# add grid}
\NormalTok{ax.grid(}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# add legend}
\NormalTok{ax.legend([}\StringTok{"y = x\^{}2"}\NormalTok{], loc }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"upper left"}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# show the plot}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-9-output-1.png}}

\subsection{Creating Complex Plots with Multiple
Subplots}\label{creating-complex-plots-with-multiple-subplots}

To help illustrate subplots in matplotlib, we can cover two scenarios:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  subplots that don't overlap and
\item
  subplots inside other subplots
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Plotting non-overlapped
subplots}\label{plotting-non-overlapped-subplots}

This is the most common use case, where multiple plots are placed next
to each other in a grid, without overlap. The \texttt{plt.subplots()}
function allows for a clean layout where each plot is contained in its
own space. You can specify the number of rows and columns to create a
grid of subplots.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{flowers\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sns.load\_dataset(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}iris\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{tips\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sns.load\_dataset(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}tips\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{flights\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sns.load\_dataset(}\StringTok{"flights"}\NormalTok{).pivot(index}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"month"}\NormalTok{, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"year"}\NormalTok{, values}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"passengers"}\NormalTok{)}


\NormalTok{fig, axes }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}

\CommentTok{\# Pass the axes into seaborn}
\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{].set\_title(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Sepal Length vs. Sepal Width\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.scatterplot(x}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{flowers\_df.sepal\_length, }
\NormalTok{                y}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{flowers\_df.sepal\_width, }
\NormalTok{                hue}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{flowers\_df.species, }
\NormalTok{                s}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{, }
\NormalTok{                ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}

\CommentTok{\# Use the axes for plotting}
\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{].set\_title(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Distribution of Sepal Width\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.histplot(flowers\_df.sepal\_width, ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{].legend([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Setosa\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Versicolor\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Virginica\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}

\CommentTok{\# Pass the axes into seaborn}
\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{].set\_title(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Restaurant bills\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.barplot(x}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}day\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, y}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\_bill\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, hue}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}sex\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, data}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{tips\_df, ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}

\CommentTok{\# Pass the axes into seaborn}
\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{].set\_title(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Flight traffic\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.heatmap(flights\_df, cmap}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Blues\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{axes[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{plt.tight\_layout(pad}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-10-output-1.png}}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The \texttt{plt.tight\_layout()} ensures the subplots do not overlap
  by adjusting the spacing automatically.
\item
  Seaborn and pandas are wrappers of Matplotlib. To create a
  Seaborn/pandas plot in a specific Matplotlib subplot, you pass the
  \texttt{ax} parameter to the its plotting function. This allows you to
  use their visualization capabilities while fully controlling the
  layout of the plot using Matplotlib's \texttt{plt.subplots()}
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Plotting Nested Subplots (Subplots Inside Other
Subplots)}\label{plotting-nested-subplots-subplots-inside-other-subplots}

You can create a subplot inside another plot using \texttt{add\_axes()}
or \texttt{inset\_axes()} from matplotlib's \texttt{Axes} object. This
is useful for creating insets or focusing on a specific region within a
larger plot.

Syntax of \texttt{add\_axes()}

\texttt{ax\ =\ fig.add\_axes({[}left,\ bottom,\ width,\ height{]})}

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  left: The x-position (horizontal starting point) of the axes, as a
  fraction of the figure width (0 to 1).
\item
  bottom: The y-position (vertical starting point) of the axes, as a
  fraction of the figure height (0 to 1).
\item
  width: The width of the axes, as a fraction of the figure width (0 to
  1).
\item
  height: The height of the axes, as a fraction of the figure height (0
  to 1).
\end{itemize}

Below is an example demonstrating the use of \texttt{add\_axes()}. You
can also explore the \texttt{inset\_axes()} method for creating inset
plots with more flexibility

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# create inset axes within the main plot axes  }

\NormalTok{np.random.seed(}\DecValTok{19680801}\NormalTok{)  }\CommentTok{\# Fixing random state for reproducibility.}

\CommentTok{\# create some data to use for the plot}
\NormalTok{dt }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.001}
\NormalTok{t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{10.0}\NormalTok{, dt)}
\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{t[:}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{/} \FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{)  }\CommentTok{\# impulse response}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.randn(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(t))}
\NormalTok{s }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.convolve(x, r)[:}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(x)] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ dt  }\CommentTok{\# colored noise}

\NormalTok{fig, main\_ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots()}
\NormalTok{main\_ax.plot(t, s)}
\NormalTok{main\_ax.set\_xlim(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{main\_ax.set\_ylim(}\FloatTok{1.1} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(s), }\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(s))}
\NormalTok{main\_ax.set\_xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}time (s)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{main\_ax.set\_ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}current (nA)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{main\_ax.set\_title(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Gaussian colored noise\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# this is an inset axes over the main axes}
\NormalTok{right\_inset\_ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ fig.add\_axes([}\FloatTok{.65}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.6}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{], facecolor}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}k\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{right\_inset\_ax.hist(s, }\DecValTok{400}\NormalTok{, density}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{right\_inset\_ax.}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(title}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Probability\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, xticks}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[], yticks}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[])}

\CommentTok{\# this is another inset axes over the main axes}
\NormalTok{left\_inset\_ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ fig.add\_axes([}\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.6}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{], facecolor}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}k\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{left\_inset\_ax.plot(t[:}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(r)], r)}
\NormalTok{left\_inset\_ax.}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(title}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Impulse response\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, xlim}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{.2}\NormalTok{), xticks}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[], yticks}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[])}

\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-11-output-1.png}}

\subsubsection{Bar plots with Pandas}\label{bar-plots-with-pandas}

\textbf{Purpose of bar plots}: Barplots are used to visualize any
aggregate statistics of a continuous variable with respect to the
categories or levels of a categorical variable.

Bar plots can be made using the pandas \texttt{bar} function with the
DataFrame or Series, just like the line plots and scatterplots.

Let us visualise the locations from where the the complaints are coming.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ nyc\_party\_complaints[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Location Type\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].value\_counts().plot.bar(ylabel }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Number of complaints\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax.yaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-13-output-1.png}}

In the above code, we use \texttt{ax.yaxis.set\_major\_formatter} to
format the y-axis labels in a currency style. From the above plot, we
observe that most of the complaints come from residential buildings and
houses, as one may expect.

For categorical variables, we can use the \texttt{.value\_counts()}
method to get the statistical frequency of each unique value.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{nyc\_party\_complaints[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Location Type\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].value\_counts()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Location Type

Street/Sidewalk                42353
Store/Commercial               17617
Club/Bar/Restaurant            15766
Park/Playground                 3036

Name: count, dtype: int64
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\NormalTok{ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ nyc\_party\_complaints[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Month\_of\_the\_year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].value\_counts().sort\_index().plot.bar(ylabel }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Number of complaints\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{                                                                              xlabel }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"Month"}\NormalTok{)}

\subsubsection{Bar plots with confidence intervals with
Seaborn}\label{bar-plots-with-confidence-intervals-with-seaborn}

We'll group the data to obtain the total complaints for each
\emph{Location Type, Borough, Month\_of\_the\_year, and
Hour\_of\_the\_day}. Note that you'll learn grouping data in later
chapters, so you may ignore the next code block. The grouping is done to
shape the data in a suitable form for visualization.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Grouping the data to make it suitable for visualization using Seaborn. Ignore this code block until learn chapter 9.}
\NormalTok{nyc\_complaints\_grouped }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ nyc\_party\_complaints[[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Location Type\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Borough\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Month\_of\_the\_year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Latitude\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Hour\_of\_the\_day\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]].groupby([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Location Type\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Borough\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Month\_of\_the\_year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Hour\_of\_the\_day\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Latitude\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].agg([(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}complaints\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}count\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)]).reset\_index()}
\NormalTok{nyc\_complaints\_grouped.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us create a bar plot visualizing the average number of complaints

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sns.barplot(x}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"Hour\_of\_the\_day"}\NormalTok{, y }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}complaints\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,  data}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{nyc\_complaints\_grouped)}

\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-21-output-1.png}}

From the above plot, we observe that most of the complaints are made
around midnight. However, interestingly, there are some complaints at
each hour of the day.

Note that the above barplot shows the mean number of complaints in a
month at each hour of the day. The black lines are the 95\% confidence
intervals of the mean number of complaints.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\texttt{pyplot}: a convenience wrapper
around the object-oriented
interface}{pyplot: a convenience wrapper around the object-oriented interface}}\label{pyplot-a-convenience-wrapper-around-the-object-oriented-interface}

While the pyplot interface is simpler for quick, basic plots, it
ultimately wraps around the object-oriented structure of Matplotlib,
meaning that it's built on top of the object-oriented interface.

\section{Creating Subplots with
Seaborn}\label{creating-subplots-with-seaborn}

We previously demonstrated how Seaborn integrates seamlessly with
Matplotlib's object-oriented interface, allowing you to pass the
\texttt{ax} argument to any Seaborn function, thereby directing the plot
to a specific axis within a subplot grid.

Additionally, Seaborn offers a more convenient and simplified approach
to creating subplots, thanks to its high-level functions and built-in
integration with Matplotlib. Here's how Seaborn makes working with
subplots easier:

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using
\texttt{Facetgrid}}{Using Facetgrid}}\label{using-facetgrid}

Seaborn's \texttt{FacetGrid} function make it very easy to create facet
grids or subplots based on data dimensions (such as categories), which
would require more manual effort with Matplotlib.

You can use the \texttt{row} and \texttt{col} parameters to control how
the data is split into subplots along these dimensions.

\begin{Shaded}

\NormalTok{tips\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sns.load\_dataset(}\StringTok{"tips"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{tips\_df.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\NormalTok{g.}\BuiltInTok{map}\NormalTok{(sns.histplot, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\_bill\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}r\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using
\texttt{Pairplot}}{Using Pairplot}}\label{using-pairplot}

Pairplots are used to visualize the association between all
variable-pairs in the data. In other words, pairplots simultaneously
visualize the scatterplots between all variable-pairs.

Let us visualize the pair-wise association of tips variables in the tips
dataset

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sns.pairplot(tips\_df )}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-26-output-1.png}}

Let us visualize the pair-wise association of nutrition variables in the
starbucks drinks data.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{starbucks\_drinks }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}datasets/starbucks{-}menu{-}nutrition{-}drinks.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.pairplot(starbucks\_drinks)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Advanced_Data_Visualization_files/figure-pdf/cell-27-output-1.png}}

In the above pairplot, note that:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The histograms on the diagonal of the grid show the distribution of
  each of the variables.
\item
  Instead of a histogram, we can visualize the density plot with the
  argument kde = True.
\item
  The scatterplots in the rest of the grid are the pair-wise plots of
  all the variables.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Static Plots with
GeoPandas}\label{static-plots-with-geopandas}

A \textbf{shapefile} is a widely-used format for storing geographic
information system (GIS) data, specifically vector data. It contains
geometries (like points, lines, and polygons) that represent features on
the earth's surface, along with associated attributes for each feature,
such as names, populations, or other data relevant to the feature.

\subsubsection{Components of a
Shapefile}\label{components-of-a-shapefile}

A shapefile isn't a single file but a collection of files with the same
name and different extensions, which work together to store geographic
and attribute data:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{.shp}: Stores the geometry (shapes of features, like points,
  lines, polygons).
\item
  \texttt{.shx}: Contains an index to quickly access geometries in the
  .shp file.
\item
  \texttt{.dbf}: A table storing attributes associated with each
  feature.
\end{itemize}

There may also be other optional files (e.g., .prj for projection
information).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Create figure and axis}
\NormalTok{fig, ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{))}

\CommentTok{\# Plot your GeoDataFrame}
\NormalTok{chicago }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gpd.read\_file(}\VerbatimStringTok{r\textquotesingle{}datasets/chicago\_boundaries\textbackslash{}geo\_export\_26bce2f2{-}c163{-}42a9{-}9329{-}9ca6e082c5e9.shp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{chicago.plot(column}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}community\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ax, legend}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{, legend\_kwds}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{\{}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}ncol\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}bbox\_to\_anchor\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: (}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)\})}

\CommentTok{\# Add title (optional)}
\NormalTok{plt.title(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Chicago Community Areas\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Next, we will add the Divvy bicycle stations on top of the chicago

\subsection{Dataset: Bicycle Sharing in
Chicago}\label{dataset-bicycle-sharing-in-chicago}

Divvy is Chicagoland's bike share system (in collaboration with Chicago
Department of Transportation), with 6,000 bikes available at 570+
stations across Chicago and Evanston. Divvy provides residents and
visitors with a convenient, fun and affordable transportation option for
getting around and exploring Chicago.

Divvy, like other bike share systems, consists of a fleet of specially
designed, sturdy and durable bikes that are locked into a network of
docking stations throughout the region. The bikes can be unlocked from
one station and returned to any other station in the system. People use
bike share to explore Chicago, commute to work or school, run errands,
get to appointments or social engagements, and more.

Divvy is available for use 24 hours/day, 7 days/week, 365 days/year, and
riders have access to all bikes and stations across the system.

We will be using divvy trips in the year of 2013

In the Divvy dataset, each trip record includes the latitude and

precise locations of each station, making it possible to visually

stations on a map, we can better understand the geographic distribution
and accessibility of Divvy's bike-sharing network.

\subsection{Interactive Plotting}\label{interactive-plotting}

Alongside static plots, \texttt{geopandas} can create interactive maps
based on the
\href{https://python-visualization.github.io/folium/latest/}{folium}
library.

Creating maps for interactive exploration mirrors the API of static
\href{https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/reference/api/geopandas.GeoDataFrame.plot.html}{plots}
in an
\href{https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/reference/api/geopandas.GeoDataFrame.explore.html}{explore()}
method of a GeoSeries or GeoDataFrame.

Here's an explanation of how \texttt{explore()} works and its key
features:

Key Features of \texttt{explore()}:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Interactive Map Display:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When you call explore() on a Geodataframe (gdf), it launches an
  interactive map widget directly within your Jupyter notebook.
\item
  This map allows you to pan, zoom, and interact with the geometries
  (points, lines, polygons) in your Geodataframe.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Layer Control:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  explore() automatically adds the geometries from your Geodataframe as
  layers on the map.
\item
  Each geometry type (points, lines, polygons) is displayed with
  appropriate styling and markers.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  Tooltip Information:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When you hover over a geometry in the map, explore() displays tooltip
  information that typically includes attribute data associated with
  that geometry.
\item
  This feature is useful for inspecting specific details or properties
  of individual features in your geospatial dataset.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Search and Filter:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  explore() provides basic search and filter functionalities directly on
  the map.
\item

\textbf{Purpose:} Histogram and density plots visualize the distribution
of a continuous variable.

A histogram plots the number of observations occurring within discrete,
evenly spaced bins of a random variable, to visualize the distribution
of the variable. It may be considered a special case of a bar plot as
bars are used to plot the observation counts.

A density plot uses a kernel density estimate to approximate the
distribution of random variable.

\section{Handling missing data}\label{handling-missing-data}

Missing values in a dataset can occur due to several reasons such as
breakdown of measuring equipment, accidental removal of observations,
lack of response by respondents, error on the part of the researcher,
etc.

Let us read the dataset \emph{GDP\_missing\_data.csv}, in which we have
randomly removed some values, or put missing values in some of the
columns.

We'll also read \emph{GDP\_complete\_data.csv}, in which we have not
removed any values. We'll use this data later to assess the accuracy of
our guess or estimate of missing values in
\emph{GDP\_missing\_data.csv}.

\subsection{Types of Missing Values}\label{types-of-missing-values}

In data science, missing values typically fall into three main types,
each requiring different handling strategies:

\subsubsection{Missing Completely at Random
(MCAR)}\label{missing-completely-at-random-mcar}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Definition}: Missing values are entirely independent of any
  variables in the dataset.
\item
  \textbf{Example}: A respondent accidentally skips a question on a
  survey.
\item
  \textbf{Impact}: MCAR data can usually be ignored or imputed without
  biasing the analysis.
\item
  \textbf{Handling}: Simple imputation methods, like filling with mean
  or median values, are often appropriate.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Missing at Random (MAR)}\label{missing-at-random-mar}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Definition}: The likelihood of a value being missing is
  related to other observed variables but not to the missing data
  itself.
\item
  \textbf{Example}: People with higher incomes may be less likely to
  report their spending, but income data itself is not missing.
\item
  \textbf{Impact}: Ignoring MAR values may bias results, so careful
  imputation based on related variables is recommended.
\item
  \textbf{Handling}: More complex imputation methods, like conditional
  mean imputation or predictive modeling, are suitable.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Missing Not at Random
(MNAR)}\label{missing-not-at-random-mnar}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Definition}: The probability of missingness is related to the
  missing data itself, meaning the value is systematically missing.
\item
  \textbf{Example}: Patients with severe health conditions might be less
  likely to report their health status, or students with low scores may
  be less likely to submit their grades.
\item
  \textbf{Impact}: MNAR is the most challenging type, as missing values
  may introduce significant bias.
\item
  \textbf{Handling}: Solutions often include sensitivity analysis, data
  augmentation, or modeling techniques that account for the missing
  mechanism, though sometimes domain-specific approaches are necessary.
\end{itemize}

Understanding the type of missing data helps in selecting the right
imputation method and mitigating potential biases in the analysis.

\subsubsection{Questions}\label{questions}

\paragraph{}\label{section-47}

Why can we ignore observations with missing values without risking
skewing the analysis or trends in the case of \textbf{Missing Completely
at Random (MCAR)}?

\paragraph{}\label{section-48}

Why could ignoring missing values lead to biased results for
\textbf{Missing at Random (MAR)} and \textbf{Missing Not at Random
(MNAR)} data?

\paragraph{}\label{section-49}

For the datset consisting of GDP per capita, think of hypothetical
scenarios in which the missing values of GDP per capita can correspond
to \textbf{MCAR / MAR / MNAR}.

\subsection{Methods for Handling missing
values}\label{methods-for-handling-missing-values}

\subsubsection{Removing Missing values}\label{removing-missing-values}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Row/Column Removal}: Use {[}\texttt{df.dropna()}{]}
  (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dropna.html)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    When to Use: if the missing values are few or the rows/columns are
    not critical.
  \item
    Risks: Can reduce the dataset's size, potentially losing valuable
    information.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Let us drop the rows containing even a single value from
\texttt{gdp\_missing\_values\_data}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_no\_missing\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.dropna()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By default, \texttt{df.dropna()} will drop any row that contains at
least one missing value, leaving only the rows that are completely free
of missing values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Shape of gdp\_no\_missing\_data}
\NormalTok{gdp\_no\_missing\_data.shape}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(42, 12)
\end{verbatim}

Using \texttt{df.dropna()} to remove rows with missing values can
sometimes lead to a significant reduction in data, which can be
problematic if much of the data is valuable and non-missing. For
example:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Impact of Default Behavior}: Dropping rows with even a single
  missing value reduced the number of rows from 155 to 42! This drastic
  reduction happens because, by default, dropna() removes any row with
  at least one missing value, keeping only rows that are completely
  complete.
\item
  \textbf{Loss of Non-Missing Data}: Even though some columns may have
  very few missing values (e.g., at most 10), using dropna() without
  modification results in losing all non-missing data in affected rows.
  This is typically a poor choice, especially when valuable, non-missing
  data is removed unnecessarily.
\end{itemize}

To avoid losing too much data, you can adjust the behavior of
\texttt{dropna()} using these parameters:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{how} Parameter

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Controls the criteria for dropping rows or columns.
  \item
    \texttt{how=\textquotesingle{}any\textquotesingle{}} (default):
    Drops rows or columns if any values are missing.
  \item
    `how=`all': Drops rows or columns only if all values are missing
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \texttt{thresh} Parameter

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Sets a minimum number of non-missing values required to retain the
    row or column.
  \item
    Useful when you want to keep rows or columns with substantial, but
    not complete, data.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

If a few values of a column are missing, we can possibly estimate them
using the rest of the data, so that we can (hopefully) maximize the
information that can be extracted from the data. However, if most of the
values of a column are missing, it may be harder to estimate its values.

In this dataset, we see that around 50\% values of the
\texttt{contraception} column is missing. Thus, we'll drop the column as
it may be hard to impute its values based on a relatively small number
of non-missing values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Deleting column with missing values in almost half of the observations}
\NormalTok{gdp\_missing\_values\_data.drop([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}contraception\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,inplace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{gdp\_missing\_values\_data.shape}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(155, 11)
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Imputing Missing values}\label{imputing-missing-values}

There are an unlimited number of ways to impute missing values. Some
imputation methods are provided in the
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/missing_data.html}{Pandas
documentation}.

The best way to impute them will depend on the problem:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{For MCAR}: Simple imputation is generally acceptable.
\item
  \textbf{For MAR}: Imputation should consider relationships with other
  variables, such as using conditional mean imputation.
\item
  \textbf{For MNAR}: Imputation requires careful analysis, and domain
  knowledge is essential to avoid bias.
\end{itemize}

Below are some of the most common methods. Recall that we randomly
introduced missing values in \texttt{gdp\_missing\_values\_data}, while
the actual values are preserved in \texttt{gdp\_complete\_data}.

We will apply these methods to \texttt{gdp\_missing\_values\_data}. To
evaluate each method's effectiveness in imputing missing values, we'll
compare the imputed gdpPerCapita values with the actual values and
calculate the \texttt{Root\ Mean\ Square\ Error} (RMSE).

To visualize the imputed vs actual values, let's define a helper
function

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Index of rows with missing values for GDP per capita}
\NormalTok{null\_ind\_gdpPC }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.index[gdp\_missing\_values\_data.gdpPerCapita.isnull()]}

\CommentTok{\#Defining a function to plot the imputed values vs actual values }
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted(y):}
\NormalTok{    fig, ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    plt.rc(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}xtick\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, labelsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }
\NormalTok{    plt.rc(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}ytick\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, labelsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }
\NormalTok{    x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_complete\_data.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}
    \CommentTok{\# y = y.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}]}
\NormalTok{    plt.scatter(x,y.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{    z}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{np.polyfit(x,y.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    p}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{np.poly1d(z)}
\NormalTok{    plt.plot(x,x,color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}orange\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Actual GDP per capita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,fontsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Imputed GDP per capita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,fontsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    ax.yaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    plt.rc(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}axes\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, labelsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)  }\CommentTok{\# Set all axis labels to fontsize 10}
    \CommentTok{\# plt.title(\textquotesingle{}Actual vs Imputed values for GDP per capita\textquotesingle{},fontsize=20)}
\NormalTok{    rmse }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(np.mean((y.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x)}\OperatorTok{**}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    plt.text(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{50000}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}RMSE = }\SpecialCharTok{\%.2f}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\OperatorTok{\%}\NormalTok{rmse, fontsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{Mean/Median/Mode Imputation}\label{meanmedianmode-imputation}

This approach replaces missing values with the mean or median of the
column.

Let's impute missing values in the column by substituting them with the
average of the non-missing values. Imputing with the mean tends to
minimize the sum of squared differences between actual values and
imputed values, especially in cases where data is Missing Completely at
Random (MCAR). However, this might not hold true for other types of
missing data, such as Missing at Random (MAR) or Missing Not at Random
(MNAR).

Let us impute missing values in the column as the average of the
non-missing values of the column. The sum of squared differences between
actual values and the imputed values is likely to be smaller if we
impute using the mean. However, this may not be true in cases other than
MCAR (Missing completely at random).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Extracting the columns with missing values}
\NormalTok{columns\_with\_missing }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [col }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ col }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.columns }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data[col].isnull().}\BuiltInTok{any}\NormalTok{()]}
\NormalTok{columns\_with\_missing}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
['economicActivityFemale',
 'lifeMale',
 'infantMortality',
 'gdpPerCapita',
 'economicActivityMale',
 'illiteracyMale',
 'illiteracyFemale',
 'lifeFemale']
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Imputing missing values using the mean}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_mean }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data[columns\_with\_missing].fillna(gdp\_missing\_values\_data[columns\_with\_missing].mean())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted(gdp\_imputed\_data\_mean)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-15-output-1.png}}

Here, since all columns with missing values are numerical, we could use
the mean to impute these values. Using the mean is generally suitable
only for numerical data, as it represents a central tendency specific to
numbers. For categorical data, however, mean imputation would be
inappropriate. Instead, the mode, which identifies the most frequently
occurring value, is a more suitable choice for imputing missing values
in categorical columns.

\paragraph{Conditional Imputation: Use other related variables to
predict missing
values}\label{conditional-imputation-use-other-related-variables-to-predict-missing-values}

There are three approaches within this category; please see the details
below.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Imputing missing values based on correlated variables in the
  data}
\end{itemize}

If a variable is highly correlated with another variable in the dataset,
we can approximate its missing values using the trendline with the
highly correlated variable.

Let us visualize the distribution of GDP per capita for different
continents.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.rcParams[}\StringTok{"figure.figsize"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.boxplot(x }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,y}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-16-output-1.png}}

We observe that there is a distinct difference between the GDPs per
capita of some of the contents. Let us impute the missing GDP per capita
of a country as the mean GDP per capita of the corresponding continent.
This imputation should be better than imputing the missing GDP per
capita as the mean of all the non-missing values, as the GDP per capita
of a country is likely to be closer to the mean GDP per capita of the
continent, rather the mean GDP per capita of the whole world.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Finding the mean GDP per capita of the continent {-} please defer the understanding of this code to chapter 9.}
\NormalTok{avg\_gdpPerCapita }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].groupby(gdp\_missing\_values\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]).mean()}
\NormalTok{avg\_gdpPerCapita}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
continent
Africa            7638.178571
Asia             25922.750000
Europe           45455.303030
North America    19625.210526
Oceania          15385.857143
South America    15360.909091
Name: gdpPerCapita, dtype: float64
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Creating a copy of missing data to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_group\_mean }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.copy()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Replacing missing GDP per capita with the mean GDP per capita for the corresponding continent}

\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_group\_mean.gdpPerCapita }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{\textbackslash{}}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_group\_mean[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].fillna(gdp\_imputed\_data\_group\_mean[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{map}\NormalTok{(avg\_gdpPerCapita))}
\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted(gdp\_imputed\_data\_group\_mean)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-19-output-1.png}}

Note that the imputed values are closer to the actual values, and the
RMSE has further reduced as expected.

Suppose we wish to impute the missing values of each numeric column with
the average of the non-missing values of the respective column
corresponding to the continent of the observation. The above logic can
be extended to each column as shown in the code below.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{all\_columns\_imputed\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.iloc[:,[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{]].}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x:}\OperatorTok{\textbackslash{}}
\NormalTok{x.fillna(gdp\_imputed\_data\_group\_mean[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{map}\NormalTok{(x.groupby(gdp\_missing\_values\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]).mean())))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Using Regression}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Let us identify the variable highly correlated with GDP per capita.}
\NormalTok{gdp\_missing\_values\_data.select\_dtypes(include}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}number\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{).corrwith(gdp\_missing\_values\_data.gdpPerCapita)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
economicActivityFemale    0.078332
lifeMale                  0.579850
infantMortality          -0.572201
gdpPerCapita              1.000000
economicActivityMale     -0.134108
illiteracyMale           -0.479143
illiteracyFemale         -0.448273
lifeFemale                0.615954
dtype: float64
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#The variable *lifeFemale* has the strongest correlation with GDP per capita. Let us use it to impute missing values of GDP per capita.}

\CommentTok{\#  Extract the variables lifeFemale and GDP per capita}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.lifeFemale}
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.gdpPerCapita}

\CommentTok{\#  Identify non{-}missing indices}
\NormalTok{idx\_non\_missing }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.isfinite(x) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ np.isfinite(y)}

\CommentTok{\# Fit a linear regression model (degree=1) to predict GDP per capita given lifeFemale}
\NormalTok{slope\_intercept\_trendline }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.polyfit(x[idx\_non\_missing],y[idx\_non\_missing],}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)   }\CommentTok{\#Finding the slope and intercept for the trendline}
\NormalTok{compute\_y\_given\_x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.poly1d(slope\_intercept\_trendline)}

\CommentTok{\#Creating a copy of missing data to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_lr }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.copy()}

\CommentTok{\#Imputing missing values of GDP per capita using the linear regression model}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_lr.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{compute\_y\_given\_x(gdp\_missing\_values\_data.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeFemale\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted(gdp\_imputed\_data\_lr)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-23-output-1.png}}

\textbf{KNN: K-nearest neighbor}

In this method, we'll impute the missing value of the variable as the
mean value of the \(K\)-nearest neighbors having non-missing values for
that variable. The neighbors to a data-point are identified based on
their Euclidean distance to the point in terms of the standardized
values of rest of the variables in the data.

Let's consider a toy example to understand missing value imputation by
KNN. Suppose we have to impute missing values in a toy dataset, named as
\texttt{toy\_data} having 4 observations and 3 variables.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Toy example {-} A 4x3 array with missing values}
\NormalTok{nan }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.nan}
\NormalTok{toy\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, nan], [}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{], [nan, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{], [}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{]])}
\NormalTok{toy\_data}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array([[ 1.,  2., nan],
       [ 3.,  4.,  3.],
       [nan,  6.,  5.],
       [ 8.,  8.,  7.]])
\end{verbatim}

We'll use some functions from the \emph{sklearn} library to perform the
KNN imputation. It is much easier to directly use the algorithm from
\emph{sklearn}, instead of coding it from scratch.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Library to compute pair{-}wise Euclidean distance between all observations in the data}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ sklearn }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ metrics}

\CommentTok{\#Library to impute missing values with the KNN algorithm}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ sklearn }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ impute}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We'll use the \emph{sklearn} function
\href{https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.pairwise.nan_euclidean_distances.html}{nan\_euclidean\_distances()}
to compute the Euclidean distance between all pairs of observations in
the data.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#This is the distance matrix containing the distance of the ith observation from the jth observation at the (i,j) position in the matrix}
\NormalTok{metrics.pairwise.nan\_euclidean\_distances(toy\_data,toy\_data)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array([[ 0.        ,  3.46410162,  6.92820323, 11.29158979],
       [ 3.46410162,  0.        ,  3.46410162,  7.54983444],
       [ 6.92820323,  3.46410162,  0.        ,  3.46410162],
       [11.29158979,  7.54983444,  3.46410162,  0.        ]])
\end{verbatim}

Note that the size of the above matrix is 4x4. This is because the
\((i,j)^{th}\) element of the matrix is the distance of the \(i^{th}\)
observation from the \(j^{th}\) observation. The matrix is symmetric
because the distance of \(i^{th}\) observation to the \(j^{th}\)
observation is the same as the distance of the \(j^{th}\) observation to
the \(i^{th}\) observation.

We'll use the \emph{sklearn} function
\href{https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.impute.KNNImputer.html}{KNNImputer()}
to impute the missing value of a column in \texttt{toy\_data} as the
mean of the values of the \(K\) nearest neighbors to the observation
that have non-missing values for that column.

Let us impute the missing values in \texttt{toy\_data} using the values
of \(K=2\) nearest neighbors from the corresponding observation.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#imputing missing values with 2 nearest neighbors, where the neighbors have equal weights}

\CommentTok{\#Define an object of type KNNImputer}
\NormalTok{imputer }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ impute.KNNImputer(n\_neighbors}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\#Use the object method \textquotesingle{}fit\_transform\textquotesingle{} to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{imputer.fit\_transform(toy\_data)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array([[1. , 2. , 4. ],
       [3. , 4. , 3. ],
       [5.5, 6. , 5. ],
       [8. , 8. , 7. ]])
\end{verbatim}

The third observation was the closest to the \(2nd\) and \(4th\)
observations based on the Euclidean distance matrix. Thus, the missing
value in the \(3rd\) row of the \texttt{toy\_data} has been imputed as
the mean of the values in the \(2nd\) and \(4th\) observations for the
corresponding column. Similarly, the \(1st\) observation is the closest
to the \(2nd\) and \(3rd\) observations. Thus the missing value in the
\(1st\) row of \texttt{toy\_data} has been imputed as the mean of the
values in the \(1st\) and \(2nd\) observations for the corresponding
column.

Let us use KNN to impute the missing values of \texttt{gdpPerCapita} in
\texttt{gdp\_missing\_values\_data}. We'll use only the numeric columns
of the data in imputing the missing values. Also, we'll ignore
\texttt{contraception} as it has a lot of missing values, and thus may
not be useful.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Considering numeric columns in the data to use KNN}
\NormalTok{num\_cols }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}\OperatorTok{+}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{9}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{num\_cols}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
\end{verbatim}

Before computing the pair-wise Euclidean distance of observations, we
must standardize the data so that all columns are at the same scale.
This will avoid columns with a higher magnitude of values having a
higher weight in determining the Euclidean distance. Unless there is a
reason to give a higher weight to a column, we assume all columns to
have the same weight in the Euclidean distance computation.

We can use the code below to scale the data. However, after imputing the
missing values, the data is to be scaled back to the original scale, so
that each variable is in the same units as in the original dataset.
However, if the code below is used, we'll lose the orginal scale of each
of the columns.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Scaling data to compute equally weighted distances from the \textquotesingle{}k\textquotesingle{} nearest neighbors}
\NormalTok{scaled\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.iloc[:,num\_cols].}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x:(x}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x.}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{())}\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{(x.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{()}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x.}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{()))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To alleviate the problem of losing the orignial scale of the data, we'll
use the
\href{https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler.html}{MinMaxScaler}
object of the \emph{sklearn} library. The object will store the original
scale of the data, which will help transform the data back to the
original scale once the missing values have been imputed in the
standardized data.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Scaling data {-} using sklearn}

\CommentTok{\#Create an object of type MinMaxScaler}
\NormalTok{scaler }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sk.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler()}

\CommentTok{\#Use the object method \textquotesingle{}fit\_transform\textquotesingle{} to scale the values to a standard uniform distribution}
\NormalTok{scaled\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(scaler.fit\_transform(gdp\_missing\_values\_data.iloc[:,num\_cols]))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Imputing missing values with KNNImputer}

\CommentTok{\#Define an object of type KNNImputer}
\NormalTok{imputer }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ impute.KNNImputer(n\_neighbors}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, weights}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"uniform"}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\#Use the object method \textquotesingle{}fit\_transform\textquotesingle{} to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{imputed\_arr }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ imputer.fit\_transform(scaled\_data)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Scaling back the scaled array to obtain the data at the original scale}

\CommentTok{\#Use the object method \textquotesingle{}inverse\_transform\textquotesingle{} to scale back the values to the original scale of the data}
\NormalTok{unscaled\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scaler.inverse\_transform(imputed\_arr)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Note the method imputes the missing value of all the columns}
\CommentTok{\#However, we are interested in imputing the missing values of only the \textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{} column}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_knn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.copy()}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_knn.loc[:,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ unscaled\_data[:,}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Visualizing the accuracy of missing value imputation with KNN}
\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted(gdp\_imputed\_data\_knn)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-34-output-1.png}}

Note that the RMSE is the lowest in this method. It is because this
method imputes missing values as the average of the values of
``similar'' observations, which is smarter and more robust than the
previous methods.

We chose \(K=3\) in the missing value imputation for GDP per capita.
However, the value of \(K\) is typically chosen using a method known as
cross validation. We'll learn about cross-validation in the next course
of the sequence.

\paragraph{Forward Fill/Backward Fill}\label{forward-fillbackward-fill}

To fill missing values in a column by copying the value of the previous
or next non-missing observation, we can use forward fill (propagating
the last valid observation forward) or backward fill (propagating the
next valid observation backward).

Below, we demonstrate forward fill. To perform backward fill instead,
simply replace \texttt{ffill} with \texttt{bfill}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Filling missing values: Method 1{-} Naive way}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_ffill }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_values\_data.ffill()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us next check how good is this method in imputing missing values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted(gdp\_imputed\_data\_ffill)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-36-output-1.png}}

We observe that the accuracy of imputation is poor as GDP per capita can
vary a lot across countries, and the data is not sorted by GDP per
capita. There is no reason why the GDP per capita of a country should be
close to the GDP per capita of the country in the observation above it.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Checking if any missing values are remaining}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data\_ffill.isnull().}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Outlier detection and
handling}\label{outlier-detection-and-handling}

An outlier is an observation that is significantly different from the
rest of the data. Outlier detection and handling are important in data
science because outliers can significantly impact the quality, accuracy,
and interpretability of data analysis and model performance. Here are
the main reasons why it's crucial to address outliers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Preventing Skewed Results:} Outliers can distort statistical
  measures, such as the mean and standard deviation, leading to
  misleading interpretations of the data. For example, a few extreme
  values can inflate the mean, making the data seem larger than it is in
  reality.
\item
  \textbf{Improving Model Accuracy:} Many machine learning algorithms
  are sensitive to outliers and can perform poorly if outliers are
  present. For instance, in linear regression, outliers can
  disproportionately affect the model by pulling the line of best fit
  toward them, reducing predictive accuracy.
\item
  \textbf{Enhancing Robustness of Models:} Identifying and handling
  outliers can make models more robust and stable. By minimizing the
  influence of extreme values, models become less sensitive to noise,
  which improves generalization and reduces overfitting.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Outlier detection}\label{outlier-detection}

Outlier detection is crucial for identifying unusual values in your data
that may need to be investigated, removed, or transformed. Here are
several popular methods for detecting outliers:

\subsubsection{Statistical Methods}\label{statistical-methods}

Visualization helps us identify potential outliers. To address them
effectively, we need to extract these outlier instances using a defined
threshold. Two commonly used statistical methods for this purpose are
the Z-Score method and the Interquartile Range (IQR) (Tukey's fences).

\paragraph{Z-Score (Standard Score)}\label{z-score-standard-score}

Calculates how many standard deviations a data point is from the mean.
Commonly, data points with a Z-score greater than 3 (or less than -3)
are considered outliers.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ scipy }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ stats}

\CommentTok{\# Calculate Z{-}scores and identify outliers}
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}z\_score\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ stats.zscore(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_z\_score\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}z\_score\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{3}

\CommentTok{\# Filter to show only the outliers}
\NormalTok{z\_score\_outliers }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_z\_score\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]]}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(z\_score\_outliers.shape)}
\NormalTok{z\_score\_outliers.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{IQR method (Tukey's fences)}\label{iqr-method-tukeys-fences}

John Tukey proposed that observations outside the range
\([Q1 - 1.5(Q3-Q1), Q3+1.5(Q3-Q1)]\) are outliers, where \(Q1\) and
\(Q3\) are the lower \((25\%)\) and upper \((75\%)\) quartiles
respectively. Let us detect outliers based on this threshold.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Calculate the first and third quartiles, and the IQR}
\NormalTok{Q1 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.percentile(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{25}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Q3 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.percentile(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{75}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{IQR }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q3 }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Q1}

\CommentTok{\# Define the lower and upper bounds for outliers}
\NormalTok{lower\_bound }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q1 }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{1.5} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ IQR}
\NormalTok{upper\_bound }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q3 }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1.5} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ IQR}

\CommentTok{\# Add a new column to indicate IQR outliers}
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_IQR\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ lower\_bound) }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ upper\_bound)}

\CommentTok{\# Filter to show only the IQR outliers}
\NormalTok{iqr\_outliers }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_IQR\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]]}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(iqr\_outliers.shape)}
\NormalTok{iqr\_outliers.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{When to use each:}\label{when-to-use-each}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Use IQR when:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Data is skewed
  \item
    You don't want to assume any distribution
  \item
    You want a more sensitive detector
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Use Z-score when:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Data is approximately normal
  \item
    You want a more conservative approach
  \item
    You need a method that's easily interpretable
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

The actual number of outliers marked by each method will depend on your
specific dataset's distribution and characteristics.

\subsection{Common Methods for Handling
outliers}\label{common-methods-for-handling-outliers}

Once we identify outlier instances using statistical methods, the next
step is to handle them. Below are some commonly used approaches:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Removing Outliers}: Discarding extreme values if they are
  likely due to errors or are irrelevant for the analysis.
\item
  \textbf{Winsorizing}: Capping/flooring outliers to a specific
  percentile to reduce their influence without removing them completely.
\item
  \textbf{Replacing with the median}: Replacing outlier values with the
  median of the remaining data. The median is less affected by extreme
  values than the mean, making it an ideal choice for imputation when
  dealing with outliers
\item
  \textbf{Transforming Data}: Applying transformations (e.g., log,
  square root) to reduce the impact of outliers.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ method\_removal():}
    \CommentTok{"""Method 1: Remove outliers"""}
\NormalTok{    data\_cleaned }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[}\OperatorTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]][}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ data\_cleaned}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ method\_capping():}
    \CommentTok{"""Method 2: Capping (Winsorization)"""}
\NormalTok{    data\_capped }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].copy()}
\NormalTok{    data\_capped[data\_capped }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ lower\_bound] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ lower\_bound}
\NormalTok{    data\_capped[data\_capped }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ upper\_bound] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ upper\_bound}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ data\_capped}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ method\_mean\_replacement():}
    \CommentTok{"""Method 3: Replace with median"""}
\NormalTok{    data\_median }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].copy()}
\NormalTok{    median\_value }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[}\OperatorTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]][}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].median()}
\NormalTok{    data\_median[college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}is\_outlier\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ median\_value}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ data\_median}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ method\_log\_transformation():}
    \CommentTok{"""Method 4: Log transformation"""}
\NormalTok{    data\_log }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log1p(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ data\_log}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Your Practice:} Try each method and compare their results to see
how they differ in handling outliers.

In real-world applications, handling outliers should be approached on a
case-by-case basis. However, here are some general recommendations:

\textbf{Recommendations for Different Scenarios:}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Data Removal:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Use when: You have a large dataset and can afford to lose data
  \item
    Pros: Simple, removes all outlier influence
  \item
    Cons: Loss of data, potential loss of important information
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Capping (Winsorization):

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Use when: You want to preserve data count while limiting extreme
    values
  \item
    Pros: Preserves data size, reduces impact of outliers
  \item
    Cons: Artificial boundary creation, potential loss of genuine
    extreme events
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Median Replacement:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Use when: The data is normally distributed, and outliers are
    verified as errors or anomalies not representing true values
  \item
    Pros: Maintains data size, simple to implement
  \item
    Cons: Reduces variance, may not represent the true distribution
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Log Transformation:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Use when: Data has a right-skewed distribution, and you want to
    reduce the impact of large outliers.
  \item
    Pros: Reduces skewness, minimizes the effect of extreme values, can
    make data more normal-like.
  \item
    Cons: Only applicable to positive values, may not be effective for
    extremely high outliers.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\section{Data binning}\label{data-binning}

Data binning is a powerful technique in data analysis where continuous
numerical data is grouped into discrete intervals or ``bins.'' Imagine
it as sorting items into distinct categories or ``buckets'' based on
their values, making it easier to observe trends, patterns, and
groupings within large datasets. We encounter binning in everyday life
without even realizing it.

For example, consider age groups: instead of listing every individual
age, we often refer to broader categories like ``under 20,'' ``20-30,''
``30-40,'' or ``40 and over.'' This binning approach helps simplify data
interpretation and comparison across different age groups. Another
common example is tax brackets. Tax rates are often applied to ranges of
income, like ``up to \$11,000,'' ``\$11,001 to \$44,725,'' and so forth.
Here, income values are grouped into bins to determine applicable tax
rates, making complex tax data easier to manage and understand.

\begin{verbatim}
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Key reasons for binning:}\label{key-reasons-for-binning}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Better intepretation of data\\
\item
  Making better recommendations\\
\item
  Smooth data, reduce noise
\end{enumerate}

Examples:

\textbf{Binning to better interpret data}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The number of flu cases everyday may be binned to seasons such as
  fall, spring, winter and summer, to understand the effect of season on
  flu.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Binning to make recommendations:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
  A doctor may like to group patient age into bins. Grouping patient
  ages into categories such as Age \textless=12,
  12\textless Age\textless=18, 18\textless Age\textless=65,
  Age\textgreater65 may help recommend the kind/doses of covid vaccine a
  patient needs.
\item
  A credit card company may want to bin customers based on their spend,
  as ``High spenders'', ``Medium spenders'' and ``Low spenders''.
  Binning will help them design customized marketing campaigns for each
  bin, thereby increasing customer response (or revenue). On the other
  hand, they use the same campaign for customers withing the same bin,
  thus minimizng marketing costs.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Binning to smooth data, and reduce noise}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  A sales company may want to bin their total sales to a weekly /
  monthly / yearly level to reduce the noise in day-to-day sales.
\end{enumerate}

Using our college dataset, let's apply binning to better interpret the
relationship between instructional expenditure per student
(\texttt{Expend}) and graduation rate (\texttt{Grad.Rate}) for U.S.
universities, and make relevant recommendations

Here is the previous scatterplot of `Grad.Rate' vs `Expend' with a
trendline.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# scatter plot of Expend vs Grad.Rate}
\NormalTok{ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{sns.regplot(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college, x }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"Expend"}\NormalTok{, y }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"Grad.Rate"}\NormalTok{,scatter\_kws}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{\{}\StringTok{"color"}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"orange"}\NormalTok{\}, line\_kws}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{\{}\StringTok{"color"}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"blue"}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expenditure per student\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax.set\_ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Graduation rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-49-output-1.png}}

The trendline indicates a positive correlation between \texttt{Expend}
and \texttt{Grad.Rate}. However, there seems to be a lot of noise and
presence of outliers in the data, which makes it hard to interpret the
overall trend.

\subsection{Common binning methods:}\label{common-binning-methods}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Equal-width:} Divides range into equal-sized intervals
\item
  \textbf{Equal-size:} Places equal number of observations in each bin
\item
  \textbf{Custom:} Based on domain knowledge (like age groups above)
\end{itemize}

We'll bin \texttt{Expend} to see if we can better analyze its
association with \texttt{Grad.Rate}. However, let us first visualize the
distribution of \texttt{Expend}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Visualizing the distribution of expend}
\NormalTok{ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{sns.histplot(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college, x}\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-50-output-1.png}}

The distribution of \texttt{Extend} is right skewed with potentially
some extremely high outlying values.

\subsubsection{Binning with equal width
bins}\label{binning-with-equal-width-bins}

We'll use the Pandas function
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html}{cut()}
to bin \texttt{Expend}. This function creates bins such that all bins
have the same width.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Using the cut() function in Pandas to bin "Expend"}
\NormalTok{Binned\_expend }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.cut(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{,retbins }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Binned\_expend}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
