The
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html}{cut()}
function returns a tuple of length 2. The first element of the tuple are

values for the bins.

Let us find the number of universities in each bin.

\begin{Shaded}

The bin \texttt{High\ expend} consists of only 5 universities, or 0.6\%
of all the universities in the dataset. These universities may be
outliers that are skewing the trend (as also evident in the histogram
above).

Let us see if we get the correct trend with the outliers removed from
the data.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Data without outliers}
\NormalTok{college\_data\_without\_outliers }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college[((college.Expend}\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{lower\_bound) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (college.Expend}\OperatorTok{\textless{}=}\NormalTok{upper\_bound))]}

\NormalTok{Binned\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.cut(college\_data\_without\_outliers[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{,labels }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Low expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Med expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}High expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],retbins }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{college\_data\_without\_outliers.loc[:,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Binned\_data[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sns.barplot(x }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, y }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Grad.Rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college\_data\_without\_outliers)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\NormalTok{    plt.axvline(Binned\_data[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][i], }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{,color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}red\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expenditure per student\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Graduation rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

Instead of removing outliers, we can address the issue by binning
observations into equal-sized bins, ensuring each bin has the same
number of observations. Let's explore this approach next.

\subsubsection{Binning with equal sized
bins}\label{binning-with-equal-sized-bins}

Let us bin the variable \texttt{Expend} such that each bin consists of
the same number of observations.

We'll use the Pandas function
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.qcut.html}{qcut()}
to make equal-sized bins (in contrast to equal-width bins in the
previous section).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Using the Pandas function qcut() to create bins with the same number of observations}
\NormalTok{Binned\_expend }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.qcut(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{,retbins }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Binned\_expend[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Each bin has the same number of observations with \texttt{qcut()}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].value\_counts()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Expend_bin
(3185.999, 7334.333]    259
(7334.333, 9682.333]    259
(9682.333, 56233.0]     259
Name: count, dtype: int64
\end{verbatim}

Let us visualize the \texttt{Expend} bins over the distribution of the
\texttt{Expend} variable.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Visualizing the bins for instructional expediture on a student}
\NormalTok{sns.}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(font\_scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.25}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.rcParams[}\StringTok{"figure.figsize"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{9}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{sns.histplot(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college, x}\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.vlines(Binned\_expend[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{,color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}red\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expenditure per student\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Graduation rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

Note that the bin-widths have been adjusted to have the same number of
observations in each bin. The bins are narrower in domains of high

Let us again make the barplot visualizing the average graduate rate with
level of instructional expenditure per student.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.qcut(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{,labels }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Low expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Med expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}High expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{a}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{sns.barplot(x }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, y }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Grad.Rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-67-output-1.png}}

Now we see the same trend that we saw in the scatterplot, but without
the noise. We have smoothed the data. Note that making equal-sized bins
helps reduce the effect of outliers in the overall trend.

Suppose this analysis was done to provide recommendations to
universities for increasing their graduation rate. With binning, we can
can provide one recommendation to \emph{`Low expend'} universities, and
another one to \emph{`Med expend'} universities. For example, the
recommendations can be:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{`Low expend'} universities can expect an increase of 9
  percentage points in \texttt{Grad.Rate}, if they migrate to the
  \emph{`Med expend'} category.
\item
  \emph{`Med expend'} universities can expect an increase of 7
  percentage points in \texttt{Grad.Rate}, if they migrate to the
  \emph{`High expend'} category.
\end{enumerate}

The numbers in the above recommendations are based on the table below.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{college.groupby(college.Expend\_bin, observed}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Grad.Rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Expend_bin
Low expend     57.343629
Med expend     66.057915
High expend    72.988417
Name: Grad.Rate, dtype: float64
\end{verbatim}

We can also provide recommendations based on the confidence intervals of
the mean graduation rate (\texttt{Grad.Rate}). The confidence intervals,
calculated below, are derived using a method known as bootstrapping. For
a detailed explanation of bootstrapping, please refer to
\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_(statistics)}{this
article on Wikipedia}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Bootstrapping to find 95\% confidence intervals of Graduation Rate of US universities based on average expenditure per student}
\NormalTok{confidence\_intervals }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{\}}

\CommentTok{\# Loop through each expenditure bin}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ expend\_bin, data\_sub }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ college.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, observed}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{\# Generate bootstrap samples for the graduation rate}
\NormalTok{    samples }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.choice(data\_sub[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Grad.Rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(data\_sub)), replace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Calculate the mean of each sample}
\NormalTok{    sample\_means }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ samples.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Calculate the 95\% confidence interval}
\NormalTok{    lower\_bound }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.percentile(sample\_means, }\FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    upper\_bound }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.percentile(sample\_means, }\FloatTok{97.5}\NormalTok{)}
    
    \CommentTok{\# Store the result in the dictionary}
\NormalTok{    confidence\_intervals[expend\_bin] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(lower\_bound, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(upper\_bound, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}

\CommentTok{\# Print the results}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ expend\_bin, ci }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ confidence\_intervals.items():}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"95\% Confidence interval of Grad.Rate for }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{expend\_bin}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ universities = [}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{ci[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{, }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{ci[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{]"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
95% Confidence interval of Grad.Rate for Low expend universities = [55.36, 59.36]
95% Confidence interval of Grad.Rate for Med expend universities = [64.15, 67.95]
95% Confidence interval of Grad.Rate for High expend universities = [71.03, 74.92]
\end{verbatim}

Apart from equal-width and equal-sized bins, custom bins can be created
using the \emph{bins} argument. Suppose, bins are to be created for
\texttt{Expend} with cutoffs
\(\$10,000, \$20,000, \$30,000... \$60,000\). Then, we can use the
\emph{bins} argument as in the code below:

\subsubsection{Binning with custom bins}\label{binning-with-custom-bins}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binned\_expend }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.cut(college.Expend,bins }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{70000}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)),retbins}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Visualizing the bins for instructional expediture on a student}
\NormalTok{ax}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{sns.histplot(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ college, x}\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.vlines(Binned\_expend[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{,color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}red\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expenditure per student\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Graduation rate\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-71-output-1.png}}

Next, let's create a custom bin with unequal sizes and widths.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Create bins and labels}
\NormalTok{bins }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(), }\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{40000}\NormalTok{, college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{()]}
\NormalTok{labels }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Low Expenditure\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Medium Expenditure\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}High Expenditure\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}

\CommentTok{\# Binning the \textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{} column}
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_Binned\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.cut(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], bins}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{bins, labels}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{labels)}

\CommentTok{\# Visualizing the bins using a histogram}
\NormalTok{ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sns.histplot(data}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{college, x}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, kde}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Add vertical lines for the bin edges (the bin edges are the values in \textquotesingle{}bins\textquotesingle{})}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ bin\_edge }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ bins[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]:  }\CommentTok{\# skip the first and last bins since they are the edges}
\NormalTok{    plt.vlines(bin\_edge, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, ax.get\_ylim()[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}red\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Add labels and formatting}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expenditure per student\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Frequency\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Display the plot}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data cleaning and preparation_files/figure-pdf/cell-72-output-1.png}}

As custom bin-cutoffs can be specified with the \texttt{cut()} function,
custom bin quantiles can be specified with the \texttt{qcut()} function.

\section{Dummy / Indicator variables}\label{dummy-indicator-variables}

Dummy or indicator variables are binary variables created to represent
categorical data in numerical form, typically used in regression and
machine learning models. Each category is represented by a separate
dummy variable with values of 0 or 1.

\subsection{Purpose:}\label{purpose}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Enables categorical data} to be used in quantitative analysis:
  Models like linear regression and many machine learning algorithms
  require numerical input, making dummy variables essential for handling
  categorical data.
\item
  \textbf{Preserves information}: Converts categorical information into
  a format that models can interpret without losing meaning.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{When to use dummy
variables}\label{when-to-use-dummy-variables}

Dummy variables are especially useful in:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Regression models:} For categorical predictors, such as
  region, gender, or type of product.
\item
  \textbf{Machine learning algorithms:} Many models, including
  tree-based methods, can benefit from dummy variables for categorical
  features.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{How to Create Dummy
variables}\label{how-to-create-dummy-variables}

The pandas library in Python has a built-in function,
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.get_dummies.html}{\texttt{pd.get\_dummies()}},
to generate dummy variables. If a column in a DataFrame has \(k\)
distinct values, we will get a DataFrame with \(k\) columns containing
0s and 1s

Let us make dummy variables with the equal-sized bins we created for the
average instruction expenditure per student.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Using the Pandas function qcut() to create bins with the same number of observations}
\NormalTok{Binned\_expend }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.qcut(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{],}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{,retbins }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{,labels }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Low\_expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Med\_expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}High\_expend\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Binned\_expend[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Making dummy variables based on the levels (categories) of the \textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{} variable}
\NormalTok{dummy\_Expend }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.get\_dummies(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The dummy data \texttt{dummy\_Expend} has a value of \(1\) if the
observation corresponds to the category referenced by the column name.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dummy\_Expend.head()}
\end{Highlighting}

\CommentTok{\#Concatenating the dummy variables to the original data}
\NormalTok{college }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.concat([college,dummy\_Expend],axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using \texttt{drop\_first} to Avoid
Multicollinearity}{Using drop\_first to Avoid Multicollinearity}}\label{using-drop_first-to-avoid-multicollinearity}

In cases like linear regression, you may want to drop one dummy variable
to avoid multicollinearity (perfect correlation between variables).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# create dummy variables, dropping the first to avoid multicollinearity}
\NormalTok{dummy\_Expend }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.get\_dummies(college[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Expend\_bin\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{, drop\_first}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# add the dummy variables to the original dataset}
\NormalTok{college }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.concat([college, dummy\_Expend], axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\chapter{Data Grouping and
Aggregation}\label{data-grouping-and-aggregation}

Grouping and aggregation are essential in data science because they
enable meaningful analysis and insights from complex and large-scale
datasets. Here are key reasons why they are important:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Data Summarization:} Grouping allows you to condense large
  amounts of data into concise summaries. Aggregation provides
  statistical summaries (e.g., mean, sum, count), making it easier to
  understand data trends and characteristics without needing to examine
  every detail.
\item
  \textbf{Insights Across Categories:} Grouping by categories, like
  regions, demographics, or time periods, lets you analyze patterns
  within each group. For example, aggregating sales data by region can
  reveal which areas are performing better, or grouping customer data by
  age group can highlight consumer trends.
\item
  \textbf{Time Series Analysis:} In time-series data, grouping by time
  intervals (e.g., day, month, quarter) allows you to observe trends
  over time, which can be crucial for forecasting, seasonal analysis,
  and trend detection.
\item
  \textbf{Reducing Data Complexity:} By summarizing data at a higher
  level, you reduce complexity, making it easier to visualize and
  interpret, especially in large datasets where working with raw data
  could be overwhelming.
\end{itemize}

In this chapter, we are going to see grouping and aggregating using
pandas. Grouping and aggregating will help to achieve data analysis
easily using various functions. These methods will help us to the group
and summarize our data and make complex analysis comparatively easy.

Througout this chapter, we will use \emph{gdp\_lifeExpectancy.csv},
let's read the csv file to pandas dataframe first

\section{Grouping by a single column}\label{grouping-by-a-single-column}

\texttt{groupby()} allows you to split a DataFrame based on the values
in one or more columns. First, we'll explore grouping by a single
column.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Syntax of
\texttt{groupby()}}{Syntax of groupby()}}\label{syntax-of-groupby}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{DataFrame.groupby(by="column\_name")} -- Groups data by the
  specified column.
\end{itemize}

Consider the life expectancy dataset. suppose we want to group by the
observations by \texttt{continent} by passing it as an argument to the
\texttt{groupby()} method.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Creating a GroupBy object}
\NormalTok{grouped }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\CommentTok{\#This will split the data into groups that correspond to values of the column \textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The \texttt{groupby()} method returns a GroupBy object.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#A \textquotesingle{}GroupBy\textquotesingle{} objects is created with the \textasciigrave{}groupby()\textasciigrave{} function}
\BuiltInTok{type}\NormalTok{(grouped)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
pandas.core.groupby.generic.DataFrameGroupBy
\end{verbatim}

The GroupBy object \texttt{grouped} contains the information of the
groups in which the data is distributed. Each observation has been
assigned to a specific group of the column(s) used to group the data.
However, note that the dataset is not physically split into different
DataFrames. For example, in the above case, each observation is assigned
to a particular group depending on the value of the \texttt{continent}
for that observation. However, all the observations are still in the
same DataFrame \texttt{data}.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Attributes and methods of the
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/groupby.html}{\emph{GroupBy}}
object}{Attributes and methods of the GroupBy object}}\label{attributes-and-methods-of-the-groupby-object}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\texttt{keys}}{keys}}\label{keys}

The object(s) grouping the data are called \emph{key(s)}. Here
\texttt{continent} is the group key. The keys of the \emph{GroupBy}
object can be seen using Its \texttt{keys} attribute.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Key(s) of the GroupBy object}
\NormalTok{grouped.keys}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
'continent'
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.GroupBy.ngroup.html}{\texttt{ngroups}}}{ngroups}}\label{ngroups}

The number of groups in which the data is distributed based on the keys
can be seen with the \texttt{ngroups} attribute.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#The number of groups based on the key(s)}
\NormalTok{grouped.ngroups}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
5
\end{verbatim}

The group names are the \emph{keys} of the dictionary, while the row
labels are the corresponding \emph{values}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Group names}
\NormalTok{grouped.groups.keys()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
dict_keys(['Africa', 'Americas', 'Asia', 'Europe', 'Oceania'])
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}

\section{Data aggregation within
groups}\label{data-aggregation-within-groups}

\subsection{Common Aggregation
Functions}\label{common-aggregation-functions}

Aggregation functions are essential for summarizing and analyzing data
in pandas. These functions allow you to compute summary statistics for
your data, making it easier to identify trends and patterns.

Below are some of the most commonly used aggregation functions when
working with grouped data in pandas:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{mean()}} -- Calculates the \textbf{average} value of
  the group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{sum()}} -- Computes the \textbf{total} value by
  summing all elements in the group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{min()}} -- Finds the \textbf{minimum} value in the
  group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{max()}} -- Finds the \textbf{maximum} value in the
  group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{count()}} -- Returns the \textbf{number of
  occurrences} or entries in the group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{median()}} -- Finds the \textbf{middle value} in the
  sorted group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{std()}} -- Calculates the \textbf{standard deviation},
  measuring the spread or variation in the values of the group.
\end{itemize}

Each of these functions can help summarize and provide insights into
different aspects of the grouped data.

Consider the life expectancy dataset, let's find the mean life
expectancy, population and GDP per capita for each country during the
period of 1952 -2007.

Next, we'll find the mean statistics for each group with the
\texttt{mean()} method. The method will be applied on all columns of the
DataFrame and all groups.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Grouping the observations by \textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{grouped\_country }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.drop ([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], axis }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{).groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\#Finding the mean stastistic of all columns of the DataFrame and all groups}
\NormalTok{grouped\_country.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Multiple aggregations and Custom aggregation
using
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.agg.html}{\texttt{agg()}}}{Multiple aggregations and Custom aggregation using agg()}}\label{multiple-aggregations-and-custom-aggregation-using-agg}

\subsubsection{Multiple aggregations}\label{multiple-aggregations}

Directly applying the aggregate methods of the \emph{GroupBy} object
such as mean, count, etc., lets us apply only one function at a time.
Also, we may wish to apply an aggregate function of our own, which is
not there in the set of methods of the \emph{GroupBy} object, such as
the range of values of a column.

The \texttt{agg()} function of a \emph{GroupBy} object lets us aggregate
data using:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Multiple aggregation functions
\item
  Custom aggregate functions (in addition to in-built functions like
  mean, std, count etc.)
\end{enumerate}

Consider the life expectancy dataset, Let us use the agg() method of the
GroupBy object to simultaneously find the mean and standard deviation of
the \emph{gdpPercap} for each country.

For aggregating by multiple functions, we pass a list of strings to
agg(), where the strings are the function names.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{grouped\_country[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].agg([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}std\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]).sort\_values(by }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,ascending }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{).head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\toprule\noalign{}
& mean & std \\
country & & \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

\subsubsection{Custom aggregation}\label{custom-aggregation}

In addition to the mean and standard deviation of the gdpPercap of each
country, let us also include the range of gdpPercap in the table above
using lambda function

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{grouped\_country[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].agg(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: x.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ x.}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

country

                         ...

Name: gdpPercap, Length: 142, dtype: float64

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# define a function that calculates the range}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ range\_func(x):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ x.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ x.}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# apply the range function to the \textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{} column besides the mean and standard deviation}
\NormalTok{grouped\_country[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].agg([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}std\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, range\_func]).sort\_values(by }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}range\_func\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, ascending }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Distinct aggregate functions on multiple
columns}\label{distinct-aggregate-functions-on-multiple-columns}

For aggregating by multiple functions, we pass a list of strings to
\texttt{agg()}, where the strings are the function names.

For aggregating by multiple functions \& changing the column names
resulting from those functions, we pass a list of tuples to
\texttt{agg()}, where each tuple is of length two, and contains the new
column name as the first object and the function to be applied as the
second object of the tuple.

For aggregating by multiple functions such that a distinct set of
functions is applied to each column, we pass a dictionary to
\texttt{agg()}, where the keys are the column names on which the
function is to be applied, and the values are the list of strings that
are the function names, or a list of tuples if we also wish to name the
aggregated columns.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# We can use a list to apply multiple aggregation functions to a single column, and a dictionary to specify different functions for multiple columns}
\CommentTok{\# Use string names for the aggregation functions}
\NormalTok{grouped\_country.agg(\{}\StringTok{"gdpPercap"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"mean"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"std"}\NormalTok{], }\StringTok{"lifeExp"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"median"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"std"}\NormalTok{], }\StringTok{"pop"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"max"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"min"}\NormalTok{]\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Grouping by Multiple
Columns}\label{grouping-by-multiple-columns}

Above, we demonstrated grouping by a single column, which is useful for
summarizing data based on one categorical variable. However, in many
cases, we need to group by multiple columns. Grouping by multiple
columns allows us to create more detailed summaries by accounting for
multiple categorical variables. This approach enables us to analyze data
at a finer granularity, revealing insights that might be missed with
single-column grouping alone.

\subsection{Basic Syntax for Grouping by Multiple
Columns}\label{basic-syntax-for-grouping-by-multiple-columns}

Use \texttt{groupby()} with a list of column names to group data by
multiple columns.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{DataFrame.groupby(by={[}"col1",\ "col2"{]})}
\end{itemize}

Consider the life expectancy dataset, we can group by both country and
continent to analyze \texttt{gdpPercap}, \texttt{lifeExp}, and
\texttt{pop} trends for each country within each continent, providing a
more comprehensive view of the data.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Grouping by multiple columns}
\NormalTok{grouped\_continent\_contry }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])[ }\StringTok{"lifeExp"}\NormalTok{].agg([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}std\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}max\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}min\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]).sort\_values(by }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, ascending }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{grouped\_continent\_contry}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Understanding Hierarchical (Multi-Level)
Indexing}\label{understanding-hierarchical-multi-level-indexing}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Grouping by multiple columns creates a hierarchical index (also called
  a multi-level index).
\item
  This index allows each level (e.g., continent, country) to act as an
  independent category that can be accessed individually.
\end{itemize}

In the above output, \texttt{continent} and \texttt{country} form a
two-level hierarchical index, allowing us to drill down from
continent-level to country-level summaries.

Breaking Down Grouping and Aggregation

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Grouping by Multiple Columns}:\\
  In this example, we are grouping the data by three columns:
  \texttt{continent}, \texttt{country}, and \texttt{year}. This creates
  groups based on unique combinations of these columns.
\item
  \textbf{Aggregating Multiple Variables}:\\
  We apply multiple aggregation functions (\texttt{mean}, \texttt{std},
  \texttt{max}, and \texttt{min}) to multiple variables
  (\texttt{lifeExp}, \texttt{pop}, and \texttt{gdpPercap}).
\end{itemize}

This type of operation is commonly referred to as \textbf{``multi-column
grouping with multiple aggregations''} in pandas. It's a powerful
approach because it allows us to obtain a detailed statistical summary
for each combination of grouping columns across several variables.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Advanced Operations within groups:
\texttt{apply()}, \texttt{transform()}, and
\texttt{filter()}}{Advanced Operations within groups: apply(), transform(), and filter()}}\label{advanced-operations-within-groups-apply-transform-and-filter}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.GroupBy.apply.html}{\texttt{apply()}}
on groups}{Using apply() on groups}}\label{using-apply-on-groups}

The \texttt{apply()} function applies a custom function to each group,
allowing for flexible operations. The function can return either a
scalar, Series, or DataFrame.

\textbf{Example}: Consider the life expectancy dataset, find the top 3
life expectancy values for each continent

We'll first define a function that sorts a dataset by decreasing life
expectancy and returns the top 3 rows. Then, we'll apply this function
on each group using the \texttt{apply()} method of the \emph{GroupBy}
object.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Define a function to get the top 3 rows based on life expectancy for each group}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ top\_3\_life\_expectancy(group):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ group.nlargest(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Defining the groups in the data}
\NormalTok{grouped\_gdpcapital\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now we'll use the \texttt{apply()} method to apply the
\texttt{top\_3\_life\_expectancy()} function on each group of the object
\texttt{grouped\_gdpcapital\_data}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Apply the function to each continent group}
\NormalTok{top\_life\_expectancy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)[[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]].}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(top\_3\_life\_expectancy).reset\_index(drop}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Display the result}
\NormalTok{top\_life\_expectancy.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& continent & country & year & lifeExp & gdpPercap \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & Africa & Reunion & 2007 & 76.442 & 7670.122558 \\
1 & Africa & Reunion & 2002 & 75.744 & 6316.165200 \\
2 & Africa & Reunion & 1997 & 74.772 & 6071.941411 \\
3 & Americas & Canada & 2007 & 80.653 & 36319.235010 \\
4 & Americas & Canada & 2002 & 79.770 & 33328.965070 \\
\end{longtable}

The \texttt{top\_3\_life\_expectancy()} function is applied to each
group, and the results are concatenated internally with the
\texttt{concat()} function. The output therefore has a hierarchical
index whose outer level indices are the group keys.

We can also use a lambda function instead of separately defining the
function \texttt{top\_3\_life\_expectancy()}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\CommentTok{\# Use a lambda function to get the top 3 life expectancy values for each continent}
\NormalTok{top\_life\_expectancy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}
\NormalTok{    gdp\_lifeExp\_data}
\NormalTok{    .groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)[[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]]  }\CommentTok{\# Avoid adding group labels in the index}
\NormalTok{    .}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: x.nlargest(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    .reset\_index(drop}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Display the result}
\NormalTok{top\_life\_expectancy.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& continent & country & year & lifeExp & gdpPercap \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

1 & Africa & Reunion & 2002 & 75.744 & 6316.165200 \\
2 & Africa & Reunion & 1997 & 74.772 & 6071.941411 \\
3 & Americas & Canada & 2007 & 80.653 & 36319.235010 \\
4 & Americas & Canada & 2002 & 79.770 & 33328.965070 \\

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.transform.html}{\texttt{transform()}}
on
Groups}{Using transform() on Groups}}\label{using-transform-on-groups}

The \texttt{transform()} function applies a function to each group and
returns a Series aligned with the original DataFrame's index. This makes
it suitable for adding or modifying columns based on group-level
calculations.

Recall that in the data cleaning and preparation chapter, we imputed
missing values based on correlated variables in the dataset.

In the example provided, some countries had missing values for GDP per
capita. To handle this, we imputed the missing GDP per capita for each
country using the average GDP per capita of its corresponding continent.

Now, we'll explore an alternative approach using \texttt{groupby()} and
\texttt{transform()} to perform this imputation.

Let us read the datasets and the function that makes a visualization to
compare the imputed values with the actual values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Importing data with missing values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_missing\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./Datasets/GDP\_missing\_data.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\#Importing data with all values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_complete\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./Datasets/GDP\_complete\_data.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Index of rows with missing values for GDP per capita}
\NormalTok{null\_ind\_gdpPC }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_data.index[gdp\_missing\_data.gdpPerCapita.isnull()]}

\CommentTok{\#Defining a function to plot the imputed values vs actual values }
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted():}
\NormalTok{    fig, ax }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ plt.subplots(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    plt.rc(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}xtick\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, labelsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }
\NormalTok{    plt.rc(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}ytick\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, labelsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }
\NormalTok{    x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_complete\_data.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_imputed\_data.loc[null\_ind\_gdpPC,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    plt.scatter(x,y)}
\NormalTok{    z}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{np.polyfit(x,y,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    p}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{np.poly1d(z)}
\NormalTok{    plt.plot(x,x,color}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}orange\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Actual GDP per capita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,fontsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Imputed GDP per capita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,fontsize}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    ax.xaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    ax.yaxis.set\_major\_formatter(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}$}\SpecialCharTok{\{x:,.0f\}}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    rmse }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(((x}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{y).}\BuiltInTok{pow}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)).mean())}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"RMSE="}\NormalTok{,rmse)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Approach 1:} Using the approach we used in the previous chapter

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Finding the mean GDP per capita of the continent}
\NormalTok{avg\_gdpPerCapita }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].groupby(gdp\_missing\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]).mean()}

\CommentTok{\#Creating a copy of missing data to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_data.copy()}

\CommentTok{\#Replacing missing GDP per capita with the mean GDP per capita for the corresponding continent}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ cont }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ avg\_gdpPerCapita.index:}
\NormalTok{    gdp\_imputed\_data.loc[(gdp\_imputed\_data.continent}\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{cont) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (gdp\_imputed\_data.gdpPerCapita.isnull()),}
                     \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{avg\_gdpPerCapita[cont]}
\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
RMSE= 25473.20645170116
\end{verbatim}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data aggregation_files/figure-pdf/cell-45-output-2.png}}

\textbf{Approach 2:} Using the \texttt{groupby()} and
\texttt{transform()} methods.

The \texttt{transform()} function is a powerful tool for filling missing
values in grouped data. It allows us to apply a function across each
group and align the result back to the original DataFrame, making it
perfect for filling missing values based on group statistics.

In this example, we use \texttt{transform()} to impute missing values in
the \texttt{gdpPerCapita} column by filling them with the mean
\texttt{gdpPerCapita} of each continent:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#Creating a copy of missing data to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_data.copy()}

\CommentTok{\#Grouping data by continent}
\NormalTok{grouped }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_missing\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\#Imputing missing values with the mean GDP per capita of the continent}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grouped[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].transform(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: x.fillna(x.mean()))}

\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
RMSE= 25473.20645170116
\end{verbatim}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data aggregation_files/figure-pdf/cell-46-output-2.png}}

Using the \texttt{transform()} function, missing values in gdpPerCapita
for each group are filled with the group's mean \texttt{gdpPerCapita}.
This approach is not only more convenient to write but also faster
compared to using for loops. While a for loop imputes missing values one
group at a time, \texttt{transform()} performs built-in operations (like
mean, sum, etc.) in a way that is optimized internally, making it more
efficient.

Let's use \texttt{apply()} instead of \texttt{transform()} with
\texttt{groupby()}

Please copy the code below and run it in your notebook:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\#Creating a copy of missing data to impute missing values}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data = gdp\_missing\_data.copy()}

\NormalTok{\#Grouping data by continent}
\NormalTok{grouped = gdp\_missing\_data.groupby(\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{})}

\NormalTok{\#Applying the lambda function on the \textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{} column of the groups}
\NormalTok{gdp\_imputed\_data[\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}] = grouped[\textquotesingle{}gdpPerCapita\textquotesingle{}].apply(lambda x: x.fillna(x.mean()))}

\NormalTok{plot\_actual\_vs\_predicted()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Why we ran into this error? and \texttt{apply()} doesn't work?

Here's a deeper look at why \texttt{apply()} doesn't work as expected
here:

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Behavior of \texttt{groupby().apply()}
vs.~\texttt{groupby().transform()}}{Behavior of groupby().apply() vs.~groupby().transform()}}\label{behavior-of-groupby.apply-vs.-groupby.transform}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{groupby().apply()}}: This method applies a function to
  each group and returns the result with a hierarchical (multi-level)
  index by default. This hierarchical index can make it difficult to
  align the result back to a single column in the original DataFrame.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{groupby().transform()}}: In contrast,
  \texttt{transform()} is specifically designed to apply a function to
  each group and return a Series that is aligned with the original
  DataFrame's index. This alignment makes it directly compatible for
  assignment to a new or existing column in the original DataFrame.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Why \texttt{transform()} Works for
Imputation}{Why transform() Works for Imputation}}\label{why-transform-works-for-imputation}

When using \texttt{transform()} to fill missing values, it applies the
function (e.g., \texttt{fillna(x.mean())}) based on each group's
statistics, such as the mean, while keeping the result aligned with the
original DataFrame's index. This allows for smooth assignment to a
column in the DataFrame without any index mismatch issues.

Additionally, \texttt{transform()} applies the function to each element
in a group independently and returns a result that has the same shape as
the original data, making it ideal for adding or modifying columns.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.filter.html}{\texttt{filter()}}
on Groups}{Using filter() on Groups}}\label{using-filter-on-groups}

The \texttt{filter()} function filters entire groups based on a
condition. It evaluates each group and keeps only those that meet the
specified criteria.

Example: Keep only the countries where the mean life expectancy is
greater than 70

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# keep only the continent where the mean life expectancy is greater than 74}
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{filter}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: x[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].mean() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{74}\NormalTok{)[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].unique()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array(['Oceania'], dtype=object)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# keep only the country where the mean life expectancy is greater than 74}
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{filter}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: x[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].mean() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{74}\NormalTok{)[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].unique()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array(['Australia', 'Canada', 'Denmark', 'France', 'Iceland', 'Italy',
       'Japan', 'Netherlands', 'Norway', 'Spain', 'Sweden', 'Switzerland'],
      dtype=object)
\end{verbatim}

Using \texttt{.nunique()} get the number of countries that satisfy this
condition

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{filter}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: x[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].mean() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{74}\NormalTok{)[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].nunique()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
12
\end{verbatim}

\section{Sampling data by group}\label{sampling-data-by-group}

If a dataset contains a large number of observations, operating on it
can be computationally expensive. Instead, working on a sample of entire
observations is a more efficient alterative. The \texttt{groupby()}
method combined with \texttt{apply()} can be used for stratified random
sampling from a large dataset.

Before taking the random sample, let us find the number of countries in
each continent.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data.continent.value\_counts()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
continent
Africa      624
Asia        396
Europe      360
Americas    300
Oceania      24
Name: count, dtype: int64
\end{verbatim}

Let us take a random sample of 650 observations from the entire dataset.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sample\_lifeExp\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.sample(}\DecValTok{650}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, let us see the number of countries of each continent in our sample.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sample\_lifeExp\_data.continent.value\_counts()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
continent
Africa      241
Asia        149
Europe      142
Americas    109
Oceania       9
Name: count, dtype: int64
\end{verbatim}

Some of the continent have a very low representation in the data. To
rectify this, we can take a random sample of 130 observations from each
of the 5 continents. In other words, we can take a random sample from
each of the continent-based groups.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{evenly\_sampled\_lifeExp\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x:x.sample(}\DecValTok{130}\NormalTok{, replace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{), include\_groups}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{group\_sizes }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ evenly\_sampled\_lifeExp\_data.groupby(level}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{).size()}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(group\_sizes)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
continent
Africa      130
Americas    130
Asia        130
Europe      130
Oceania     130
dtype: int64
\end{verbatim}

The above stratified random sample equally represents all the continent.

\section{\texorpdfstring{\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.corr.html}{\texttt{corr()}}:
Correlation by
group}{corr(): Correlation by group}}\label{corr-correlation-by-group}

The
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.corr.html}{\texttt{corr()}}
method of the \emph{GroupBy} object returns the correlation between all
pairs of columns within each group.

\textbf{Example:} Find the correlation between \texttt{lifeExp} and
\texttt{gdpPercap} for each continent-country level combination.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x:x[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{].corr(x[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]), include\_groups}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
continent  country       
Africa     Algeria           0.904471
           Angola           -0.301079
           Benin             0.843949
           Botswana          0.005597
           Burkina Faso      0.881677
                               ...   
Europe     Switzerland       0.980715
           Turkey            0.954455
           United Kingdom    0.989893
Oceania    Australia         0.986446
           New Zealand       0.974493
Length: 142, dtype: float64
\end{verbatim}

Life expectancy is closely associated with GDP per capita across most
continent-country combinations.

\section{\texorpdfstring{\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.pivot_table.html}{\texttt{pivot\_table()}}}{pivot\_table()}}\label{pivot_table}

The \texttt{pivot\_table()} function in pandas is a powerful tool for
performing groupwise aggregation in a structured format, similar to
Excel's pivot tables. It allows you to create a summary of data by
grouping and aggregating it based on specified columns. Here's an
overview of how \texttt{pivot\_table()} works for groupwise aggregation:

Note that \texttt{pivot\_table()} is the same as \texttt{pivot()} except
that \texttt{pivot\_table()} aggregates the data as well in addition to
re-arranging it.

\textbf{Example:} Consider the life expectancy dataset, calculate the
average life expectancy for each country and year combination

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pd.pivot\_table(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data, values }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,index }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, columns }\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,aggfunc }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,margins }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\toprule\noalign{}

1997 & 2002 & 2007 & All \\

\textbf{Explanation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{values}: Specifies the column to aggregate (e.g.,
  \texttt{lifeExp} in our example).
\item
  \textbf{index}: Groups by the rows based on the \texttt{country}
  column.
\item
  \textbf{columns}: Groups by the columns based on the \texttt{year}
  column.
\item
  \textbf{aggfunc}: Uses \texttt{mean} to calculate the average life
  expectancy.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Common Aggregation Functions in \texttt{pivot\_table()}}

You can use various aggregation functions within \texttt{pivot\_table()}
to summarize data:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{mean}} -- Calculates the average of values within each
  group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{sum}} -- Computes the total of values within each
  group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{count}} -- Counts the number of non-null entries
  within each group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{min}} and \textbf{\texttt{max}} -- Finds the minimum
  and maximum values within each group.
\end{itemize}

We can also use custom \emph{GroupBy} aggregate functions with
\texttt{pivot\_table()}.

\textbf{Example}: Find the \(90^{th}\) percentile of life expectancy for
each country and year combination

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pd.pivot\_table(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data, values }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,index }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, columns }\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,aggfunc }\OperatorTok{=} \KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x:np.percentile(x,}\DecValTok{90}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{\texorpdfstring{\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.crosstab.html}{\texttt{crosstab()}}}{crosstab()}}\label{crosstab}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Basic Usage of
\texttt{crosstab()}}{Basic Usage of crosstab()}}\label{basic-usage-of-crosstab}

The \texttt{crosstab()} method is a special case of a pivot table for
computing group frequncies (or size of each group).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# create a basic crosstab to see counts of countries in each continent}
\NormalTok{pd.crosstab(gdp\_lifeExp\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], columns}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}count\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
col\_0 & count \\
continent & \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Africa & 624 \\
Americas & 300 \\
Asia & 396 \\
Europe & 360 \\
Oceania & 24 \\
\end{longtable}

Use the \texttt{margins=True} argument to add totals (row and column
margins) to the table. The \texttt{All} row and column provide totals
for each age group and gender category.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# create a crosstab to see counts of countries in each continent and year}
\NormalTok{pd.crosstab(gdp\_lifeExp\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], gdp\_lifeExp\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], margins}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This table shows the count of each year in each continent group, helping

We may often use it to check if the data is representative of all groups

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Using \texttt{crosstab()} with Aggregation
Functions}{Using crosstab() with Aggregation Functions}}\label{using-crosstab-with-aggregation-functions}

You can specify a \texttt{values} column and an aggregation function
(\texttt{aggfunc}) to summarize numerical data for each combination of
categorical variables.

\textbf{Example:} find the mean life expectancy for each continent and
year

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# find the mean life expectancy for each country in each continent and year}
\NormalTok{pd.crosstab(gdp\_lifeExp\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], gdp\_lifeExp\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], values}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], aggfunc}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Independent Study}\label{independent-study-9}

\subsection{Practice exercise 1}\label{practice-exercise-1-5}

Read the table consisting of GDP per capita of countries from the
webpage:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\_per\_capita
.

To only read the relevant table, read the tables that contain the word
\emph{`Country'}.

Estimate the GDP per capita of each country as the average of the
estimates of the three agencies - IMF, United Nations and World Bank.

We need to do a bit of data cleaning before we could directly use the
\texttt{groupby()} function. Follow the steps below:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Drop the ``Year'' column
\item
  Drop the level 1 column name (innermost level column)
\item
  Apply the following function on all the columns of the ``Estimate'' to
  convert them to numeric:
  \texttt{f\ =\ lambda\ x:pd.to\_numeric(x,errors\ =\ \textquotesingle{}coerce\textquotesingle{})}
\item
  Set the Country/Territory column as the index
\item
  Convert all other columns into numeric and coerce errors using
  `errors='coerce'`
\item
  Drop rows with NaN values
\item
  Find the average GDP per capital across the three agencies
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dfs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_html(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\_per\_capita\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, match }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{gdp\_data  }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ dfs[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{gdp\_data.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& Country/Territory & \multicolumn{2}{l}{%
IMF{[}4{]}{[}5{]}} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{%
World Bank{[}6{]}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{%
United Nations{[}7{]}} \\
& Country/Territory & Estimate & Year & Estimate & Year & Estimate &
Year \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & Monaco & --- & --- & 240862 & 2022 & 240535 & 2022 \\
1 & Liechtenstein & --- & --- & 187267 & 2022 & 197268 & 2022 \\
2 & Luxembourg & 135321 & 2024 & 128259 & 2023 & 125897 & 2022 \\
3 & Bermuda & --- & --- & 123091 & 2022 & 117568 & 2022 \\
4 & Switzerland & 106098 & 2024 & 99995 & 2023 & 93636 & 2022 \\
\end{longtable}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Flatten the MultiIndex to access column names}

\chapter{Data Reshaping and
Enrichment}\label{data-reshaping-and-enrichment}

In this chapter, we will explore how to reshape and enrich data using
pandas. Data reshaping and enriching are essential steps in data
preprocessing because they help transform raw data into a more
structured, useful, and meaningful format that can be effectively used
for analysis or modeling.

\begin{verbatim}
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
\end{verbatim}

\section{Data Reshaping}\label{data-reshaping}

Data reshaping involves altering the structure of the data to suit the
requirements of the analysis or modeling process. This is often needed
when the data is in a format that is difficult to analyze or when it
needs to be organized in a specific way.

\subsection{Why Data Reshaping is
Important:}\label{why-data-reshaping-is-important}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Improves Data Organization}: Raw data may be in a long format,
  where each observation is recorded on a separate row, or it may be in
  a wide format, where the same variable is spread across multiple
  columns. Reshaping allows you to reorganize the data into a format
  that is more suitable for analysis, such as turning multiple columns
  into a single column (melting) or aggregating rows into summary
  statistics (pivoting).
\item
  \textbf{Facilitates Analysis}: Some analysis techniques require
  specific data formats. For example, many machine learning algorithms
  require data in a matrix form, where each row represents a sample and
  each column represents a feature. Reshaping helps to convert data into
  this format.
\item
  \textbf{Simplifies Visualization}: Visualizing data is easier when it
  is in the right shape. For instance, plotting categorical data across
  time is easier when the data is in a tidy format, rather than having
  multiple variables spread across columns.
\item
  \textbf{Efficient Grouping and Aggregation}: In some cases, you may
  want to group data by certain categories or time periods, and
  reshaping can help aggregate data effectively for summarization.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Wide vs.~Long Data Format in Data
Reshaping}\label{wide-vs.-long-data-format-in-data-reshaping}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Wide Format}: Each variable in its own column; each row
  represents a unit, and data for multiple variables is spread across
  columns.
\item
  \textbf{Long Format}: Variables are stacked into one column per
  variable, with additional columns used to indicate time, categories,
  or other distinctions, leading to a greater number of rows.
\end{itemize}

To reshape between these two formats, you can use pandas functions such
as \texttt{pivot\_table()}, \texttt{melt()}, \texttt{stack()}, and
\texttt{unstack()}. Let's next take a look at each of these methods one
by one.

Throughout this section, we will continue using the
\emph{gdp\_lifeExpectancy.csv} dataset. Let's start by reading the CSV
file into a pandas DataFrame.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Pivoting ``long'' to ``wide'' using
\texttt{pivot\_table()}}{Pivoting ``long'' to ``wide'' using pivot\_table()}}\label{pivoting-long-to-wide-using-pivot_table}

In the last chapter, we learned that \texttt{pivot\_table()} is a
powerful tool for performing groupwise aggregation in a structured
format. The \texttt{pivot\_table()} function is used to reshape data by
specifying columns for the index, columns, and values.

\subsubsection{Pivoting a single column}\label{pivoting-a-single-column}

Consider the life expectancy dataset. Let's calculate the average life
expectancy for each combination of country and year.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data\_pivot }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.pivot\_table(index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], columns}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, values}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, aggfunc}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_data\_pivot.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llllllllllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& year & 1952 & 1957 & 1962 & 1967 & 1972 & 1977 & 1982 & 1987 & 1992 &
1997 & 2002 & 2007 \\
continent & country & & & & & & & & & & & & \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\multirow{5}{=}{Africa} & Algeria & 43.077 & 45.685 & 48.303 & 51.407 &
54.518 & 58.014 & 61.368 & 65.799 & 67.744 & 69.152 & 70.994 & 72.301 \\
& Angola & 30.015 & 31.999 & 34.000 & 35.985 & 37.928 & 39.483 & 39.942
& 39.906 & 40.647 & 40.963 & 41.003 & 42.731 \\
& Benin & 38.223 & 40.358 & 42.618 & 44.885 & 47.014 & 49.190 & 50.904 &

& Botswana & 47.622 & 49.618 & 51.520 & 53.298 & 56.024 & 59.319 &

48.122 & 49.557 & 50.260 & 50.324 & 50.650 & 52.295 \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Explanation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{values}: Specifies the column to aggregate (e.g.,
  \texttt{lifeExp} in our example).
\item
  \textbf{index}: Groups by the rows based on the \texttt{continent} and
  \texttt{country} column.
\item
  \textbf{columns}: Groups by the columns based on the \texttt{year}
  column.
\item
  \textbf{aggfunc}: Uses \texttt{mean} to calculate the average life
  expectancy.
\end{itemize}

With values of \texttt{year} as columns, it is easy to compare any
metric for different years.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#visualizing the change in life expectancy of all countries in 2007 as compared to that in 1957, i.e., the overall change in life expectancy in 50 years. }
\NormalTok{sns.scatterplot(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data\_pivot, x }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1957}\NormalTok{,y}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2007}\NormalTok{,hue }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.lineplot(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data\_pivot, x }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1957}\NormalTok{,y }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1957}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data wrangling_files/figure-pdf/cell-6-output-1.png}}

Observe that for some African countries, the life expectancy has
decreased after 50 years. It is worth investigating these countries to
identify factors associated with the decrease.

Another way to visualize a pivot table is by using a heatmap, which
represents the 2D table as a matrix of colors, making it easier to
interpret patterns and trends.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Plotting a heatmap to visualize the life expectancy of all countries in all years, figure size is set to 15x10}
\NormalTok{plt.figure(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{plt.title(}\StringTok{"Life expectancy of all countries in all years"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{sns.heatmap(gdp\_lifeExp\_data\_pivot)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{Data wrangling_files/figure-pdf/cell-7-output-1.png}}

\textbf{Common Aggregation Functions in \texttt{pivot\_table()}}

You can use various aggregation functions within \texttt{pivot\_table()}
to summarize data:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{mean}} -- Calculates the average of values within each
  group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{sum}} -- Computes the total of values within each
  group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{count}} -- Counts the number of non-null entries
  within each group.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{min}} and \textbf{\texttt{max}} -- Finds the minimum
  and maximum values within each group.
\end{itemize}

We can also define our own custom aggregation function and pass it to
the \texttt{aggfunc} parameter of the \texttt{pivot\_table()} function

\textbf{For Example:} Find the \(90^{th}\) percentile of life expectancy
for each country and year combination

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pd.pivot\_table(data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data, values }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,index }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, columns }\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}year\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,aggfunc }\OperatorTok{=} \KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x:np.percentile(x,}\DecValTok{90}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Stacking and Unstacking using
\texttt{stack()} and
\texttt{unstack()}}{Stacking and Unstacking using stack() and unstack()}}\label{stacking-and-unstacking-using-stack-and-unstack}

Stacking and unstacking are powerful techniques used to reshape
DataFrames by moving data between rows and columns. These operations are
particularly useful when working with \textbf{multi-level index} or
\textbf{multi-level columns}, where the data is structured in a
hierarchical format.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{stack()}: Converts columns into rows, which means it
  ``stacks'' the data into a long format.
\item
  \texttt{unstack()}: Converts rows into columns, reversing the effect
  of \texttt{stack()}.
\end{itemize}

Let's use the GDP per capita dataset and create a DataFrame with a
multi-level index (e.g., continent, country) and multi-level columns
(e.g., lifeExp , gdpPercap, and pop).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# calculate the average and standard deviation of life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita for countries across the years.}

\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gdp\_lifeExp\_data.groupby([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}continent\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}country\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])[[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}pop\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}gdpPercap\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]].agg([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}std\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

gdpPercap} \\

\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
