The resulting DataFrame has two levels of index and two levels of
columns, as shown below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# check the level of row and column index}
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.index.nlevels}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
2
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.columns.nlevels}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
2
\end{verbatim}

if you want to see the data along with the index and columns (in a more
accessible way), you can directly print the \texttt{.index} and
\texttt{.columns} attributes.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.index}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
MultiIndex([( 'Africa',                  'Algeria'),
            ( 'Africa',                   'Angola'),
            ( 'Africa',                    'Benin'),
            ( 'Africa',                 'Botswana'),
            ( 'Africa',             'Burkina Faso'),
            ( 'Africa',                  'Burundi'),
            ( 'Africa',                 'Cameroon'),
            ( 'Africa', 'Central African Republic'),
            ( 'Africa',                     'Chad'),
            ( 'Africa',                  'Comoros'),
            ...
            ( 'Europe',                   'Serbia'),
            ( 'Europe',          'Slovak Republic'),
            ( 'Europe',                 'Slovenia'),
            ( 'Europe',                    'Spain'),
            ( 'Europe',                   'Sweden'),
            ( 'Europe',              'Switzerland'),
            ( 'Europe',                   'Turkey'),
            ( 'Europe',           'United Kingdom'),
            ('Oceania',                'Australia'),
            ('Oceania',              'New Zealand')],
           names=['continent', 'country'], length=142)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.columns}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
MultiIndex([(  'lifeExp', 'mean'),
            (  'lifeExp',  'std'),
            (      'pop', 'mean'),
            (      'pop',  'std'),
            ('gdpPercap', 'mean'),
            ('gdpPercap',  'std')],
           )
\end{verbatim}

As seen, \textbf{the index and columns each contain tuples}. This is the
reason that when performing data subsetting on a DataFrame with
multi-level index and columns, you need to supply a tuple to specify the
exact location of the data.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.loc[(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Americas\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}United States\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}lifeExp\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}mean\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
73.4785
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.columns.values}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array([('lifeExp', 'mean'), ('lifeExp', 'std'), ('pop', 'mean'),
       ('pop', 'std'), ('gdpPercap', 'mean'), ('gdpPercap', 'std')],
      dtype=object)
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Understanding the \texttt{level} in
multi-level index and
columns}{Understanding the level in multi-level index and columns}}\label{understanding-the-level-in-multi-level-index-and-columns}

The \texttt{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data} dataframe have two levels of
index and two level of columns, You can reference these levels in
various operations, such as grouping, subsetting, or performing
aggregations. The \texttt{level} parameter helps identify which part of
the multi-level structure you're working with.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.index.get\_level\_values(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index(['Africa', 'Africa', 'Africa', 'Africa', 'Africa', 'Africa', 'Africa',
       'Africa', 'Africa', 'Africa',
       ...
       'Europe', 'Europe', 'Europe', 'Europe', 'Europe', 'Europe', 'Europe',
       'Europe', 'Oceania', 'Oceania'],
      dtype='object', name='continent', length=142)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.index.get\_level\_values(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.columns.get\_level\_values(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index(['lifeExp', 'lifeExp', 'pop', 'pop', 'gdpPercap', 'gdpPercap'], dtype='object')
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.columns.get\_level\_values(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index(['mean', 'std', 'mean', 'std', 'mean', 'std'], dtype='object')
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.columns.get\_level\_values(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index(['mean', 'std', 'mean', 'std', 'mean', 'std'], dtype='object')
\end{verbatim}

As seen above, the outermost level corresponds to \texttt{level=0}, and
it increases as we move inward to the inner levels. The innermost level
can be referred to as \texttt{-1}.

Now, let's use the level number in the \texttt{droplevel()} method to
see how it works. The syntax for this method is as follows:

\texttt{DataFrame.droplevel(level,\ axis=0)}

\subsection{Summary of Common Reshaping
Functions}\label{summary-of-common-reshaping-functions}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1364}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5364}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3273}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Function
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Description
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\texttt{pivot()} & Reshape data by creating new columns from existing
ones. & Pivot data on index/columns. \\
\texttt{melt()} & Unpivot data, turning columns into rows. & Convert
wide format to long. \\
\texttt{stack()} & Convert columns to rows. & Move column data to
rows. \\
\texttt{unstack()} & Convert rows back to columns. & Move row data to
columns. \\
\texttt{.T} & Transpose the DataFrame (swap rows and columns). &
Transpose the entire DataFrame. \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Practical Use Cases:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pivoting:} Useful for time series analysis or when you want to
  group and summarize data by specific categories.
\item
  \textbf{Melting:} Helpful when you need to reshape wide data for
  easier analysis or when preparing data for machine learning
  algorithms.
\item
  \textbf{Stacking/Unstacking:} Useful when you are working with
  hierarchical index DataFrames.
\item
  \textbf{Transpose:} Helpful for reorienting data for analysis or
  visualization.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Converting from Multi-Level Index to Single-Level Index
DataFrame}\label{converting-from-multi-level-index-to-single-level-index-dataframe}

If you're uncomfortable working with DataFrames that have multi-level
indexes and columns, you can convert them into single-level DataFrames
using the methods you learned in the previous chapter:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{reset\_index()}
\item
  Flattening the multi-level columns
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# reset the index to convert the multi{-}level index to a single{-}level index}
\NormalTok{gdp\_lifeExp\_multilevel\_data.reset\_index()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\toprule\noalign{}
& continent & country & \multicolumn{2}{l}{%

\section{Data Enriching}\label{data-enriching}

\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/merging.html}{Data
enriching} involves enhancing your existing dataset by adding additional
data, often from external sources, to make your dataset more insightful.

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{index_files/mediabag/merging_join_multi_d.png}}

There are 3 common methods for data enriching:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Merging using \texttt{merge()}}: Combining datasets based on a
  common key.
\item
  \textbf{Joining using \texttt{join()}}: Using indices to combine data.
\item
  \textbf{Concatenation using \texttt{concat()}}: Stacking DataFrames
  vertically or horizontally.
\end{itemize}

Let's first load the existing data

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_existing }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.read\_csv(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}./datasets/LOTR.csv\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_existing.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_existing.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(4, 3)
\end{verbatim}

\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_external.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_external.head()}
\end{Highlighting}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Combining based on common keys:
\texttt{merge()}}{Combining based on common keys: merge()}}\label{combining-based-on-common-keys-merge}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_merge }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.merge(df\_existing, df\_external)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_enriched\_merge.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_merge.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(2, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID & FirstName & Skills & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 50 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 39 \\
\end{longtable}

You can also do this way

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_merge }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ df\_existing.merge(df\_external)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_enriched\_merge.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_merge.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(2, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID & FirstName & Skills & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 50 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 39 \\
\end{longtable}

By default, the \texttt{merge()} function in pandas performs an
\textbf{inner join}, which combines two DataFrames based on the
\textbf{common keys shared by both}. Only the rows with matching keys in
both DataFrames are retained in the result.

This behavior can be observed in the following code:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_merge }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.merge(df\_existing, df\_external, how}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}inner\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_enriched\_merge.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_merge.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(2, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID & FirstName & Skills & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 50 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 39 \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{When you may use inner join?} You should use inner join when you
cannot carry out the analysis unless the observation corresponding to
the \emph{key column(s)} is present in both the tables.

\textbf{Example:} Suppose you wish to analyze the association between
vaccinations and covid infection rate based on country-level data. In
one of the datasets, you have the infection rate for each country, while
in the other one you have the number of vaccinations in each country.
The countries which have either the vaccination or the infection rate
missing, cannot help analyze the association. In such as case you may be
interested only in countries that have values for both the variables.
Thus, you will use inner join to discard the countries with either value
missing.

In \texttt{merge()}, the \texttt{how} parameter specifies the type of
merge to be performed, the default option is \texttt{inner}, it could
also be \texttt{left}, \texttt{right}, and \texttt{outer}.

These join types give you flexibility in how you want to merge and
combine data from different sources.

Let's see how each of these works using our dataframes defined above

\textbf{Left Join}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Returns all rows from the left DataFrame and the matching rows from
  the right DataFrame.
\item
  Missing values (\texttt{NaN}) are introduced for non-matching keys
  from the right DataFrame.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_merge\_lft }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.merge(df\_existing, df\_external, how}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}left\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_merge\_lft.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_merge\_lft.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(4, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID & FirstName & Skills & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 50.0 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 39.0 \\
2 & 1003 & Gandalf & Spells & NaN \\
3 & 1004 & Pippin & Fireworks & NaN \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{When you may use left join?} You should use left join when the
primary variable(s) of interest are present in the one of the datasets,
and whose missing values cannot be imputed. The variable(s) in the other
dataset may not be as important or it may be possible to reasonably
impute their values, if missing corresponding to the observation in the
primary dataset.

\textbf{Examples:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  Suppose you wish to analyze the association between the covid
  infection rate and the government effectiveness score (a metric used
  to determine the effectiveness of the government in implementing
  policies, upholding law and order etc.) based on the data of all
  countries. Let us say that one of the datasets contains the covid
  infection rate, while the other one contains the government
  effectiveness score for each country. If the infection rate for a
  country is missing, it might be hard to impute. However, the
  government effectiveness score may be easier to impute based on GDP
  per capita, crime rate etc. - information that is easily available
  online. In such a case, you may wish to use a left join where you keep
  all the countries for which the infection rate is known.
\item
  Suppose you wish to analyze the association between demographics such
  as age, income etc. and the amount of credit card spend. Let us say
  one of the datasets contains the demographic information of each
  customer, while the other one contains the credit card spend for the
  customers who made at least one purchase. In such as case, you may
  want to do a left join as customers not making any purchase might be
  absent in the card spend data. Their spend can be imputed as zero
  after merging the datasets.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Right join}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Returns all rows from the right DataFrame and the matching rows from
  the left DataFrame.
\item
  Missing values (\texttt{NaN}) are introduced for non-matching keys
  from the left DataFrame.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_merge\_right }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.merge(df\_existing, df\_external, how}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}right\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_merge\_right.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_merge\_right.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(5, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID & FirstName & Skills & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 50 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 39 \\
2 & 1006 & Legolas & NaN & 2931 \\
3 & 1007 & Elrond & NaN & 6520 \\
4 & 1008 & Barromir & NaN & 51 \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{When you may use right join?} You can always use a left join
instead of a right join. Their purpose is the same.

\subsubsection{outer join}\label{outer-join}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Returns all rows from both DataFrames, with \texttt{NaN} values where
  no match is found.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_merge\_outer }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.merge(df\_existing, df\_external, how}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}outer\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_merge\_outer.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_merge\_outer}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(7, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID & FirstName & Skills & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 50.0 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 39.0 \\
2 & 1003 & Gandalf & Spells & NaN \\
3 & 1004 & Pippin & Fireworks & NaN \\
4 & 1006 & Legolas & NaN & 2931.0 \\
5 & 1007 & Elrond & NaN & 6520.0 \\
6 & 1008 & Barromir & NaN & 51.0 \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{When you may use outer join?} You should use an outer join when
you cannot afford to lose data present in either of the tables. All the
other joins may result in loss of data.

\textbf{Example:} Suppose I took two course surveys for this course. If
I need to analyze student sentiment during the course, I will take an
outer join of both the surveys. Assume that each survey is a dataset,
where each row corresponds to a unique student. Even if a student has
answered one of the two surverys, it will be indicative of the
sentiment, and will be useful to keep in the merged dataset.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Combining based on Indices:
\texttt{join()}}{Combining based on Indices: join()}}\label{combining-based-on-indices-join}

Unlike \texttt{merge()}, \texttt{join()} in pandas combines data based
on the \textbf{index}. When using \texttt{join()}, you must specify the
\texttt{suffixes} parameter if there are overlapping column names, as it
does not have default values. You can refer to the official function
definition here:
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.join.html}{pandas.DataFrame.join}.

Please copy the code below and run it in your notebook:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_join = df\_existing.join(df\_external)}
\NormalTok{print(df\_enriched\_join.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_join.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let's set the suffix to fix this issue

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_join }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ df\_existing.join(df\_external, lsuffix }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\_existing\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,rsuffix }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\_external\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_enriched\_join.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_join.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(4, 6)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FellowshipID\_existing & FirstName\_existing & Skills &
FellowshipID\_external & FirstName\_external & Age \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1001 & Frodo & Hiding & 1001 & Frodo & 50 \\
1 & 1002 & Samwise & Gardening & 1002 & Samwise & 39 \\
2 & 1003 & Gandalf & Spells & 1006 & Legolas & 2931 \\
3 & 1004 & Pippin & Fireworks & 1007 & Elrond & 6520 \\
\end{longtable}

As can be observed, \textbf{\texttt{join()} merges DataFrames using
their index and performs a left join}.

Now, let's set the ``FellowshipID'' column as the index in both
DataFrames and see what happens.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# set the index of the dataframes as the "FellowshipID" column}
\NormalTok{df\_existing.set\_index(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}FellowshipID\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, inplace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{df\_external.set\_index(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}FellowshipID\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, inplace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# join the two dataframes}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_join }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ df\_existing.join(df\_external, lsuffix }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\_existing\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{,rsuffix }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\_external\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_enriched\_join.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_enriched\_join}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(4, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FirstName\_existing & Skills & FirstName\_external & Age \\
FellowshipID & & & & \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1001 & Frodo & Hiding & Frodo & 50.0 \\
1002 & Samwise & Gardening & Samwise & 39.0 \\
1003 & Gandalf & Spells & NaN & NaN \\
1004 & Pippin & Fireworks & NaN & NaN \\
\end{longtable}

In this case, \texttt{df\_enriched\_join} will contain all rows from
\texttt{df\_existing} and the corresponding matching rows from
\texttt{df\_external}, with \texttt{NaN} values for non-matching
entries.

Similar to \texttt{merge()}, you can change the type of join in
\texttt{join()} by explicitly specifying the \texttt{how} parameter.
However, this explanation will be skipped here, as the different join
types have already been covered in the \texttt{merge()} section above.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Stacking vertically or horizontally:
\texttt{concat()}}{Stacking vertically or horizontally: concat()}}\label{stacking-vertically-or-horizontally-concat}

\texttt{concat()} is used in pandas to concatenate DataFrames along a
specified axis, either rows or columns. Similar to \texttt{concat()} in
NumPy, it defaults to concatenating along the rows.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# let\textquotesingle{}s concatenate the two dataframes using default setting}
\NormalTok{df\_concat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.concat([df\_existing, df\_external])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_concat.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_concat}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(9, 3)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& FirstName & Skills & Age \\
FellowshipID & & & \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1001 & Frodo & Hiding & NaN \\
1002 & Samwise & Gardening & NaN \\
1003 & Gandalf & Spells & NaN \\
1004 & Pippin & Fireworks & NaN \\
1001 & Frodo & NaN & 50.0 \\
1002 & Samwise & NaN & 39.0 \\
1006 & Legolas & NaN & 2931.0 \\
1007 & Elrond & NaN & 6520.0 \\
1008 & Barromir & NaN & 51.0 \\
\end{longtable}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Concatenating along columns (horizontal)}
\NormalTok{df\_concat\_columns }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.concat([df\_existing, df\_external], axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(df\_concat\_columns.shape)}
\NormalTok{df\_concat\_columns}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Missing values after data
enriching}\label{missing-values-after-data-enriching}

Using either of the approaches mentioned above may introduce missing
values for unmatched entries. Handling these missing values is crucial
for maintaining the quality and integrity of your dataset after merging
or joining DataFrames. It is important to choose a method that best fits
your data and analysis goals, and to document your decisions regarding
missing value handling for transparency in your analysis.

\textbf{Question}: Read the documentations of the Pandas DataFrame
methods \texttt{merge()} and \texttt{concat()}, and identify the
differences. Mention examples when you can use (i) either, (ii) only
\texttt{concat()}, (iii) only \texttt{merge()}

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  If we need to merge datasets using row indices, we can use either
  function.
\item
  If we need to stack datasets one on top of the other, we can only use
  \texttt{concat()}
\item
  If we need to merge datasets using overlapping columns we can only use
  \texttt{merge()}
\end{enumerate}

For a comprehensive user guide, please refer to the
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/merging.html}{official
documentation}.

\section{Independent Study}\label{independent-study-10}

\subsection{Practice exercise 1}\label{practice-exercise-1-6}

You are given the life expectancy data of each continent as a separate
*.csv file.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-63}

Visualize the change of life expectancy over time for different
continents.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-64}

Appending all the data files, i.e., stacking them on top of each other
to form a combined datasets called ``data\_all\_continents''

\subsection{Practice exercise 2}\label{practice-exercise-2-6}

\subsubsection{Preparing GDP per capita
data}\label{preparing-gdp-per-capita-data}

Read the GDP per capita data from
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_countries\_by\_GDP\_(nominal)\_per\_capita

Drop all the \texttt{Year} columns. Use the
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.drop.html}{\texttt{drop()}}
method with the \texttt{columns}, \texttt{level} and \texttt{inplace}
arguments. Print the first 2 rows of the updated DataFrame. If the first
row of the DataFrame has missing values for all columns, drop that row
as well.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-65}

Drop the inner level of column labels. Use the \texttt{droplevel()}
method. Print the first 2 rows of the updated DataFrame.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-66}

Convert the columns consisting of GDP per capita by \emph{IMF, World
Bank}, and the \emph{United Nations} to numeric. Apply a lambda function
on these columns to convert them to numeric. Print the number of missing
values in each column of the updated DataFrame.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Merging datasets with \emph{similar} values
in the \emph{key}
column}{Merging datasets with similar values in the key column}}\label{merging-datasets-with-similar-values-in-the-key-column}

We suspect that population of more countries may be available in
\texttt{population\_data}. However, due to unclean country names, the
observations could not merge. For example, the country \emph{Guinea
Bissau} is mentioned as \emph{GuineaBissau} in
\texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data} and \emph{Guinea-Bissau} in
\texttt{population\_data}. To resolve this issue, we'll use a different
approach to merge datasts. We'll merge the population of a country to an
observation in the GDP per capita dataset, whose name in
\texttt{population\_data} is the most \emph{`similar'} to the name of
the country in \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data}.

\subsubsection{}\label{section-74}

Proceed as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  For each country in \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data}, find the
  \texttt{country} with the most \emph{`similar'} name in
  \texttt{population\_data}, based on the similarity score. Use the
  lambda function provided below to compute the similarity score between
  two strings \emph{(The higher the score, the more similar are the
  strings. The similarity score is \(1.0\) if two strings are exactly
  the same).}
\item
  Merge the population of the most \emph{`similar'} country to the
  country in \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data}. The merged dataset must
  include 5 columns - the country name as it appears in
  \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data}, the GDP per capita, the country name
  of the most \emph{`similar'} country as it appears in
  \texttt{population\_data}, the population of that country, and the
  similarity score between the country names.
\item
  After creating the merged dataset, \textbf{print} the rows of the
  dataset that have similarity scores less than 1.
\end{enumerate}

Use the function below to compute the similarity score between the
\texttt{Country} names of the two datasets:

\texttt{from\ difflib\ import\ SequenceMatcher}

\texttt{similar\ =\ lambda\ a,b:\ SequenceMatcher(None,\ a,\ b).ratio()}

\textbf{Note: You may use one \texttt{for} loop only for this particular
question. However, it would be perfect if don't use a \texttt{for} loop}

\textbf{Hint:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Define a function that computes the index of the observation having
  the most \emph{`similar'} country name in \texttt{population\_data}
  for an observation in \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data}. The function
  returns a Series consisting of the most \emph{`similar'} country name,
  its population, and its similarity score \emph{(This function can be
  written with only one line in its body, excluding the return statement
  and the definition statement. However, you may use as many lines as
  you wish)}.
\item
  Apply the function on the \texttt{Country} column of
  \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data}. A DataFrame will be obtained.
\item
  Concatenate the DataFrame obtained in (2) with
  \texttt{gdp\_per\_capita\_data} with the pandas \texttt{concat()}
  function.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Majors/Minors: Nested lists of student
majors.}\label{majorsminors-nested-lists-of-student-majors.}

Below is the list consisting of the majors / minors of students of the
course STAT303-1 Fall 2023. This data is a list of lists, where each
sub-list \emph{(smaller list within the outer larger list)} consists of
the majors / minors of a student. Most of the students have majors /
minors in one or more of these four areas:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Math / Statistics / Computer Science
\item
  Humanities / Communication
\item
  Social Sciences / Education
\item
  Physical Sciences / Natural Sciences / Engineering
\end{enumerate}

There are some students having majors / minors in other areas as well.

\section{GDP per capita \& social
indicators}\label{gdp-per-capita-social-indicators}

Read the file \emph{social\_indicator.txt} with python. Set the first
column as the index when reading the file. How many observations and
variables are there in the data?

\emph{(4 points)}

\subsection{}\label{section-100}

Which variables have the strongest and weakest correlations with GDP per
capita? Note that \texttt{lifeFemale} and \texttt{lifeMale} are the
female and male life expectancies respectively.

Note that only when the magnitude of the correlation is considered when
judging a correlation as strong or weak.

\emph{(4 points)}

\subsection{}\label{section-101}

Does the male economic activity \emph{(in the column
\texttt{economicActivityMale})} have a positive or negative correlation
with GDP per capita? Did you expect the positive/negative correlation?
If not, why do you think you are observing that correlation?

\emph{(4 points)}

\subsection{}\label{section-102}

What is the rank of the US amongst all countries in terms of GDP per
capita? Which countries lie immediately above, and immediately below the
US in the ranking in terms of GDP per capita? The country having the
highest GDP per capita ranks 1.

Note that:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The US is mentioned as \emph{United States} in the data.
\item
  The country with the highest GDP per capita will have rank 1, the
  country with the second highest GDP per capita will have rank 2, and
  so on.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Hint:}
\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.rank.html}{rank()}

\emph{(4 points)}

\subsection{}\label{section-103}

Which country or countries rank among the top 20 in terms of each of
these social indicators - \texttt{economicActivityFemale},
\texttt{economicActivityMale}, \texttt{gdpPerCapita},
\texttt{lifeFemale}, \texttt{lifeMale}? For each of these social
indicators, the country having the largest value ranks 1 for that
indicator.

\emph{(6 points)}

\textbf{Hint:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Use
  \href{https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rank.html}{rank()}.
  Note that this method is different from the method given in the hint
  of the previous question. This method is of the DataFrame class, while
  the one in the previous question is of the Series class. \emph{This
  part of the hint is just for your understanding. You don't need to
  write any code in this part.}
\item
  Using \texttt{rank()}, get the DataFrame consisting of the ranks of
  countries on each of the relevant social indicators \emph{(one line of
  code)}.
\item
  In the DataFrame obtained in (2), filter the rows for which the
  maximum rank is less than or equal to 20 \emph{(one line of code)}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{}\label{section-104}

On which social indicator among \texttt{economicActivityFemale},
\texttt{economicActivityMale}, \texttt{gdpPerCapita},
\texttt{lifeFemale}, \texttt{lifeMale}, \texttt{illiteracyFemale},
\texttt{illiteracyMale}, \texttt{infantMortality}, and
\texttt{totalfertilityrate} does the US have its worst ranking, and what
is the rank? Note that for \texttt{illiteracyFemale},
\texttt{illiteracyMale}, and \texttt{infantMortality}, the country
having the lowest value will rank 1, in contrast to the other social
indicators.

\emph{(8 points)}

\subsection{}\label{section-105}

Find all the countries that have a lower GDP per capita than the US,
despite having lower illiteracy rates (for both genders), higher
economic activity (for both genders), higher life expectancy (for both
genders), and lower infant mortality rate than the US?

\emph{(6 points)}

indicators}\label{gdp-per-capita-vs-social-indicators}

questions below, assume that all numeric columns, \textbf{except GDP per
capita}, are social indicators.

\subsection{}\label{section-106}

Use the column \texttt{geographic\_location} to create a new column
called \texttt{continent}. Merge the values of the
\texttt{geographic\_location} column appropriately to obtain 6 distinct
values for the \texttt{continent} column -- \emph{Asia, Africa, North
America, South America, Europe} and \emph{Oceania}. Drop the column
\texttt{geographic\_location}. Print the first 5 observations of the
updated DataFrame.

\emph{(8 points)}

\textbf{Hint:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Use \texttt{value\_counts()} to see the values of
  \texttt{geographic\_location}. The code
  \texttt{if\ \textquotesingle{}Asia\textquotesingle{}\ in\ \textquotesingle{}something\textquotesingle{}}
  will return \texttt{True} if `\emph{something}' contains the string
  `\emph{Asia}', for example, if `\emph{something}' is `\emph{North
  Asia}', the code with return True. \emph{This part of the hint is just
  for your understanding. You don't need to write any code in this
  part.}
\item
  Apply a lambda function on the Series \texttt{geographic\_location} to
  replace a string that contains `\emph{Asia}' with `\emph{Asia}',
  replace a string that contains `\emph{Europe}' with `\emph{Europe}',
  and replace a string that contains `\emph{Africa}' with
  `\emph{Africa}'. \emph{This will be a single line of code.}
\item

  \((y_1, y_2, ..., y_p)\) is
  \(|x_1 - y_1| + |x_2 - y_2| + ... + |x_p-y_p|\), where \(|.|\) stands
  for absolute value (for example, \(|-2| = 2;  |3| = 3\)).
\end{enumerate}

Check the datatype of the variables using the \texttt{dtypes} attribute

Write a function that accepts a Pandas Series \emph{(or a column of a
Pandas DataFrame object)} as argument, and if the datatype of the Series
is non-numeric, does the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Checks if at least 10 values of the Series contain a digit in them.
\item
  If at least 10 values are found to contain a digit, then:

  A. Eliminate the characters \texttt{\textasciitilde{}}, \texttt{+},
  and \texttt{,} from all the values of the Series.

  B. Convert the Series to numeric (with coercion if needed).
\item
  If at least 10 values are NOT found to contain a digit, then:

  A. If the values of the Series are \emph{`Yes'} and \emph{`No'}, then
  replace \emph{`Yes'} with \emph{1} and \emph{`No'} with \emph{0}. The
  Series datatype must change to numeric as well.

  B. If the values of the Series are \emph{`Agree'} and
  \emph{`Disagree'}, then replace \emph{`Agree'} with \emph{1} and
  \emph{`Disagree'} with \emph{0}. The Series datatype must change to
  numeric as well.
\end{enumerate}
